This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for calculating the ground state of a $d$-dimensional hypercube governed by the Schrödinger equation. Under the premise that the ground state can be found within a specific type of neural network weight configuration known as Data-Driven Reduced Basis Methods, we derive a tight estimate of the generalization error in terms of the smallest non-zero eigenvalue of the associated linear operator and the complexity of the neural network. The collection of all such operators is considered. The resulting analysis is then supported numerically, and the associated convergence rates are optimized through the use of Gaussian random basis functions. These basis functions allow the ground state to be approximated directly within a neural network, rather than through the conventional approach of optimizing it through training. The findings of this study could potentially be extended to other types of reduced basis method approaches, and may offer insights useful for tackling other difficult PDE-based problems. The generalization performance of the neural network is also compared against an alternative method involving direct minimization on a high-dimensional grid. The results were produced with the help of the DeepSARD-scan library, a newly-developed, systematic approach for testing the performance of implicit model-reducing techniques. The newly obtained results represent the first generalization performance analysis of neural networks for solving such problems, and are in line with what is known from previous studies on the subject. The source code for the DeepSARD-scan library is available at: https://github.com/mathnext/deep-sard-scan. The source code for our numerical experiments is available at: https://github.com/mathnext/deep-sard-scan-submits. The intricacy of the human nervous system makes studying simpler organisms, such as C. Elegans, valuable for gaining insights into brain activity. With well-documented behavioural and structural biology, C. Elegans serves as a suitable model for testing simulation techniques and modelling approaches. Traditional white-box models that rely on internal details of these neural networks are inadequate for capturing the complex responses to stimuli or lead to unrealistic simulations. In this research, we use data-driven methods with advanced recurrent neural networks, such as LSTMs and GRUs, to simulate C. Elegans' nervous system and compare the models in terms of performance, training speed, and accuracy. Notably, GRU models with 4 hidden units exhibit similar performance to LSTMs with 8 hidden units while requiring significantly less computation and training time, demonstrating the effectiveness of this regression approach. Furthermore, our work highlights the importance of continuing research in behaviour modelling to refine the understanding of C. Elegans' nervous system and its interaction with environmental stimuli. While this study primarily focuses on C. Elegans, the techniques employed are widely applicable to various neural networks found in more complex organisms, including humans. As such, these techniques hold considerable potential for advancing our understanding of higher-level brain activity. However, to model human neuroscience accurately, additional systems would need to be simulated, such as the visual processing system, similar to those already successfully modelled in C. Elegans with its response to stimuli. With further development and refinement, our technique has the potential to contribute significantly to theoretical neuroscience and simulated cognitive modelling. Moreover, this approach may lead to various real-world applications, such as simulation, prediction, and control of biological and artificial neural networks. In particular, simulated models of neurological disorders could aid in developing treatments while overcoming ethical and cost constraints associated with the disease. As an example, studying C. Elegans' response to caffeine and alcohol has shed light on its effects on sleep and locomotion, illustrating the practical value of simulated modelling in biological and pharmaceutical research. A novel, straightforward sorting method is applied to permutations: repeatedly insert the permutation's initial element into the corresponding position, stopping once it becomes 1. This process yields a distinct structural pattern involving the set of all permutations, with permutations beginning with 1 at the top and those without fixed points, known as derangements, at the bottom. Observing this pattern from a different perspective and tracing it from top to bottom leads to a similar pattern where elements are successively fixed in place. Examining a random permutation under this view and considering a version of the classic 'coupon collector' problem, where each draw is replaced, yields valuable insights into the time needed for all elements of a random permutation to become fixed. In more detail, we investigate the pattern formed when following this sorting process for all natural number permutations up to a certain length n, denoting this pattern as the 'n-fold fixed point forest.' Exploring a simplified version of this pattern, where only elements up to a given k are part of the permutation, reveals itself to be useful in studying the pattern's structure. Notably, the pattern's scale-free nature becomes apparent when looking at a distanced version of this pattern, where the distance corresponds to the length of all leading identical elements. When studying a set of natural number permutations based on the length of all leading identical elements, the pattern's structure exhibits remarkable properties. In more detail, the distribution of this length can be determined theoretically, displaying characteristics of a logarithmic distribution, with similar tendencies observed for other descriptive metrics, such as the pattern's growth and the separation times between distinct structural phases. Similar properties are found for a broader set of permutations, including those where the initial elements are fixed from the start, where we investigate a version of the 'coupon collector' problem, or when considering combinations rather than permutations. Eventually, a comparative analysis is conducted to reveal which structures exhibit similar patterns and which exhibit distinct properties. Firstly, the pattern's growth exhibits similarities regardless of the set used. Secondly, the distribution of the pattern's length tends to be different for even n and odd n, where it displays characteristics of a normal distribution for even n and a lognormal distribution for odd n. Lastly, structural phases were found only for specific types of structures where the pattern's length is used as the criterion. Nonetheless, such an approach reveals the pattern's descriptive metrics to be highly descriptive of the underlying structure, where growth rates and distribution shapes exhibit distinct characteristics depending on the length of all leading identical elements, denoted as k. with every irreducible character of H resulting in a multiplicity-free 
character of G. Specifically, we identify the strong Gelfand pairs of SL(2, 
p) when p is a prime number. For p equals 2, 3, or 5, we determine all the 
strong pairs, whereas for p equals 7, 11, or 13, we identify nearly all the 
strong pairs, with one exception for each such p. For p equals 31 or larger, 
all the strong pairs are calculated. Additionally, we provide a descriptive 
characterization that identifies which irreducible characters of a specific 
two-partition of SL(2, p) are multiplicity-free. Furthermore, we identify 
the strong Gelfand pairs of a more general version of SL(2, p), which also 
considers the cases of quadratic residues. This work is especially significant 
as it finds the first known instance of a multiplicity-free family of irreducible 
characters in a non-abelian group that surpasses a large prime squared, with 
such a character corresponding to the two-partition (7, 3). With further 
investigation, we discover that for p equals 2, 5, or 7, all the strong pairs 
involve partitions of odd numbers. In contrast, for p equals 13 or larger, all 
the strong pairs involve partitions of even numbers. Finally, for these latter 
cases, we offer heuristic reasoning as to why this transition occurs, specifically, 
why strong pairs are associated with odd numbers for small primes and with even 
numbers for large primes. This is based on how the Plancharel formula applies to 
cyclic groups and their subgroups. However, the formula involves logarithms, 
which for small primes results in a two-partition of an odd number, while for 
larger primes it results in a two-partition of an even number. This justifies

generalizing to the group of matrices, a different (non-integer) version of

The early K-type star K2-138, hosting six planets, particularly five proposed to be in a prolonged chain of 3:2 mean motion resonances, necessitates the analysis of its planets' potential resonant behavior. By using existing parameters in N-body simulations, our analysis confirms that nearly all simulations (99.2%) produce a chain of 3:2 resonances; however, fewer (11%) demonstrate a five-planet resonance chain. We successfully employ resonances to confine the orbital periods and masses of the planets. We examine the likelihood of this system forming in situ and through disk migration, as well as explore the potential planetary compositions using a computational planet structure model. Our results indicate that the possible mass range for the planets corresponds to our planet formation models, supporting in situ formation of the 3:2 resonance chain. Additionally, our model suggests that the possible mass range for the planets corresponds to their currently observed radii. Lastly, our planet structure model places the possible Compositional Boundaries in a similar area on an mass-radius diagram when compared to the exoplanet hunter algorithm. Limited observational data, particularly regarding the planets' transits, prevents determining the orbital inclinations with certainty. We propose that future transit observations and radial velocity measurements of K2-138's planets could potentially yield significant insights into their possible ring-like configurations. To fill this gap, we develop the first integrated design of analog transmit precoders and digital receive combiners for multicasting in mmWave systems, with each device having multiple phases and multiple antennas. By combining semidefinite relaxation, alternating optimization and Cholesky decomposition, we sequentially optimize the digital and analog components at the transmitter and receivers. The proposed method leads to significant performance improvements. Notably, with a fixed hybrid precoder at the transmitter, the receiver can achieve perfect full-dimensionality, and vice versa. It outperforms a scheme that optimizes a hybrid precoder for multicasting using alternating optimization, with a better success rate of having a positive mutual information for all users. In 2002, Biss researched a type of fibration known as the rigid fibration (initially called the rigid covering fibration), exhibiting properties akin to covering spaces. This study establishes a connection between general topological spaces and their corresponding rigid fibrations. This relationship enables a commutative diagram involving homotopy groups and quasitopological homotopy groups, resulting in further significant outcomes in this domain. Specifically, in the instance of n-ramified rigid fibrations (a type of covering space), a well-known sequence involving homotopy groups is generalised to rigid fibrations. This study also demonstrates that if a topological space X is a product of two subspaces, it is homeomorphic to the pushout of two other subspaces and a rigid fibration, constructed from their respective fundamental groups. This generalised sequence is utilised to establish the inverse Grothendieck isomorphism for one-dimensional rigid fibrations. Lastly, in one-dimensional rigid fibrations, a connection is established between their fundamental groups and the linear groups of their corresponding fields. This was accomplished by introducing a novel field adaptation of the Baas-Connective-cup-product sequence, involving quasitopological homotopy groups, the fundamental groups, and linear groups of the one-dimensional rigid fibrations in question. A simplified variant of this sequence is also proven for specific instances of these spaces. The establishment of this connection leads to several key outcomes, notably new isomorphisms between the fundamental groups and linear groups of the one-dimensional rigid fibrations in question, including an extension to the Grothendieck isomorphism. These novel outcomes also imply the existence of further sequences in the domain of one-dimensional covering spaces. Ultimately, a comprehensive list of the one-dimensional rigid fibrations over the interval is derived through a detailed analysis. This study serves as the first comprehensive investigation into the rigorous fibrations in the literature. As a result, the outcomes of this research are applicable to a broad range of subfields, encompassing one-dimensional rigid fibrations, the rigidity of fibrations, quasitopological fibrations, covering space theory, the Grothendieck isomorphism, and fundamental group sequences. This unification of perspectives provides a more complete and reliable explanation for the process of Pauli crystal formation. This analysis involves summing a series of fermion states, and the resulting expression for energy is proportional to the number of fermions, which can be positive or negative depending on the combination of variables involved. This research further uses numerical calculations to determine the dimensions of Pauli crystals, and the study includes a comparison with existing theoretical models through the use of an effective potential. The findings suggest that the lack of negative energy in the original model is a consequence of the neglect of higher harmonic oscillations. This study aims to introduce a dynamic neural network framework, known as ZNN, which utilizes the characteristics of exponential functions in time-varying matrix-related problems to drive the predictive computation process. By leveraging the initial conditions and problem-specific errors that arise from time variations, ZNN formulates differential equations that facilitate swift and efficient solving of various problems. To grasp the fundamental concepts of ZNN, this work provides an foundational review, highlighting the crucial factors that contribute to its rapid solving ability. These factors are the inherent properties of the exponential function, the one-step iteration framework, problem-related matrix properties, and initial conditions. To further illustrate the unique computations of ZNN, this study presents two time-varying matrix-related problems, providing a comprehensive review of the predicting computing theory that underpins ZNN. Additionally, a comparison of the iterative frameworks that underpin ZNN highlights the significant advantages of this theory, namely, fast convergence, problem-dependent initialization, and flexible design. To demonstrate the underlying one-step iteration framework of ZNN, this work proposes several modified, extended versions of ZNN, which can tackle more complex problems, such as linear Sylvester equations, tensor multiplication, and multi-body systems of differential equations. Moreover, some recent extensions of ZNN are reviewed in the context of state-space representation, instantiating the predicting computing theory of ZNN. Finally, this study concludes by highlighting four potential research directions that could further refine the ZNN framework. These directions are one-step solvers for problems that involve coupled nonlinear equations, extended versions of ZNN that can be used to solve more complex problems, integrated designing of predicting computing frameworks, and applications of ZNN that involve data-driven methods, such as neural networks. By exploring these research directions, we aim to further refine the fundamental concepts of ZNN and predict its future development. To make the content of this study more accessible, I have included two appendices that provide a detailed explanation of the underlying theory and a comparative analysis of the solving frameworks that are related to ZNN. The first appendix is dedicated to the review of several one-step solvers for problems that involve time-varying linear matrix-related problems, while the second appendix is dedicated to the review of predicting computing frameworks that can be used to solve time-varying matrix-related problems, such as neural networks and other predicting computing frameworks. To the best of our knowledge, these appendices are not available in the existing literature, further highlighting the significant contributions that this study can make to the fields of ZNN and predicting computing theory. The edge states, in particular, are predicted to be nearly zero-gap states, analogous to those found at the magic angle but governed by a different mechanism. The findings provide a framework for the stable existence of flat bands under quantum constraints. The study also highlights the distinct characteristics of strong magnetic fields versus those resulting from twist angles in twisted graphene systems. The edge states' exceptional robustness to twist angles but not magnetic fields underscores this distinction. The study concludes with a examination of proposed quasi-Nodal topological metal predictions and their uncertainty in the context of strong magnetic fields. Transmission system operators utilize unit commitment as crucial tools for determining the most cost-effective and feasible generation schedules. Researchers have been investigating constraint screening, a technique that can expedite the solution process for large-scale unit commitment problems by reducing the number of unnecessary constraints. Current constraint screening methods rely on optimizing load and generation, but this approach tends to be conservative and leaves a considerable percentage of constraints intact. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a machine learning-based model to predict costs given load inputs, enabling more effective optimization and constraint screening in unit commitment problems. By incorporating cost perspectives and machine learning, the proposed model outperforms conventional approaches, significantly reducing computational time across various scenarios. Moreover, the proposed model can also facilitate constraint screening by identifying the most relevant constraints to quickly solve unit commitment problems. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model significantly accelerates solution processing times, decreasing the computational time by up to 70.5% to 80.7% compared to other methods. Notably, the proposed model shows considerable potential for online applications, as it reduces computational time from around 100 to 300 seconds to less than 30 seconds. Overall, the proposed model is an invaluable tool for solving unit commitment problems efficiently. Researchers frequently apply synthetic control techniques to determine the effect of treatment on a single treated entity within data sets that span multiple periods. The goal of synthetic control is to create a weighted average of units without treatment that mimics the treated entity's pre-intervention outcome trajectory. Initially, the weights used in synthetic control calculations are derived by correlating pre-intervention outcomes of the treated entity with those of units without treatment. It has been discovered, however, that traditional estimation techniques can be inconsistent. To resolve this challenge, this paper introduces a novel analytical framework, which formalizes the process of making causal inferences and estimating the effect of treatment on the treated. The new framework enables the reutilization of units previously considered unsuitable for the purpose, thereby ensuring the consistent estimation of synthetic control weights. The treated entity's outcomes can be contrasted with those of the synthetic control in the post-intervention period to create a time series. By employing techniques from the field of time-series analysis, this enables the accurate estimation of the effect of treatment on the treated entity. The presented methodology can be extended to assess treatment effects on groups of entities receiving treatment at various points in time. The presented theoretical model was tested using simulated data and applied to real-world data from the field of medicine, specifically the effect of bariatric surgery on weight loss. The results of the study indicate that the continuous learning of weights from pre-intervention data leads to a more reliable estimation of treatment effects. The presented findings provide the basis for a new, stable method of calculating synthetic control weights, which can be utilized with or without machine learning components. The code used in this study has been made public and is available on GitHub for public access. The presented theoretical model can be applied to a variety of unit treatment scenarios and is not limited to situations involving time series data. A cutting-edge approach has been developed to accurately identify genuine hadronic tau decays in the CMS detector, distinguishing them from those originating from quarks, gluons, electrons, and muons. By incorporating insights from complex detector operations, this novel method utilizes a sophisticated deep neural network to analyze intricate patterns of energy within the CMS detector. As a result, it exhibits marked performance improvements over its predecessor, particularly in effectively differentiating between tau decays and quark/gluon jets, with gains in efficiency of up to 30%. Additionally, analysis of the latest CMS data from proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV has confirmed the validity of this advanced approach. Furthermore, research into varying energy configurations of the CMS detector has revealed relatively consistent levels of background suppression relative to true signal detection. This study represents a significant step forward in applying neural network technology to particle physics research, particularly in the complex context of jet patterns. Such breakthrough methods will play a crucial role in the CMS detector's detection of 3-body decays in the presence of jets in future analyses. [Figure 1 is a related illustration]

Future sky surveys, notably the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), are projected to observe approximately 10 million time-varying celestial sources each night for a decade, sending real-time data streams to brokers for evaluation. Brokers will then utilize machine learning to filter these sources and select the most relevant for various scientific applications. Our investigation explores the merits and complexities of employing Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) in classification tasks, especially those requiring uncertainty quantification. When trained as a single model, BNNs provide uncertainty levels via their predictive probability distribution functions (PDFs), enabling them to portray the reliability of the classification outcome. We analyzed the influence of training time, network architecture, and stochastic training techniques on uncertainty estimation by employing BNNs on simulated LSST tasks. Our results indicate that uncertainty estimates may be unreliable for the majority of sources, possibly due to the prevalence of outliers. Notably, BNNs with an additional softmax layer performed better than their conventional counterparts, with the inclusion of stochastic training showing variable effects depending on the specific task. While uncertainty estimates may be improved with longer training, further research is needed to fully appreciate the benefits and limitations of utilizing BNNs in brokering tasks for scientific scientific applications. Specifically, subclassification could be a viable use case for BNNs. Our work is also supplemented by additional resources, including our code and experimental plans. Potential future investigations could involve comparing BNN performance to that of other algorithms, such as Gaussian Processes, to determine the feasibility of incorporating BNNs in the Rubin brokerage. Our investigation is part of a broader research effort focused on employing machine learning in the Rubin brokerage process, led by Dr. Jennifer Schneider (University of Arizona). Further details about the project, including meeting notes and documents, are available through the DESCL webpage. The project is intended to explore various ranking and classification applications, supported by NASA and the LSST Collaboration. Our research is meant to contribute to a future ranking and brokering software package, with the goal of ultimately influencing the science requirements specification process for the LSST Observation Data System. The science team is currently working to define the requirements for various brokering tasks and SciML algorithms can provide valuable input in this regard. Ultimately, our research aims to ensure that the brokering process and associated algorithms are optimized for maximum scientific effectiveness in areas such as the search for Transiting Exo-Earths. To achieve this goal, we are soliciting feedback from the broader LSST science and software communities

The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Our study extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn when n is 3 or greater, and also explores its implications in the contexts of combinatorics and computer science. Specifically, our findings demonstrate that any Coxeter element within Bn can be represented as a product of two standard generators raised to various powers. Moreover, our reduction heuristic can be used to identify the unique shortest Coxeter element corresponding to any given reduced word. Notably, this computational method is efficient enough to operate in O(n^2.5.69) time. Our study also supplies evidence that the proposed standard generator set is inherently finite. Lastly, our theoretical considerations are supported by the accompanying algorithm 'coxword Reduction,' which has been verified for the type B Coxeter group through implementation. The type B Coxeter group's properties, as uncovered in our study, are likely to also apply to other Coxeter groups of type F and I. Specifically, our reduction heuristic can be used to identify the unique shortest Coxeter element corresponding to any given reduced word in these groups as well. Our algorithms for the type B Coxeter group 'coxword Reduction' and type F Coxeter group 'coxword Reduction2' have been published online at https://github.com/Lei-QI/coxword-type-B.git and https://github.com/Lei-QI/coxword-type-F.git, respectively. Our research was inspired by findings indicating that the symmetric group Sn's standard generators can be represented as a product of two generating sets, each with a maximum length of n. These ideas were developed during a visit to the University of Haifa, supported by the NSFC grant no. 12171017, the Natural Science Foundation of Jiangsu Province, and an NSFC grant no. 12171017. Additionally, our research was also influenced by discussions with Dr. Shwartz and Dr. Li. Two related variations of the well-known knapsack problem are the Set-Union Knapsack Problem and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem. Both involve selecting items from a set to maximize an objective while adhering to a budget limit and a set of nonnegative item values, as well as elements weighted for coverage. Unfortunately, these problems are NP-hard, making exact solutions computationally costly. However, we propose a novel local search algorithm that finds high-quality solutions efficiently, typically finding 87-94% of the optimal value within a short processing time. This algorithm outperforms existing approaches, including a recently improved local search, while also showcasing improved quality and faster processing times on large-scale instances. What's more, our approach has been fully described and publicly made available to ensure its applicability and reproducibility. Our experiments show the efficacy of our algorithm on various benchmark datasets. Furthermore, our results suggest that the Best-First strategy, which evaluates the cost of transitioning between neighboring solutions, surpasses the Random-Reset strategy in achieving higher quality solutions. While both Random-Reset and Best-First methods exhibit comparable processing times, the significant improvement in solution quality suggests that Best-First be utilized in practice. Lastly, our analytical comparisons with the publicly available solution-finder, called BMEC, show that our algorithm yields significantly better results, with quality improvements ranging from 10% to 30% and up to 20% faster processing times on various benchmark datasets. Specifically, our approach outperforms existing algorithms by finding 100% perfect optimal values on the BMEC BDT1000 dataset. Although perfect optimal values were found on the BMEC BDT2000 and BDT3000 datasets with a larger dataset size, our algorithm's relative gap to optimality (RGTO) is 0.031 and 0.012, respectively. These results indicate the significant improvement in solution quality of the proposed algorithm, which outperforms existing approaches. What's more, our approach has been fully described and publicly made available to ensure its applicability and reproducibility. Our algorithm's successful performance on the leading dataset BDT3000 with a large size suggests the significant improvement in solution quality, which surpasses existing algorithms by a margin of 0.012. Notably, our analytical comparisons show the substantial improvement in solution quality of the proposed algorithm, which outperforms existing algorithms. In the photon-photon interaction that occurs during ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, electron-positron pairs are produced through a process called photon-photon fusion, resulting in a broad range of lepton creation in space around the collision point. Those electron-positron pairs formed near heavy nuclei are then subject to strong interactions. Researchers have used the b-space EPA model to calculate the spatial distribution of electrons and positrons produced during these collisions and studied the impact of electromagnetic interactions between the lepton pairs and nuclei. This research has focused on examining rapidity and transverse momentum distribution changes. This work presents initial findings on the movement of electrons and positrons along the rapidity axis following their creation and details on the variation in transverse momentum distribution before and after their interaction with nuclei. It's essential to consider these electromagnetic interactions in further studies on the phase and creation of quark-gluon plasma through ultra-peripheral collisions. This research aims to contribute important knowledge to such studies, crucial for understanding the characteristics of ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions. It's also hoped that such knowledge can aid researchers working with present or future experimental data in studying ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions. This research has taken into account the electromagnetic field of nuclei using a non-abergian formalism for photon-photon interaction calculations. It's also worth noting that such electromagnetic interactions between electrons/positrons and nuclei have not been widely studied in the field. This research has two possible approaches: the first presumes that electrons/positrons are born with a point charge, and the second utilizes the b-space EPA model where electrons/positrons are treated as an finite size object. We begin with the first approach in this research. It's estimated that the electromagnetic interaction cross-section of an electron/positron with a nucleus is approximately 660 megabarns. This research will be expanded by replacing the classical photon concept with the beta-space EPA model, offering a crucial bridge between QED and QCD in the study of photon-photon interactions. It's hoped that such a general approach can aid in the development of a non-linear photon-photon interaction model in the study of ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions. This research will be extended to the beta-space EPA model. It's further proposed that such electromagnetic interactions of electrons/positrons with nuclei could provide significant insight into the study of ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, potentially contributing crucial knowledge to the phase and creation studies of quark and gluon in the collision of ultra-relativistic heavy ions.

To minimize pollution, bicycle usage is experiencing a resurgence, particularly in urban environments. Despite the trend towards decreased fatalities in other traffic groups, the opposite holds true for cyclists. Therefore, tracking cyclist data is essential to improving their safety by providing city planners with data to design safer cycling routes. This study proposes a comprehensive, visually-based assessment tool to evaluate urban roads from a cyclist's point of view. This tool proposes a new set of safety indicators for cyclists and showcases its effectiveness through comparative testing with existing systems. Furthermore, the tool is designed to provide real-time feedback to city planners, enabling them to create more secure environments for cyclists through informed decision-making. After collecting relevant video data from various locations, experts annotated it to create training models for object detection and to prioritize critical elements. This path planning framework incorporates robust Control Barrier Functions to account for uncertainties, ensuring the generated path is free from obstacles and adaptable to model inaccuracies. This approach aligns with Robot Operating System (ROS) implementation for ease of use on modern robots, making it suitable for applications on various dynamics-based robots. This method successfully navigates a quadrotor around dynamic obstacles, as well as an underwater vehicle subject to model uncertainties and external disturbances. Compared to existing research, this approach delivers equivalent or improved safety standards, reduction of 2-4 times in path length, and a 2-3 times speed increase, while minimizing computational complexity and bottlenecks. This method surpasses state-of-the-art techniques with human-level performance, offering a straightforward and adaptable implementation even for novel robotic systems. This approach enables real-time path planning with a average computation time of 0.2 seconds for quadrotors and 0.6 seconds for underwater vehicles on a single CPU for continuous navigation. This path planning framework is further enhanced by integration with learned predictors, demonstrating promising results in Section 6. The novelty of this work is compounded by its comprehensive evaluation, exceeding 50 related studies in the field, and is freely accessible through open-source repositories on GitHub, further enabling its widespread adoption. This approach is designed to be used by researchers and engineers without requiring extensive expertise in optimal control, and is already utilized as the primary path planning method for various quadrotor systems. This path planning framework is further supplemented by its integration with predictive models, developed in parallel with this work, offering exceptional performance in unmanned aerial vehicles. The integration of this approach results in human-level performance, outperforming existing research on quadrotors and demonstrating substantial improvements in computational efficiency and straight-line following. For a ring $R$ possessing a cover of proper subrings, the least upper bound of the cardinalities of these subrings

This results in dilation surfaces having directional flows with unique accumulation points, known as hyperbolic closed orbits that emerge from their induced nontrivial scaling effects. A hypothesis suggests that dilation surfaces lacking these hyperbolic closed orbits are equivalent to translation surfaces. Under the assumption of the existence of specific structural components, known as horizon saddle connections, in dilation surfaces, it is shown that the hyperbolic closed orbits are found densely in the surface of a unit circle. It follows that most measured foliations on dilation surfaces with minimal disorder exhibit Morse-Smale behavior, leading to a further hypothesis that all such surfaces with minimal disorder can be classified as translation surfaces. It is proven that, if a dilation surface has a particularly uniform scaling effect, then it takes the form of a translation surface. Lastly, examples of dilation surfaces lacking certain defined structural components are demonstrated. These counter-examples show that, without additional assumptions, they exhibit complex dynamics and include both infinite directional flows and a high level of irregularity in their behavior. Specifically, they contain an infinite number of structural components, known as horizon saddle connections. This shows that the existence of these components cannot be easily assumed. These counter-examples also show that dilation surfaces with uniform scaling effects and irregular behavior are not rare examples, but rather occur frequently. They demonstrate that, in nearly all cases where the scaling effect is positive, then this surface is equivalent to a translation surface, but in cases where the scaling effect is negative, then this is not necessarily the case. These counter-examples include two types: those that are equivalent to dilation surfaces with irregular behavior and those that are not. They include examples such as semi-translation surfaces, semi-dilation surfaces, translation surfaces with reflection symmetry, and regular dilation surfaces with reflection symmetry. These examples demonstrate the important roles that reflection symmetry plays in translating results from translation surfaces to dilation surfaces, as well as in creating new examples. As the scope of Gaussian processes widens, the availability of simple mathematical solutions dwindles, prompting the need for alternative methods. Monte Carlo simulations serve as an intermediary between complicated mathematical formulas and applicable predictions through random sampling. Traditional techniques for Gaussian processes typically involve either natural Bayesian estimation or Markov chain sampling techniques. However, there are issues with both approaches - the former can fail to capture the process's non-stationary features, and the latter can be computationally costly. There are also concerns regarding the performance of these methods in capturing the process's underlying characteristics. Our approach, Pathwise Conditioning, offers a more direct and efficient means of conditioning a Gaussian process without resorting to approximate Markov chain sampling or assuming a multi-level expandable process structure. This new method leverages the process's underlying physics to derive a simple, direct, and efficient means of conditioning. Notably, our method has several key benefits: it's free from assumptions about the process's features, it's computationally efficient, it captures the process's underlying features, and it's notably faster than the Markov chain sampling technique. The method will be demonstrated in two contexts - one in dynamics, where it's used to simulate the competition between Brownian particles and an external potential, and in statics, where it's used in a system characterized by interactions. Our evaluation of the method's performance will be based on a range of measures including time spent, error rates, hydrodynamical theories, and a comparative analysis of our results, including state-of-the-art results and Markov chain sampling results, to be presented in the paper's second part. Notably, our results show that our method not only captures the process's features but also outperforms the Markov chain sampling technique in terms of efficiency. The method's integration with the Python package PyGP will also be presented along the lines of a standard Flask web framework development approach as a key component of the project. A web-based demonstration of the method's performance and its potential for generating the process's underlying features is also presented. Notably, our results show that our method's performance and features surpass those of the Markov chain sampling technique and conventional non-stationary Gaussian process methods. Notably, the method's performance and features can be accessed through a live web-based demonstration at pathwise.path.com. Furthermore, our method's integration with the Python package PyGP has also been developed and is now part of the project. This new project aims to promote the development of more efficient and feature-rich methods for Gaussian processes

One of the significant obstacles in this area is identifying meaningful spatiotemporal features, and excessive variation among successive frames, making it difficult for the model to generalize and achieve long-term predictions. We proposed the detailed motion representation, called MoDeRNN, which effectively captures velocity distribution within a region using a novel detailed-motion-cell, composed of 2-RNNs and 1 convolution layer. The model uses the proposed smoothed relative-approach error (S-R-A-E) criterion to derive quantitative details on how objects within a scene have moved. By demonstrating that minimal information on velocity and acceleration is retained across successive frames, and that the proposed model maintains a consistent error rate compared to other leading prediction methods. The proposed model also demonstrates capacity to estimate missing motion details in a scenario involving a moving camera setting. Lastly, we show that our model is capable of detecting abnormal behavior in a predictive setting which is another significant area within the field of AB-DG. The proposed model has also been tested on a new dataset called MoDeACAR, which simulates a sequence of images describing vehicles navigating a circular path and the model's ability to estimate the vehicles' future positions was then validated by comparing it with position data derived from video editing software. The new dataset in addition to confirming the effectiveness of our method, exposes several other techniques used in our model. The related source code is available at the following GitHub repository: github.com/Alireza-Sirouzi/ MoDeRNN-For-Predictive-Learning. This research focuses on bridging the gap between programming languages employing garbage collection for memory management and those leveraging advanced type systems to ensure memory safety in imperative languages. Historically, garbage collection has been used in functional languages, while imperative languages increasingly utilize type systems to safeguard memory usage. Our investigation applies existing methods for linear capabilities to ensure safe access to reference types that can be copied, with a particular emphasis on its novel extension to languages with tracing garbage collection, as well as data structures featuring explicit lifespan management. This work is related to hybrid programming that combines linear and non-linear elements, specifically in the context of the languages Rust and JavaScript. Rust is an imperative language emphasizing memory safety, while JavaScript is a multi-paradigm language with first-class functions but non-deterministic memory management. We discovered that JavaScript's garbage collection can be treated as an advancement over garbage collection, utilities, as well as symbolic representations of values in the language, with its types encompassing traditional object kinds and reference types with an additional thread-local lifetime attribute. Linear capabilities in JavaScript correspond to its context menus, providing an additional layer of symbolic checking beyond at runtime. This is implemented using a library, with a single top-level module serving as the linear module, containing all linear definitions, with the rest of the code operating within a typical JavaScript module. We developed a mechanism to ensure safe interaction between the local scope and garbage collection, with a method for obtaining a linear representation within an arbitrary scope, as well as converting a linear representation back to its original form. We demonstrated the usefulness of this approach by porting the Rust's effects monad as a JavaScript library, with a top-level module called "effects" serving as the linear module, with the rest of the code operating within a typical JavaScript module. This work is also applied to data structures featuring explicit lifespan management, with a point system governing access to values within these structures. We demonstrated the usefulness of this approach by porting the Rust's graph data structure as a JavaScript data structure, with a top-level module called "graph" serving as the linear module, with the rest of the code operating within a typical JavaScript module. This investigation led to a hybrid programming technique, with a new interpretation of functional languages employing linear capabilities, as well as an extension of the garbage collection notion to include an additional layer of symbolic checking beyond at runtime. This research provides tools for implementing advanced programming language features in languages with garbage collection, as a basis for combining languages with linear and non-linear elements. Permutation decoding has become more prominent lately, allowing it to take full advantage of codes' symmetries in parallel, which ultimately accelerates decoding processes. This work focuses on developing efficient iterative list decoders for polar codes by exploring subcodes resulting from fixed permutations that only flip output bits corresponding to an even index. This polar subcode approach leads to several beneficial outcomes, including reduced memory requirements, prevention of convergence issues, and protection of the polar code's natural symmetry, which results in improved decoder performance. Simulation experiments demonstrate that our proposed iterative list decoder exceeds the capabilities of state-of-the-art iterative decoders and even rivals some cutting-edge permutation-based list decoders. Notably, this technique shows the greatest advantage in codes with a large amount of information, where other decoders may struggle to handle the task. Moreover, our analysis reduces the complexity associated with finding the best permutation-based list decoder, making it a more manageable problem. This work also explores the technical feasibility of implementing the polar subcode approach using FPGA technology from a design perspective, which involves integrating multiple polar subcode list decoders onto a single device to improve performance. The outcomes of our design experiment reveal that a single FPGA can efficiently support a range of codes operating at extremely high data rates, which further validates the practicality of our proposed technique. Moreover, our experimental findings indicate that the time required to complete each clock cycle is directly proportional to the size of the code and independent of the code's information density, which ultimately depends on the complexity of the decoding process. Consequently, our technique uses the polar subcode approach to successfully implement some of the fastest and most efficient iterative list decoders to date. This work involves the design and optimization of our dual-encoder dual-decoder polar subcode list decoder, which significantly outperforms its competitors by achieving a frequency of over 90% for decoding accuracy at a data rate of 1 Gbps. Notably, our experimental technique using the polar subcode approach surpasses the performance of the newly developed dual-encoder dual-decoder approach, which had previously set the benchmark at 85%. Furthermore, our experimental results also reveal that when operating at a frequency of 1 Gbps, our decoder takes an average of 12-15 clock cycles to complete each decoding process. We examine the link between the choice of image co-adding technique and the final image's point spread function. This involves identifying the characteristics of co-adding algorithms that yield co-added images with well-defined point spread functions. Our investigation centers on the following key attributes of co-adding algorithms: the ability to preserve the point spread function, sensitivity to background fluctuations, effects of variable seeing, and variability in exposure times. To this end, we compare the image co-adding capabilities of Image Reduction and Analysis Software, Astrometry.net, and PyRAF, and find that PyRAF produces a well-defined point spread function in the majority of cases across different input conditions. Furthermore, we highlight certain characteristics of co-added images that can provide insight into the effects of image co-adding algorithms, including the variability of stellar widths, the presence of stellar halos, and the presence of ghost images. This study is expected to enhance our understanding of image co-adding algorithms and their implications for the analysis of deep star catalogs. Our research findings and code are publicly available on GitHub. The study primarily focuses on ground-based near-infrared observations conducted using 8 Megapixel cameras, with an emphasis on exploring whether near-infrared data can be treated similarly to short-wavelength data. If the answer is yes, this could lead to a significant increase in the dataset size, expanding to include all near-infrared light curves measured by the Second New Generation Virgo Survey and the K2 missions. This could ultimately enable us to assess whether near-infrared data are susceptible to the same biases as short-wavelength data. If the result of this investigation is positive, this could further facilitate a thorough analysis and understanding of potential sources of systematic error in the study of massive datasets. This research was supported in part by an NRC research fellowship. Image processing was performed primarily, although not exclusively, using the PyRAF package. Data analysis was conducted using a combination of PyRAF, NumPy, and PyFSP. Initially, we examined PyRAF's image co-adding capabilities by treating fake images as separate entities to ensure that our findings were not influenced by the actual data. To confirm our results, we performed a secondary analysis involving a real observation. These approaches help to ensure that our study remains grounded in observational facts that can be universally replicated. Following an extensive analysis of the effects of image co-adding algorithms, we perform a detailed comparison of PyRAF's image co-adding capabilities to those of Image Reduction and Analysis Software and Astrometry.net

This paper outlines the development of a comprehensive theoretical framework for understanding the fracture toughness of solid crystals at their most basic level. Founded on the thermodynamic dislocation theory, it begins by postulating that the behavior of dislocations in these solids must comply with the fundamental principles of thermodynamics. A critical dynamic equation derived from this framework accurately describes the dynamic behavior of dislocations in pure crystalline solids and provides a predicted critical resolidification velocity that aligns seamlessly with established theories from phenomenological materials science. Building upon this foundation, the framework uses the concepts of available and intrinsic fracture toughness to characterize the fracture process of crystalline solids, where intrinsic fracture toughness serves as a measure of the minimal effort required to break the solid. The framework's predictive capabilities were validated through numerical modeling of the fracture process in metals, yielding results consistent with empirical findings from materials science. Theoretical estimates of intrinsic fracture toughness, based on the universal properties of atoms and solids, are also developed and examined in relation to the actual strengths of minimal crystalline structures constructed from DNA and folded proteins. Theoretical estimates of intrinsic fracture toughness are finally compared with experimental strengths measured in various crystalline solids, demonstrating that the framework's predictions closely match those derived from phenomenological materials science as well as from actual experiments. The development of this foundational framework highlights the importance of applying the principles of thermodynamics to the fracture process of crystalline solids and their materials constructions. The framework shows that the fracture process of crystalline solids can be understood as a manifestation of the universal drivers of atomic and molecular arrangement, which underpin the formation of materials and biological structures. By establishing a fundamental link between thermodynamics and the fracture property of materials and biological constructions, the theoretical work paves the way for a deeper comprehension of the multifaceted relationships between matter, mechanics, and thermodynamics. The new framework further provides an innovative theoretical approach to analyze the growing presence of cracks in synthetic and natural structures, which are increasingly influenced by the increasing scale of molecular and atomic variability. By enabling a theoretical estimation of the minimum effort required to break and destroy these structures, the theoretical model can be used to provide a unified explanation for the remarkable mechanical stability and durability of various biological structures and materials that have been observed in actual systems. The theoretical estimation of the minimum effort required to break and destroy these structures is finally compared with experimental findings from various fields. The theoretical work is meant to provide a foundational contribution to the emerging fields of materials and biological constructions that is rooted in the universal principles of thermodynamics and arrangements. Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. Where the multiple SLE end, liminf of growth of these free fields can be related to stochastic evolutions of kernels associated with the underlying stochastic processes. Key values driving these evolution, such as the Bru-Wishart and Dyson models, provide a probabilistic interpretation of the imaginary surface's Markovian properties and provide an alternative to prior work linking the Gaussian free field and multiple SLE. This study draws on ideas from random matrix theory, integrable systems, and probability theory. As a consequence of the work in this study on the real line, it is predicted that the corresponding growth rate of the free field has a negative moment of the order of $\frac{1}{n^2}$, which would be the optimal possible rate. Furthermore, multiple SLE driven by the Bru-Wishart model may have a growth rate that is slightly less than the optimal order. This study draws on ideas from ideas on local times and random step functions of Bru and Wishart matrices. Concepts from integrable systems and probability theory provide additional insights. In this research, we address the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional space with smooth periodic initial conditions and obtain analytical estimates of the solution's maximum norm, tied to the initial conditions' maximum norm. We also demonstrate that these estimates are precise when the initial conditions are symmetric with respect to space inversions. Consequently, we derive a precise invariance property for the norm of the solution's vorticity. Building upon the obtained estimates, we further investigate the solution's high-frequency behavior, yielding precise estimates in the Fourier frequency domain for the vorticity and its norm. Interestingly, our analysis reveals that the Navier-Stokes equations' dissipativity constant is directly related to the initial norm's decay rate at high frequencies. Finally, in the limit where our analytical estimates converge, we arrive at a new regularity result for the Navier-Stokes equations in the maximum Lp norm, valid for p values between 1 and infinity, and conditioned on the initial data's Lp norm. This result represents an improvement and, in certain cases, a refinement of the conventional Sobolev inequality in Lorentz spaces. Moreover, when the initial data is smooth and periodic, the maximum Lp norm's regularity result even holds for an even more extensive class of integers. Ultimately, the obtained regularity result can be considered a refinement of the global in time well-posedness proof for the Cauchy problem of the Navier-Stokes equations in the maximum Lp norm, encompassing the cases where p values are not simply 2. To accomplish this achievement, we employ a novel approach based on the Helmholtz decomposition, combined with the most advanced techniques of almost-monotonicity and nonlinear decay in a Fourier space, which have been extensively developed in the recent research literature. Specifically, the methods employed here include the nonlinear decay estimates derived by Cadamuro-Mouhiadis and the almost-monotonicity method of Elgindi. We hope that the novel approach used here here can be adapted and applied to the study of other partial differential equations, such as the energy-critical dissipative wave equation, with the long-term goal of achieving a deeper understanding of the solution's decay rate in a Fourier space, tied to its initial data's profile. The algorithm's time complexity is proportional to the number of qubits, not exponentially related to the value output by the server, thus marking a substantial breakthrough. However, applying the blockchain to IoT straightforwardly yields high processing times and energy consumption. To address these limitations in supply chain management, where various IoT devices operate in parallel, a new blockchain architecture has been developed, specifically designed to incorporate a lightweight consensus protocol, known as LC4IoT. Simulations were conducted to test the performance of LC4IoT and revealed that the proposed approach consumes minimal computational power, storage space, and processing delay. Furthermore, the efficacy of LC4IoT was assessed using the Food Supply Chain (FSC) scenario, which demonstrated the system's capacity to reduce energy consumption by up to 40% and delay by 30% compared to conventional IoT applications. The results indicate that the practical applicability of the blockchain in IoT applications, such as the FSC, depends on certain criteria like hardware specifications and environmental conditions. Based on these criteria, it is found that the blockchain solution is economically feasible for the FSC within a specific time frame. The performance of the LC4IoT was evaluated in terms of energy consumption, processing delay, storage requirements, and blocking rate using realistic FSC data, which showed the suitability of the blockchain for trust establishment in various IoT ecosystems. The study highlights the importance of consensus protocol optimization to streamline the blockchain protocol, whereas the blockchain architecture remains relatively unchanged. Moreover, the choice of consensus protocol significantly affects the final outcome, and thus it should be taken into consideration during protocol design. The results of this study can be applied in diverse IoT domains such as Industry 4.0, Healthcare, Smart Home, and other environments where reliability and efficiency are paramount. With such optimizations, the blockchain may become a leading technology to establish trust in various IoT applications. Generating synthetic cell shapes realistically can contribute to developing training datasets to enhance cell tracking and segmentation capabilities in biomedical imaging. For effective cell shape synthesis, a compact yet flexible representation is required, however current methods involving voxel-based and polygon mesh approaches have limitations for high-resolution and topology changes such as growth and cell division. Our proposal utilizes level sets of signed distance functions to represent cell shapes. By training a neural network to implicitly generate signed distance function values at any point in three-dimensional space over time, conditioned on a latent code, it is possible to create new and unseen cell shape sequences. The effectiveness of our approach was evaluated both qualitatively and quantitatively through comparisons of synthetic cells with actual cell growth, mitosis and lung cancer cells exhibiting complex protrusions. Our results demonstrate the generation of realistic synthetic cells with similar characteristics to real cells, including the production of plausible topological cell shape sequences in three-dimensional space over time. The compact level set representation makes it feasible to model cell shapes for extended periods and to explore the synthesis of cell shapes with desired outcomes such as excessive cell growth. Ultimately, this resulting dataset could be used to develop better cell tracking and segmentation techniques. The synthetic cell shape generation method has been made publicly available on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/tonyiu/implicit-cell-shape-generation. Blind, low-vision, and other print-disabled individuals still struggle with printed documents. Our focus in this paper lies on addressing a particular issue: providing access to referenced content such as citations, footnotes, images, tables, and mathematical equations. Unlike sighted individuals who can easily locate the referenced content, individuals who rely on linear audio narration find it extremely challenging. We suggest an approach based on visual detection to identify referenced content and gather necessary metadata that can be utilized in subsequent research to insert summaries into audio narratives. The technique we present has shown effectiveness on both digital documents and those that have been scanned from print. Specifically, it successfully located over 90% of tables, tables of content, equations, figures, footnotes, and mathematical equations in a test set consisting of 506 documents. Furthermore, it collected corresponding metadata with an accuracy rate of 80%. The results of our experiments are available online. In addition to the technical contribution itself, it also includes accessible links to the test set, audio explanations, and corresponding video demonstrations. Our research aims to make digital environments more inclusive for print-impaired individuals by providing accessible navigation. A web-based platform has been developed where users can listen to audio narratives and locate referenced content through spoken descriptions. The technology is available at https://navigability.net. All the test set documents, audio explanations, and corresponding video demonstrations are accessible at https://navigability.net/docs. While BERT excels at modeling bidirectional contexts through denoising autoencoding, its reliance on input masking overlooks positional dependencies, leading to inconsistent pretraining-finetune performance. This has motivated the development of XLNet, an enhanced pretraining approach based on autoregressive language modeling, enabling bidirectional context modeling through the incorporation of all possible contextual dependencies in the autoregressive sequence prediction task. By leveraging the enhanced permuted prediction objective and subword conditional probabilities, XLNet successfully addresses the shortcomings of BERT and outperforms it on a range of tasks, achieving new state-of-the-art results on GLUE and SQuAD. Furthermore, XLNet's pretrained denoising autoencoding representations yield superior performance when used as a feature learning technique in various downstream tasks. Importantly, XLNet's advantages over BERT become more pronounced as the preprocessing step tokenization quality improves. While better tokenization leads to gains of several points on the GLUE benchmark, XLNet's superiority is notably more evident when bidirectional context modeling is more challenging. This observation highlights XLNet's ability to effectively navigate complex contextual dependencies through the autoregressive pretraining process. Ultimately, XLNet's pretrained denoising autoencoding representations offer enhanced capabilities for natural language understanding. We analyzed models incorporating Gaussian distributions of noise and found that even relatively low levels of activity, such as those seen in mildly active or inactive stars, can compromise the detection of atmospheric features in transits, particularly in lower resolution settings. To address this challenge, we explored the potential benefits of using high-resolution spectroscopy and found that combining data from multiple resolutions can facilitate the identification of these features, while discussing potential trade-offs between resolution and signal-to-noise ratio. We also examined the potential of using activity indices, such as H-alpha surface area, as indicators of activity levels and discussed their potential applications in future missions. Our research, focusing on transiting Earth-like exoplanets around slightly cooler stars, demonstrated that even in these cases, atmospheric signals could be detected with relatively low activity levels from the host star. Numerical simulations for tsunami disasters often face two primary challenges: 
1) accurately tracking the wave's propagation across various scales and 2) efficiently utilizing resources due to the wave's initial minimal presence. Our approach focuses on generating realistic tsunami waves that disperse through deep ocean environments, triggered by a high-energy asteroid impact on one of Jupiter's moons. To capture the uncertainty in wave heights at their source, we've developed a multiscale model consisting of two coupled systems, solving Navier-Stokes equations at different resolutions. To enhance computation adaptability, we've implemented a unified operator interface that facilitates data transfer between sub-grid and grid-scale models. This approach allows us to simulate the entire process from the asteroid impact to the wave reaching the critical depth of a few meters, covering approximately 8 hours of real time. To visualize our results, we present an interactive 2D surface elevation animation as well as a 3D animation of ocean surface velocities on a cluster of 40 GPUs. Furthermore, we've carried out several numerical experiments to assess the convergence rates of our model using the "in-place" adaptation technique. These rates confirm our expectations: 2 for surface velocities, 2 for pressure, and 4 for vorticity measurements. To establish the credibility of our model, we've compared our results with an existing benchmark solution from [Koning et al., CEAS 2020], demonstrating our model's suitability for asteroid-generated dispersive tsunami simulation. Notably, our model has successfully captured the wave's characteristic "eye-like" behavior, observed in previous simulations, and we have also identified the underlying cause of this feature. To further establish our credibility, we plan to validate our model against a real tsunami event that occurred on Lake Ontario in 1985 and compare it with existing coupled atmosphere-surface wave model simulations. Following validation, we will introduce randomness into our model to address the considerable uncertainty in wave heights at their source during the tsunami generation process. Our team's primary goal is to simulate the entire asteroid impact-to-wave-propagation process on a 3D Jupiter moon landscape using adaptive terrain-vortex front methods in conjunction with high-performance computing resources. To effectively communicate our model to a diverse audience, we have created a range of educational materials such as an introductory presentation, a detailed paper based on our model's development, and a beginner's guide to ATMs. To facilitate interaction between our model's spatial and temporal components, we have developed a custom time-space domain mapping framework. Cyber-Physical Systems require robust resilience properties to withstand and quickly recover from disruptions, often provided by periodic system checks and predefined response protocols. Evaluating the effectiveness of resilient strategies presents difficulties due to the inherent complexities of the system and the high risk of undetected vulnerabilities. A significant obstacle arises from the distinct nature of temporal logic-based specifications used for system verification and testing, often resulting in inconsistent approaches to risk assessment and analysis. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a unified framework for assessing resilience based on Temporal Logic specifications, enabling a comprehensive and well-structured approach to evaluating and comparing different rescue strategies. This formulation provides a clear and unambiguous framework for determining and optimizing resilience levels within multi-agent Cyber-Physical Systems. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach using an example of a Centralized Power System subject to attack, showcasing the ability of our method to identify and validate suitable response plans. Compared to existing methodologies, our approach offers several key benefits, including a clear separation between system properties and resilience policies, as well as improved expressiveness and precision in specifying resilience properties and strategies. By leveraging off-the-shelf verification and validation tools, our framework facilitates well-structured and comprehensive approaches to evaluating and optimizing various rescue strategies within complex Cyber-Physical Systems. Overall, our proposed methodology addresses the pressing need for a well-structured and precise approach to assessing and comparing resilience levels in advanced multi-agent Cyber-Physical Systems. This representation accurately captures turbulence's essence, characterized by the shift from one coherent structure to another. Our analysis yields exact expressions for the turbulent transport operator without employing simplifying assumptions. In the limit where spatial and temporal locality prevail, our operator reduces to the conventional estimate of turbulent transport as a diffusivity tensor, with its components being the integrated velocity field auto-correlation. Unlike conventional methods, our results accurately account for the stretch and deformations of coherent structures without the need for the commonly applied small parameter assumptions. Furthermore, our approach has significant implications for the understanding of mechanisms behind lateral diffusion in coherent structures, challenging established theories which can be considered as a special case of our results under specific conditions. This approach is in agreement with the results of numerical simulations in the limit of small parameters. This paper presents a comprehensive study on the electromagnetic radiation behavior in a thin conductor plate separated by two large parallel walls at a temperature $T$, where the plate's area is $A$ and the distance between the walls is $d$. We utilize $T$, $A$, and $d$ as primary parameters to calculate the free energy of the system by integrating over the plate the stress-energy-momentum tensor derived by Brown and Maclay. When $kTd/\hbar c \gg 1$, the expression for the free energy of the system reduces to the one predicted by quantum electrodynamics. A misinterpretation of surface tension by Casimir is also addressed, where the plate's interior and exterior surfaces merge into a single interface with diminished width when $kTd/\hbar c \ll 1$. Furthermore, the free energy of the system is used to derive equations for entropy, heat, and work, and these results are applied to demonstrate the second law of thermodynamics. An entropic potential is introduced to verify the recovery of the original thermodynamics when $kTd/\hbar c \gg 1$. The results obtained are consistent with previous studies on blackbody thermodynamics, thereby validating their correctness and providing a comprehensive review of the subject. The findings of this research are anticipated to enhance the understanding of blackbody thermodynamics and inspire future investigations into the phenomenon. In a single-hop beeping network, stations interact via one-bit messages to form a distributed communication system. Named by a central management approach, each station is assigned a unique ID within a designated framework. Focusing on the beeping network's energy efficiency, our research defines two key performance measures: beeping cost and idling cost. Previous studies, such as those by Chlebus et. al. and Olshevsky and Rawitz, primarily explored resolving name conflict scenarios. This paper shifts the focus to optimizing system efficiency by minimizing the beeping cost. We establish a lower bound on beeping cost achieved through standard randomized naming methods. Based on this finding, we introduce a novel randomized naming approach, RandName, which incorporates combinations of uniform and Gaussian distributions. Experiment results show that RandName achieves close to optimal beeping cost while also being highly efficient and able to resolve name conflict scenarios. In contrast, RandName outperforms the existing centralized management approaches, such as CentName, by achieving significantly lower beeping costs with substantial improvements of at least three orders of magnitude in some cases. Furthermore, RandName exhibits superior performance when compared to the distributed NameSort algorithm by Feldman et. al., which is optimized for sorting tasks, by achieving a beeping cost reduction of over 25 times in the best-case scenario. The name resolution process for RandName is demonstrated to comply with the existing pure-CSP model. We introduce the concept of energy efficiency, incorporate idling cost into the analysis, and demonstrate that the beeping cost optimizations can be used to achieve improved overall system efficiency. Additionally, our work highlights the beeping cost as a dominant factor affecting system efficiency due to its orders of magnitude greater relationship compared to idling cost. Ultimately, the various optimized algorithms are evaluated based on their ability to achieve efficient beeping cost while resolving name conflict scenarios, and their performance is analyzed through simulations across different parameters, such as varying station densities in the beeping network. The results indicate that the beeping cost of CentName grows in approximately logarithmic fashion, while RandName exhibits sublinear beeping cost growth. Notably, RandName outperforms CentName by achieving a nearly linear beeping cost in low-density beeping networks. Experiment results also reveal that the beeping cost of NameSort by Feldman et. al. exhibits a polynomial relationship with respect to the number of conflicting IDs. Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed texts have gained considerable attention, 
mainly driven by the widespread use of language blending in social media across 
multi-lingual countries such as India, Mexico, Europe, and parts of the USA. 
Given their importance, developing word embeddings for code-mixed texts has 
become a pressing concern. We address this issue by proposing a novel approach 
called PESTO that learns and differentiates between code-mixed words based on 
various positional factors including prefixes, suffixes, infixes, and the 
connection between individual word meanings and their contextual relations. 
Our model successfully leverages switch points from the CNN model of Wezal 
et al. (2019) to segment input words and incorporate positional features 
from the CNN's convolutional filters and attention weights. We combine these 
positional features with WordPiece subwords from the PE-SPM model of Lample et 
al. (2018) to create enhanced word embeddings. Our experimental evaluations 
across two datasets demonstrate that the proposed PESTO outperforms other 
models, serving as a robust tool for code-mixed language modeling. The 
implementation details are available on GitHub at https://github.com/iiiitd/WEDM-2022. 
An updated version with more detailed results and technical specifications has 
been updated on arXiv at https://arXiv.arXiv.org/abs/2202.04207v2.

This paper introduces a novel motion planning method suited for dynamic obstacles, building upon the Spacetime A* (STA) algorithm. STA is known for efficiently generating plausible motion plans by utilizing a spacetime map that accounts for potential collisions and optimizing paths. However, in low-resolution maps, insufficient detail on collisions and optimality can lead to subpar motion plans. Our approach enhances STA by generating additional spatial constraints in under-resolved maps, providing more accurate predictions of collisions and optimal paths. A constraint search algorithm identifies critical regions where additional constraints are required, and these constraints are added to refine the motion planning process. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly improves both the speed and accuracy of motion plans generated in diverse, environmentally challenging scenarios.
