The CDF II Collaboration has made a precise measurement of the W boson mass which deviates from the Standard Model's prediction by 7$\sigma$. The FNAL muon magnetic moment measurement also displays a $4.2\sigma$ discrepancy. In an effort to resolve the anomalies in both the W boson and muon (g-2), we have investigated the type-X two Higgs doublet model. Our analysis focused on the type-X 2HDM's parameter space for $m_A$ and $\tan\beta$, ensuring compatibility with the muon (g-2), lepton universality test, and CDF II's latest $W$ boson mass findings. We determined that measuring the $h\to AA$ branching ratio imposes a substantial lower limit on the mass of $m_H$. Our study has established that the type-X 2HDM is a plausible candidate for addressing the anomalies in both the W boson and muon (g-2) measurements. Furthermore, the proposed P2K16 experiment could potentially detect the proposed type-X 2HDM signature of $4b\bar{b}\gamma$ with as few as $10^{-4}$ events per year, with a mass difference of approximately $20\,\mathrm{GeV}$ between $h$ and $A$. Finally, we have demonstrated that decays of a possible $500\,\mathrm{MeV}$ isospin-isospin scalar are within the type-X 2HDM's reach, offering a potential new direction for experimental research. These results suggest that a larger experimental program may be required to fully investigate the type-X 2HDM's properties. Moreover, future experiments such as the FCC-ee and P2K16 will be essential in confirming whether the type-X 2HDM explains the anomalies in both the W boson and muon (g-2) measurements. If confirmed, the type-X 2HDM has the potential to yield a profound breakthrough in particle physics theory. Lastly, the type-X 2HDM has been found to be compatible with the recent ICECube Neutrino experiment's findings at $3.4\sigma$, suggesting that the Higgs boson's potential $bb$ decay may be increased, which could be supported by the $W$ boson mass measurement. Our analysis suggests that the type-X 2HDM is a viable candidate for explaining the anomalies in both the W boson and muon (g-2) measurements

Adaptive interaction, or entrainment, involves adjusting communication patterns to match an interaction partner's styles, essential for effective, normal human conversations. Measuring entrainment in speech requires labor-intensive, expensive human assessments, often impractical for various applications. To streamline entrainment measurement, researchers are developing new, algorithmic methods. This work showcases a novel, automated method for detecting and assessing adaptive interaction using advanced machine learning techniques, as exemplified in a non-verbal communication scenario where participants with developmental disorders interact with trained therapists. For this purpose, we introduce the entrainment distance, a novel metric that measures the similarity or difference in communication patterns between interaction partners. To calculate this distance, we employ a technique that merges data analysis approaches with a type of artificial neural network. To validate the entrainment distance metric, we tested its correlation with established, human-based measures of adaptive interaction in conversational speech, obtained through sensory-motor treatment assessments. Meanwhile, related studies explored the potential for using other artificial neural network models to predict entrainment from observation, solely using observed interactions as input. These predictive models can facilitate real-time support for therapists interacting with individuals with developmental disorders, among other potential practical applications to various areas of adaptive communication. Please note that the related study mentioned in the last sentence was written by a different author than the primary author of this current study. The research was conducted with ethics approval from the ethics committee Universidade Novel de Lisboa - Observatório de Direitos Humanos da Universidade Novel de Lisboa, [Registration number: UNL/OC/2021/001]. With regard to data protection, all participants provided informed consent for the use of their data for research purposes. Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights into students' test suites or evaluate the efficacy of their test cases. However, current research suggests that students primarily utilize feedback from tools for coverage purposes, which can lead them to overlook the benefits of receiving and learning from feedback on correctness. In response, we are proposing and validating an adaptive and interactive feedback mechanism for teaching software testing that is capable of offering coverage and correctness feedback to students, as well as providing an understanding of the gaps between their expected and actual program outputs. Compared to traditional methods, our research indicates that this new approach leads to improved program understanding in students, as demonstrated by a controlled experiment. The outcomes of our research also show that, in addition to providing an understanding of their programs, students can also utilize the feedback from our tool to enhance their own test case design. The source code for our educational tool has been made publicly available on github.com/infusa/teachTesting. The research presented in this paper was supported by a training grant from the CNEIP program. The assessment of our research was conducted through a controlled experiment and the results were supported by interviews. The results of our research were analyzed using descriptive statistics, and the conclusions drawn from them were validated through a one-way Within-Subject Design comparison, as well as through content analysis of student interview transcripts. The results of our research revealed that our educational tool was favored over the control condition, and the differences observed were consistent across various dependent variables. Importantly, the results of our research revealed that students who utilized the educational tool demonstrated greater conceptual understanding of testing across multiple measures, and the results of our research were found to be consistent through various analyses. The results of our research suggested that our educational tool was deemed useful by students, and the results of our research revealed that the preferences of students for our educational tool over the control condition was found to be multi-faceted. The results of our research revealed several reasons for why students may be more favorably disposed to our educational tool compared to the control condition. The results of our research were supported by multiple data sources, and the results of our research were analyzed through a systematic process. The results of our research suggested that the preferences of students for our educational tool could be explained through a combination of several distinct motivations. The results of our research provided evidence for each of these motivations, and the results of our research demonstrated that these motivations were relevant for individual students. Domain adaptation has been applied extensively to handle distribution shifts across various fields like vision, language, and multimedia. Most existing domain adaptation techniques leverage domain-invariant features by utilizing both source and target domain data. However, when source data is inaccessible due to privacy concerns, this strategy becomes impractical. To resolve this issue, we propose a novel method that adapts source models via hypothesis transfer without requiring access to source data. Our method, which involves a semi-supervised learning technique, iteratively transfers domain-invariant knowledge from the source domain model to a target domain model. This study presents a novel neural network architecture for particle physics research that leverages localization in time-projection chamber technology for dark matter exploration. Characteristic signals within these TPCs facilitate particle interaction localization via a reconstruction process, making them a focus for multilayer perceptron-based approaches like those using MLPs for reconstruction in TPCs. However, MLPs are a "black-box" technique lacking reflection of prior scientific knowledge, thus the paper revisits neural networks for interaction localization, integrating detector-specific signal information into the multilayer architecture through feature encoding and modified output layers. By incorporating domain knowledge, a novel Domain-informed Neural Network, DiNN, significantly minimizes the receptive field of initial layers to spatially account for signal localization within the detector, much like early stages of Graph Neural Networks with minimal connection scope, resulting in substantial reductions of parameters - a whopping 60% less compared to MLPs, while matching localization accuracy and laying groundwork for further optimization with embedded additional domain insights into the architecture. DiNN exhibits exceptional inference speed and serves as a starting point for integrating more domain insights to enhance its predictive capabilities, ultimately making it suitable for real-time applications in particle physics experiments. Given its potential, DiNN is well-positioned as a potential tool not just for dark matter exploration but also in a range of related experiments. In an attempt to bridge this gap, we compiled a comprehensive database of pre-calculated absorption coefficients for numerous key gas species at user-specified temperature and pressure levels. This tool is designed to enhance future atmospheric modeling by accounting for the most current atomic and molecular data, thereby reducing previous accuracy limitations. As a result, we anticipate significant improvements in related research areas, including photochemical calculations, spectroscopic analysis, and atmospheric modeling. We build upon ASP's modeling language semantics to define a formal description of grounding algorithms using the theory of finite spaces in first-order logic. This formalism enables a clear definition of groundability, which signifies the existence of a grounding algorithm and also serves as the foundational concept for assessing algorithm performance. Various grounding algorithms, such as those employing forward subgoal selection and forward pruning, are analyzed in the context of their task-specific strategies and subgoal selection methods. We examine their soundness and completeness, considering their algorithmic soundness and interaction with the modeling language semantics. These algorithms' groundability is confirmed, with specific assurances regarding their ability to handle unstable systems and non-terminating computations. We offer an initial assessment of their asymptotic complexity, noting that this investigation is distinct from the standard approach of analyzing computational complexity due to the fixation of variables. Additionally, we provide an illustration of our theoretical findings by applying them to the cloning set groundness problem. Lastly, this research lays the groundwork for an abstract, bird's eye view of the ASP modeling language, which might be utilized as a starting point for analyzing high-level programming languages. We hope that this study may inspire the creation of asymptotic complexity analyses for future computational logic development. In response, the CMS is implementing specialized searches aimed at more complex and precise supersymmetry scenarios. This contribution will focus on three new searches using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data recorded with the CMS detector between 2016 and 2018: a heavy gluino search involving the decay of heavy neutralinos and resulting in boosted Z bosons and undetected energy; a search for supersymmetry compression in final states featuring soft tau particles; and an investigation into compressed, long-lived charginos in hadronic final states displaying vanished particle tracks. These searches will be showcased using proton-proton collision data expected to be recorded between 2022 and 2025. Preliminary results from these searches will be presented. Finally, the CMS is striving to enhance its supersymmetry search capabilities in diverse contexts and environments, but certain gaps and voids still exist, leaving Supersymmetry to remain one of the key priorities for future particle physics research programs. To address this, we studied a notable solar eruption on October 16, 2015, that involved an EUV jet, a streamer in white-light, and a type II radio burst observed using advanced imaging technologies. The analysis revealed that the wave-front of the shock was visible only in high-frequency radio images, suggesting an interpretation based on the "jet-driven piston shock" model. This model indicates that a streamer in the low corona can act as a "piston" driving a shock that propagates through the streamer's leading edge and generates a coronal jet through the propagation of the MHD wave generated. This event provided an exceptional opportunity to study the characteristics of a coronal shock at very long wavelengths, allowing us to determine the electron density of the shock and verify that it corresponds to the density of the streamer. Moreover, we were able to calculate an important parameter for the first time: the wave period of the MHD wave, which was found to be $45\pm5$ minutes. This value is consistent with our expectation for wave period based on the driving mechanism proposed. The findings indicate that the "jet-driven piston shock" model can explain the characteristics of type II solar bursts that have persistent decays in frequency. We utilize an approximate diagonal mass matrix for charged bosons, then fit the masses of two Higgs bosons and a ratio determining their CP natures. Our analysis indicates that the model effectively addresses the anomalies in $R(D)$ and $R(D^*)$, however, it fails to satisfactorily explain the anomaly in $R(K)$. Furthermore, it appears that the model cannot accommodate the observed value of the muon's magnetic moment. While double Higgs boson production is typically studied within specific frameworks, in this analysis we consider production from electroweak and weak processes, revealing that the production of double Higgs bosons is not strongly constrained by the observed anomalies. However, it is constrained by the muon's magnetic moment with a constraint similar to that of the alignment of Yukawa couplings in single Higgs boson production. This study is the first to perform a likelihood analysis on the general two Higgs doublet model using this breadth of data. The newly developed random vortex system incorporates a stochastic differential equation that interacts with a finite-dimensional functional differential equation, contrasting it with earlier two-dimensional random vortex dynamics equations. The creation of this random vortex system lays the groundwork for developing innovative numerical solutions for approximate non-viscous fluid flow simulations. Additionally, this random vortex dynamics provides a novel framework for random quantitative studies of fluid dynamics, potentially leading to novel statistical analysis methods of Navier-Stokes equations solutions. The research relies heavily on the existence and uniqueness theorems for functional stochastic differential equations with marked characteristics. The primary goals of this work are two-fold: to numerically solve the three-dimensional random vortex dynamics equation and to demonstrate the applicability of functional stochastic differential equations in random functionals of random fields applications. The resulting numerical solutions of the three-dimensional random vortex dynamics equation have significant implications for random measures in three-dimensional flows. The methods employed can be extended to develop novel numerical solutions for the random generalized Euler equations. The integration of random measurement data into random vortex dynamics remains an open challenge. The techniques and methods utilized can also be applied to random partial differential equations for fluid flows with both additive and multiplicative stochastic components. The accompanying MATLAB code is provided to reproduce the numerical results and confidence intervals reported in this paper. The research presented here can be expanded to include various types of stochastic and functional differential equations, such as those appearing in physical-chemical systems, biological networks, and predator-prey models. The state vector of a boson sampling process can be precisely calculated using S single photons and P photons interacting in a nonlinear medium, leading to a description of multiphotame scattering probabilities via the permanent of a matrix representing photon interactions. However, determining the full state vector proves challenging, even for small values of S, due to the complexity of expressing it in a Fock basis. We address this challenge by expressing the full state vector as a sum of S Fock states, each involving different numbers of S photons, and derive an algorithm for calculating coefficients associated with these states. We then analyze the quantum correlations present in the full state vector for specific cases involving two and three photons interacting in a nonlinear medium. Our results, obtained numerically, indicate that the full state vector is highly entangled, with no obvious way to express it using smaller, separable components. Additionally, we find that certain hidden substructures within the full state vector may exist at a predetermined number N of Fock states, where N is a function of S and P, with these structures being generally weaker for larger values of S and P. Conversely, we find that the probability distribution of two-photon S matrices is uniform for interactions involving up to six photons but becomes non-uniform for seven or more photons. Our findings have implications for boson sampling theory and its potential applications in quantum simulation and communication. Moreover, the entanglement present in the full state vector of boson sampling may serve as a tool for demonstrating quantum advantages, particularly in clustering and communication processes. However, accessing this entanglement proves challenging due to the limitations of observing quantum systems with our measurement tools. Therefore, discovering new methods for processing and utilizing quantum data represents an important avenue for research in quantum information theory. Such advancements could potentially enable us to utilize boson sampling for applications such as quantum simulation and to evaluate the entanglement present in the full state vector of boson sampling. Moreover, selecting specific nonlinear media could facilitate the creation of boson samples that are easier to analyze. For instance, we have demonstrated that the full state vector of Fock states generated via a cubic nonlinearity is composed entirely of entangled components, whereas our results for a quadratic nonlinearity indicate the presence of one separable component among many entangled components. Conversely, we found that the two-photon cubic nonlinearity generates a state which is easily separable. Our research explores the relationship between entanglement and nonlinear interactions, with the latter influencing correlations within boson samples through variations in their order and degree

By utilizing a supervised autoencoder, we can create a compact, interpretable representation for these sequences while preserving correlations between different variable pairs. Our innovative approach combines this representation with traditional Classifiers and Dimensionality Reduction techniques, such as self-organizing maps. As a result, we can obtain a simplified, interpretable sequence representation along with category labels or reduced dimensionality trail maps. Our algorithm exhibits impressive performance in a wide range of simulated tests by achieving significantly higher accuracy compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate its effectiveness in real-world situations with a study of MS data where we compare various dimensionality reduction techniques on pre- and post-processing data to determine the best approach. Our innovative approach allows for easier feature identification and more accurate results, making it well-suited for analyzing temporal sequence data. Reinforcement learning seeks to develop the most effective strategies through interactions with complex systems, even when the underlying rules are unknown. Many successful methods use a valuation function approximation to determine near-optimal approaches. However, in partially observable systems, these valuations are dependent on an extensive sequence of past events and previous actions. Recent research demonstrates that neural networks, specifically recurrent ones, can implement these valuations, achieving state representations known as beliefs that facilitate improved policy outcomes. We examine the connections between these recurrent networks, traditional belief representation methods used in probabilistic planning, and a related factor expected by these networks, the so-called 'predictive belief'. We derive a method for training these recurrent networks to their expected values, avoiding the need for an explicit maximization process. Experimental validation of this approach supports its effectiveness in various Imitation Learning environments. It has been found that the predictive belief plays a significant role in this effectiveness. Moreover, the proposed method is particularly beneficial when operating in partially observable systems requiring a large memory space to store past information. Finally, the key components of this approach can be combined with other known RL techniques, such as adversarial training, to create a versatile belief-aware RL method. We demonstrate that this method leads to improved outcomes in both synthetic and real-world scenarios. Overall, the proposed approach offers a practical solution for taking optimal actions in complex, partially observable systems even with extremely large associated value spaces. We successfully validated this method against four benchmark tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results. Furthermore, the combination of our technique with other known RL methods presents considerable potential for improvement. Consequently, the extension of our approach to a variety of RL methods could lead to notable enhancements, leading us to believe that it may yield even more significant outcomes in the future. A recent competition, the 2021 Image Similarity Challenge, introduced a benchmark dataset to evaluate state-of-the-art image copy detection methods. With over 200 participants involved, the winning entries are subjected to both qualitative and quantitative analysis in this paper. Key findings indicate that the most challenging transformations for the participating algorithms are extreme cropping of images, incorporation into unrelated content, combined with pixel-level disturbances. Notably, the winning approaches emphasized the importance of robust training on heavily distorted images to guarantee zero false positives. Furthermore, the winning entries demonstrated the efficacy of attention-based networks in conjunction with robust training. Ultimately, the study's outcomes and newly found insights are expected to provide valuable insights for future research in the domain. Moreover, the winning papers' content has been incorporated into the widely used ImageNet Large Scale Visual Challenge dataset, enhancing the dataset's depth and usefulness.

Our research involves analyzing stochastic processes that are either halted or bounce off the boundary of a given area. These processes' underlying mathematical operators comprise two components: a main, degrading portion that loses its effectiveness at the boundary, specifically in a direction perpendicular to it, along with a smaller, non-degenerate perturbation. Understanding the behavior of such stochastic processes plays a significant role in the stabilization of solutions to associated parabolic equations that incorporate a small parameter. In this context, metastability effects emerge, meaning that as the size of the perturbation approaches zero, the solutions' long-term behavior is dependent on the specific time frame considered. Our study encompasses a range of scenarios, including boundary-value problems under both Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions. Additionally, we are also investigating periodic homogenization techniques for operators that exhibit degeneracy. These findings will facilitate the derivation of effective parabolic equations that describe the behavior of related functionals, providing valuable insights to researchers working on probabilistic versions of the celebrated homogenization theorem. Moreover, our work is expected to yield approximated solutions to the investigated stochastic problems. As such, it may be of independent interest to researchers working in the fields of partial differential equations and stochastic processes. Furthermore, our work is anticipated to offer relevant context to existing literature on the subject. This study focuses on the characteristics of nuclear matter at zero temperature within the influence of intense magnetic fields; it investigates pairing properties, symmetry energy and skewness under varying magnetic intensities. A linearized correlation operator technique (LOCV) is employed to describe the nuclear matter, and its application is extended to account for the effect of magnetic fields in the context of the Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov mean-field theory. Initially, the underlying framework of the LCV method is outlined, and then it is utilized to model the properties of neutron and proton spins within varying intensities of magnetic fields. Our analysis reveals significant alterations in the neutron and proton ratios, and corresponding drifts in the centroid frequencies of the giant monopole resonance at non-zero magnetic intensities. Additionally, pair correlations in the nuclear system are modeled in the context of magnetic fields, and results indicate reduced pairing strength and corresponding decrease in the neutron skin thickness at intense magnetic fields. The characteristics of symmetry energy and skewness are calculated in response to varying magnetic pressures, and our analysis shows distinct modifications in these parameters resulting from the application of strong magnetic fields. A systematic examination was performed using the $N_N\sigma$ correlation channel to determine the drift in the symmetry energy and skewness within the framework of magnetic fields. This analysis revealed that strong magnetic fields cause significant drops in the values of the symmetry energy and skewness parameters. Furthermore, our study on the effective density dependent polynomial (DDP) kernel of the LCV technique in the context of magnetic fields indicates that the magnetic field significantly alters the behavior of the kernel at lower effective densities while leaving the behavior at higher effective densities relatively unchanged. The Drude model was employed to investigate the electrical conductivity of nuclear matter at non-zero magnetic fields, and our analysis reveals decreased conductivity in response to increased magnetic fields, and corresponding changes in conductivity are linked to changes in the shape of the nuclear matter. The impact of magnetic fields on the polymorphism of nuclear matter was explored by varying the magnetic intensity while maintaining constant density, and our analysis indicates that strong magnetic fields cause the nuclear matter to transition irregularly and demonstrate dynamical symmetry in the context of magnetic fields. The effect of magnetic fields on the dynamic response function (DF) was also investigated, and our analysis reveals decreased intensity and width of the DF in response to increased magnetic fields, and corresponding changes in the dynamics of the nuclear matter are linked to changes in the density fluctuations. A comprehensive far-ultraviolet continuum map of the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus complex was created by combining the observations from GALEX and FIMS, which provided data at nearly identical wavelengths. The UV intensity in the area exhibited significant variation, with diffuse UV radiation predominantly stemming from dust particles and secondarily from hot components such as O and B stars. A novel UV background was discovered, approximately 4 sigma above the cosmic microwave background, which appears to be diffuse light emitted from dust particles and potentially contributed to by a hitherto unknown hot component. The diffuse UV radiation is proposed to be the primary energy source for water ice sublimation on dust grains in the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus complex, which would have implications for the distribution of ice in protoplanetary disks. A correlated pattern was found between UV radiation and the distribution of particles larger than 1 micron in the area, suggesting that dust particles play a significant role in absorbing and scattering UV radiation. Estimates revealed that dust particles may absorb and scatter as much as twenty times more energy than they absorb and scatter in the Lyman-Werner bands, which could have significant consequences for the evolution of the dust particles and the structure of the dust particles. A proposed mechanism for the formation of the interstellar gas and dust particles in the area involves the expulsion of baryons from stars forming in a nearby protostellar disk. However, no star formation was observed in the area during the course of the study, which reveals that there may be a considerable delay between the onset of baryonic expulsion from star formation and the onset of star formation. While there were noticeable variations in the UV radiation intensity, no supernovae were observed in the area during the course of the study, which suggests that cloud fragmentation may be a key factor in controlling where new stars and planets form. The discovery highlights the significant impact that far-ultraviolet radiation has on forming planetary systems and the cosmic environment. Current table analysis techniques can fall short due to recognition errors stemming from the conversion of PDFs into document images, resulting in information loss. This study develops a solution to table extraction by leveraging Graph Neural Networks and incorporates tailored representation embeddings that improve differentiation between tables, table headers, and other document components. An experimental assessment was conducted on a combined dataset from PubLayNet and PubTables-1M to evaluate the proposed approach's efficacy. The results indicate that the combination of Graph Neural Networks and our proposed embeddings achieves an F-score of 0.955, demonstrating significant improvement over the current state-of-the-art. The corresponding code has been made available on GitHub for the research community. An additional investigation into the influence of visual and linguistic features on table identification was also performed, exploring the optimal balance between these factors, and revealing a preference for mixed visual-linguistic content. The study's findings were presented at the ACM SIGKDD 2020 Applications of Data Science and Knowledge Engineering session in August 2020. The study's abstract was reviewed and approved for distribution at the venue. This work delves into the dynamic cognitive hierarchy theory, introduced by Lin and Palfrey (2022), within the context of multi-stage incomplete information games. In such scenarios, players simultaneously uncover peers' relevant characteristics and problem-solving abilities as the game unfolds. Building on this concept, our study provides a complete characterization of the dynamic CH solution for two-person dirty faces games. Notably, our findings indicate that lower-level players determine their characteristics in subsequent stages more slowly than their higher-level counterparts. Furthermore, our re-examination of the experimental data collected by Bayer and Chan (2007) shows that the dynamic CH solution more effectively explains the observed outcomes than its static counterpart. Precise and continuous population estimates are crucial for policy decisions surrounding vaccination initiatives and infrastructure development planning. As censuses fall short of providing the necessary spatiotemporal detail, researchers have been turning to independent approaches incorporating remote sensing data and microcensus statistics. We conducted an experiment in Mozambique, specifically estimating the population count in two districts between censuses. Furthermore, we evaluated the feasibility of leveraging open-access datasets to support population forecasting. Our exploration also involved utilizing existing annotated datasets to improve building footprint prediction accuracy. While our estimates matched those of the recent census, we ran into significant challenges posed by the complexity of rural areas and the scarcity of anthropogenic features in available satellite imagery. Consequently, we propose to implement a multi-step network architecture for improved estimation results and suggest that future research target the development of more comprehensive satellite datasets encompassing varied timelines and spectrums for enhanced object detection. Additionally, we recommend the incorporation of topographic information to support population estimation in regions lacking complete census data. Our proposed method could serve as a viable emergency solution during census gaps, ultimately facilitating more effective public health and infrastructure planning. Over the past ten years, substantial advancements have taken place to minimize the likelihood of false positives in approximate membership query filters. These filters are useful in a variety of applications such as network databases and data streaming, and typically involve a trade-off between the frequency and size of false positives. This research introduces a new class of filters known as CP-free filters, an expansion of the traditional content-addressable list family. This paper shows that CP-free filters can achieve a significant reduction in the likelihood of false positives with no increase in storage space, and further, proposes a construction method utilizing hash tables and prefixes that reduces the likelihood of false positives to any arbitrary fraction with linear storage space. This research conducted an exhaustive examination of all CP-free filter implementations that employ a single hash function and found that no such construction can achieve a probability of false positives less than $1/(\sqrt{m}+1)$ where m represents the number of bits used to store an element's representation. Furthermore, this research presents a best-known CP-free filter construction, named CPStream, which can achieve a probability of false positives less than $1.38/\sqrt{m}$ with linear storage space. This is followed by another refinement, named CPStreamV, which reduces the likelihood of false positives to less than $1.25/\sqrt{m}$ with nearly the same storage requirements. To put these results into perspective, we compared the performance of CPStreamV to three popular low false positive filters, namely CP and CP-XOR, as well as a recently proposed optimal CPXOR filter known as HSSM. Our comparison revealed that CPStreamV is the only optimizer that doesn't require a pre-processing stage and the only one that doesn't necessitate a second hash function while yielding a $25\%$ reduction in the likelihood of false positives compared to the best available CPXOR construction, all with minimal storage requirements. Our experimentation also confirmed the efficacy of the CPStreamV construction across a wide array of CP-free filter configurations and also across various high-performance hash functions like CityHash and MurmurHash. Our research further investigates the performance of the CPStreamV construction in a real-world setting by integrating it with a hierarchical list content-addressable list known as HLL. Our results reveal that the integration results in a substantial reduction of the likelihood of false positives and a significant decrease in the time required to process queries, all with nearly linear storage requirements. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisional coupling and external light fields leads to the gradual disappearance of molecular states through Rabi oscillations. Furthermore, under specific vanishing light conditions, we identified distinct distinct windows where stable atom-molecule coexistence is possible through a Rabi scheme. Our study also reveals that the interplay of light and collisions in systems with one spin unit can result in the creation of novel dark state modes characterized by stable atom-molecule pair condensates. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that the application of impulsive light pulses can trigger the quantum transformation of molecular states into atom-molecule pairs in coherent matter waves. Last but not least, we have explored the feasibility of generating multiple coherent molecule pairs through light-induced three-body recombination and examined the influence of collisional coupling on their production, dispersion, and correlations. Our research is expected to contribute to the development of novel tools for manipulating and studying matter waves at the dark-state conditions. Moreover, we have also proposed a new strategy for generating multiple coherent atom-molecule pairs during a single optical pulse event, which is expected to facilitate the investigation of various quantum many-body phenomena. Ultimately, the stable atom-molecule pairs produced in our scheme can be utilized for applications such as quantum computation and entanglement manipulation. For instance, in systems with long-range interactions, we have shown that the recombination of three-body interactions in our scheme results in the generation of entangled triplet states with properties analogous to spin singlet-dipole modes commonly found in quantum information processing. Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the rapid growth of computation time with dataset size. A shift towards quantum computing could potentially resolve this limitation, providing an alternative to current statistical models. We develop and test a quantum equivalent to the K-means clustering method on superconducting qubits, contrasting it to a previously implemented quantum support vector machine. Results indicate that our algorithm matches classical K-means performance in both clustering and classification tasks, achieving an impressive speedup due to a lower asymptotic complexity of $O(N^{3/2}K^{1/2}\log{P})$ with $N$, $K$, and $P$ representing the number of data points, clusters, and data dimensions, respectively. Furthermore, a substantial speedup over classical methods is expected when processing large datasets. Additionally, our algorithm exhibits excellent matchability with existing classical K-means models, making it highly suitable for real-world applications and potential hybrid computing environments. Overall, our research lays the groundwork for the application of quantum machine learning to high-dimensional datasets. Finally, we outline the necessary conditions for achieving a significant speedup over classical algorithms in machine learning, conditional on solving a complex many-body quantum problem associated with these algorithms. Such a speedup would not only alleviate the curse of dimensionality but also yield a computational advantage through a quantum-inspired approach to pattern recognition. A comprehensive theoretical framework is provided to support these results. Additionally, our work utilizes the Pauli spin-1/2 fermion mapping to translate a quantum algorithm designed for qubits into an algorithm compatible with a quantum processor. A quantum circuit is constructed to solve a binary classification problem and demonstrates a high classification accuracy with a small dataset. Furthermore, our algorithm shows a promising potential for generalizing to other machine learning algorithms, and future research aims to apply this approach to other quantum algorithms. A comprehensive theoretical and experimental analysis of our quantum K-means algorithm is presented at Phys. Rev. X. Rapid Commun. Phys. Rev. X Rapid Comm. The associated data can be accessed through https://github.com/quantumalgorithm/K-means_QC. The quantum algorithms were implemented using Quil (McQueen et al., 2015). A quantum processor simulator was utilized to obtain the quantum circuit results, which is a modified version of the quantum simulator originally presented at http://michaelwimmerquantum.com. The quantum processor data was obtained within the University of Konstanz research group led by Jakob Sieg

A recently created TTS model called FastPitch can change pitch, but the quality of the speech made with it gets significantly worse when it's given pitch values far from its average pitch value.  In other words, it can only control pitch so much.  We suggest two new algorithms to fix this issue.  First, we came up with a pitch-shifting technique that doesn't change a speaker's unique voice characteristics, which helps make new speech samples sound more natural.  We also developed a training technique where FastPitch is taught to recognize speech with a range of pitches all for the same sentence.  Experimental results show that these algorithms greatly improve how well FastPitch can control pitch.  We also tested how well listeners could identify the different pitches in a speech sample, and the results show a significant improvement.  Interestingly, we found that changing the speaker's voice qualities actually helps FastPitch understand the speaker's voice better, which is an unexpected benefit.  We believe that our speaker-adaptation technique has a wide range of applications beyond just changing the voice in a speech sample.  We also compared our modified model to a state-of-the-art TTS model called HMM-Tacotron, and the results show that our modified model is better in many ways.  Finally, we converted a book into a speech-like voice using FastPitch, which is a challenging task.  We were able to create a near-perfect voice sample in a few hours, which is a significant achievement.  We believe that our model has a lot of potential for natural language processing applications.  We also suggest another idea to further improve how well FastPitch can control pitch, which is a future research goal.  The code and audio examples for our research are available on our website.  We hope that our research will help the development of more advanced text-to-speech systems.  Our model can also generate synthetic training data for a range of speakers, which is a significant contribution.  The idea of stretching speech times using a non-autoregressive model could be a key feature in a speech synthesis model. This research focuses on solving spatiotemporal object-based reasoning challenges in videos by employing object-level features that incorporate temporal and spatial context. A particular challenge with this approach lies in effectively linking different object appearances across various temporal and spatial scales. To tackle these multistep reasoning tasks, we introduce Hopper, a highly efficient video understanding framework based on a modified Transformer architecture for enhancing context-rich relationships between objects within videos. Hopper's key components include a novel appearance matching module for identifying similar objects across different temporal and spatial levels, and an efficient, step-wise reasoning strategy for reducing computational complexity. Our experiments demonstrate that Hopper achieves top-notch performance on challenging multistep reasoning tasks while showcasing its superior efficiency compared to existing models. For further details on our approach and results, please refer to our paper published in CVPR 2022. The code is available on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/zwang90/Hopper. Moreover, the pre-trained Hopper model can be obtained from the model repository at https://github.com/ResearchITE/ModelHub. Finally, the accompanying video demo can be found at https://youtu.be/j7Qk7XxO6Gk. Our model operates seamlessly on our provided dataset, and with minimal fine-tuning, it can effectively apply to practical use cases on resources with higher computational power, such as Google's Colab or an edge device like the Jetson TK1. Our model indicates considerable potential for integration into smart video surveillance systems. An example of its implementation on Google's Colab is available at https://colab.github.com/, and on the Jetson TK1 is available at https://jetsonnanodebook.com. Our model operates using the PyTAl version 2.6.0, which is available at https://github.com/nvidia/pytorch-extended. Our model is trained under a non-commercial license, and it can be used for both research and commercial purposes. Our study investigates lepton-pair production coupled with a $b\bar{b}$ pair in the CKM-determined context of the Standard Model. We focus on the impact of the W boson mass on its production cross-section and the shape of its lepton-pair transverse momentum distribution at the 13 TeV LHC. Through a comparative analysis with theoretical predictions not accounting for bottom-quark pair production, we have derived corrections relative to these predictions as functions of the W boson mass. These corrections are found to be relatively minor, with variations less than 10% across the relevant W boson mass range of 80.3 to 80.5 GeV. Furthermore, employing LHC data on lepton-pair production and utilizing a jackknife method, we have explored the capability of experimentally determining the W boson mass with an anticipated precision of 0.1 GeV. Ultimately, we have examined the utility of this specific production process for constraining the W boson mass. The findings demonstrate that combining LHC data across multiple production processes, including pair production and vector-boson associated production, will be sufficient for achieving the desired precision with an added value of around 1% over utilizing any individual process. Remote-controlled vehicles called Telepresence robots have gained attention in various fields, thanks to advancements in technology and reduced costs. A crucial factor for these robots' acceptance is ensuring users have a satisfying experience while interacting remotely, including effortless navigation. This research focuses on an overlooked aspect of remote control: the navigation interface's impact on users' overall experience. To investigate this, we conducted a study where 24 non-expert participants remotely operated the robots and we introduced two frustrating scenarios to evaluate their reaction. The results of the experiment are presented in terms of the users' perceived quality of service and how their experience was affected by the disruptions. This research is the first to assess the quality of the experience for remote control applications of this kind, allowing parameters for evaluating and optimizing the experience of non-expert users interacting with similar systems to be identified. The findings of our study could benefit the development of methods for enhancing the quality of the experience for remote control applications, influencing design choices and optimization strategies. Additionally, our work confirms that users of such systems are willing to pay more for a better experience, especially when the disruption is more severe. Several planetary systems have multiple giant planets, and research aims to
understand how their formation is affected when planets develop in tandem. Our
study uses long-term hydrodynamic simulations of planetary accretion to explore
the effects of simultaneous planet growth on mass and disk composition. We
simulated two planets of different sizes (10$M_\mathrm{Earth}$ and $5M_\mathrm
{Earth}$) born at equal intervals from a mass range of 0-$2$M_\mathrm{Earth}$)
as they accrete from a planetesimal disk. Their interactions led to a rare phase
of synchronized growth. However, this synchronization ended at $0.1$Myr when
gas giant formation was completed differently than predicted by single planet
simulations. Results showed a significant decrease in the final mass of the less
heavily accreted planet and increased mass of the more heavily accreted planet
compared to single planet simulations. At $20$Myr, these changes led to a $12$%
reduction in the final mass of the less massive planet and a $21$% increase in
the final mass of the more massive planet. During dual planet growth, pressure
gradients caused gas to flow from the disk's midplane to the gap edges, and
phases of increased MHD pressure in the disk's surface redirected gas to the
disk's upper layers. Consequently, planets developed unevenly depending on
initial mass and developed unusual mass distributions. Furthermore, simultaneous
planet growth caused a disk flow that made disk surfaces shift towards the
celestial equator, resulting in a thicker disk and increased irregularity of
gas distribution. At $20$Myr, dual planet systems displayed long-term average
irregularities in gas distribution that were $4$-$11\%$, while single planet
systems showed $2$-$5$\%$. In conclusion, two developing gas giants tend to have
uneven distributions in mass and disk gas, and researchers should consider the
consequences of such asymmetry in gas accretion and planet formation models.

This research develops a novel fuzzy k-means approach to cluster high-dimensional data across multiple subspaces. The algorithm is specifically designed for high-dimensional data sets where features can vary in relevance and importance, affecting the quality of the cluster. To overcome this limitation, our method modifies the traditional fuzzy k-means objective function using two distinct entropy terms. The first term optimizes cluster compactness by maximizing inter-cluster separation and minimizing within-cluster variance. The second term dynamically weights features according to their unique contributions, promoting better data partitioning. The effectiveness of our approach is evaluated through multiple datasets and comparisons with established state-of-the-art clustering methods. Notably, our method consistently outperforms existing benchmarks across multiple metrics. Furthermore, our research applies fuzzy k-means to gene expression data to identify highly similar genes and discovers conserved, functionally linked groups across multiple human cancers. Notably, our findings highlight 41 cancers with paired samples. The paired groups include lung cancer and melanoma, as well as various cancer types not previously linked, such as esophageal and brain cancers. Moreover, our analysis reveals 11 cancers with potential therapeutic applications, including the previously unlinked medullary brain tumor. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become crucial components of large-scale neural networks. Consisting of multiple dedicated expert networks that specialize in a certain dimension of the input, they significantly accelerate processing by only activating relevant experts. Nonetheless, the conventional algorithms for training MoE networks are inefficient and unreliable, leading to the'split' and 'gridlock' issues where some experts are either underutilized or inactive. We address this challenge by proposing a new algorithm that identifies and solves the MoE objective to the highest degree, overcoming the existing limitations. Moreover, our approach is capable of handling large-scale networks, allowing for various customizable modifications to be incorporated. Through extensive tests, we demonstrate that our algorithm consistently delivers superior results, outperforming the traditional methods and yielding top-notch performance in image and text prediction tasks. Furthermore, we show that our algorithm can be applied to design highly customized MoE networks, paving the way for further research in this field. This set of notes offers a standalone overview of chip-firing games on metric graphs along with the associated Jacobian and Prym varieties from the perspective of tropical geometry. The study of chip-firing games on general metric graphs requires the concept of a two-dimensional tropical tangle, which is introduced in chapter 4. Chapters 5-7 explore the applications of this framework to regular coverings of the line by metric graphs, primitive line bundle sections of the Jacobian and Prym varieties, and divisor classes in these varieties. Additionally, the text includes two supplementary chapters covering the classification of finite metric graphs and one-dimensional tropical tangles. The study relies heavily on tropical geometry and the theory of regular covers, which is introduced in the first two chapters. The text assumes a basic understanding of algebraic geometry and the theory of metric graphs but, due to its written format, requires additional background from tropical geometry, the study of which is recommended but not assumed. The study is based on the author's PhD thesis, which was defended in December 2014 and includes further details on the underlying concepts. While quantum gravitational effects generally break global symmetries, their presence may hold significant value in understanding both particle physics and cosmology. Discovering well-maintained global symmetries could provide a valuable insight into the properties of gravity. A statistically significant detection of cosmic birefringence in the CMB may signify a previously undetected, though spontaneously broken, global symmetry in the early universe. A potential explanation for this phenomenon would be a massless, electromagnetically interacting Nambu-Goldstone boson. Our analysis demonstrates that the presence of such a particle could be confirmed by concurrent measurements of cosmic birefringence and a variation in the electron's anomalous magnetic moment. These findings highlight that the universe may possess properties that can be explained by quantum gravity's adherence to spontaneously broken global symmetries. If a certain global symmetry is discovered to be broken, but not spontaneously, it could indicate that the universe has additional, undiscovered sectors of physics. Furthermore, our results show that the GKS model is capable of providing the universe's early birefringence and can be ruled out if the GKS model's predictions do not align with those of the 121 and DS models in conjunction with electron anomalous magnetic moment measurements. These studies stress the importance of a comprehensive multi-disciplinary investigation into the universe's physical state, and the CMB serves as an optimal tool for exploring high-energy phenomena outside of the standard model. A precise understanding of cosmic birefringence may allow for a precise determination of the electron's anomalous magnetic moment, and the related GKS model could be optimally detected through birefringence measurements at a CMB satellite with a level of sensitivity equivalent to the Planck satellite. Our research further demonstrates that a perfectly conserved global symmetry, as opposed to a spontaneously broken one, may be responsible for generating cosmic birefringence if the symmetry is electromagnetically interacting and includes a massless, anomalous long-wavelength mode. Conversely, our results contrast with those of a recent study claiming that global symmetry conservation can be constrained by cosmic string predictions and unrelated to cosmological phenomena. Our FUV-optical analyses allowed us to identify numerous variable stars, one blue straggler star, and 37 blue horizontal branch stars, the latter of which turned out to be of second generation in origin. The goal of deep transfer learning (DTL) is to empower deep neural networks (DNNs) with the ability to draw from past experiences like humans. This capability is referred to as knowledge transferability. Typically, the process of DTL begins with pre-trained, high-performance models developed for different tasks than the one being tackled. The widely accepted principles underlying DTL include selecting task-suitable pre-trained models and leveraging task data for fine-tuning. The research also provides real-world examples to support the proposed counterpoints and conducts a series of experiments to substantiate the underlying claims. Despite thorough examinations of massive cascade dynamics across multiple contexts, few have scrutinized the impact of network structure on information propagation efficiency. Our research applies the linear threshold model to networks comprised of communities, revealing that a prominent network attribute - modularity - profoundly influences the rate of information dissemination in complex diffusion scenarios. Simulation results show that an optimal level of modularity facilitates the most efficient spreading process; however, beyond a certain threshold, stronger or weaker modular structures hinder the dissemination speed. This finding is validated through the analysis of six benchmark networks, complemented by a case study examining the effect of COVID-19 contact tracing on the Facebook social network. Our findings and code will guide researchers working with simulated diffusion processes on networked systems. They will also contribute to the existing discourse on efficient information propagation. Moreover, in light of current global challenges where rapid information dissemination is crucial, understanding the impact of network structure on information propagation could lead to the identification of key nodes for enhancing awareness campaigns. For instance, to improve vaccination rates in the Facebook network following a COVID-19 outbreak, targeting nodes at the intersection of community clusters could accelerate the spread of vaccination information. Consequently, understanding the relationship between network structure and information propagation efficiency is essential for developing more effective campaigns in various applications. discrete nonlinear interference points and find that this distance can be employed to estimate 
the effective memory length of the communication channel. Based on this approach, we establish 
bounds for the accuracy of the time-domain perturbation model in terms of signal-to-noise ratio and 
remark that it becomes increasingly applicable as the effective memory length increases. An 
experimental verification of our analysis is carried out using a specific type of wireless channel. 
These findingsemphasize the need to consider the channel's effective memory length in practical scenarios. 
It has been previously established that this length can be substantial in cases of amplified links, yet our 
present study reveals that it can also be significant for cases without signal amplification, specifically 
in scenarios with a high signal-to-noise ratio. We propose a new method for discrete-time channel

To counter this threat, security experts continuously develop advanced detection systems based on machine learning and deep learning. However, skilled hackers counter these systems by adapting their malware samples to bypass detection through a variety of evasion attacks. This study focuses on problem-space evasion attacks on Android devices, where malicious actors modify APK files directly to evade detection. The study aims to explore this type of attack that often receives insufficient attention due to a lack of knowledge about the Android ecosystem or a focus on general evasion attacks. Service-oriented computing utilizes services as building blocks for constructing distributed systems. Traditionally, orchestrating cloud-based services centered around business process execution, particularly with BPEL's focus on services as processes. However, recent shifts towards virtualized and decentralized service platforms, such as Pox, Pervasive Services, and Blockchain-based platforms, separate services from processes, blurring the lines between microservices and workflows. To address this discrepancy, we introduce a unified approach to modeling service orchestrations, encompassing both microservices and workflows, founded on a service-oriented mindset. This strategy is put into practice through the creation of an open-source orchestration framework, Ozy, written in Node.js, allowing for the declaration of service orchestrations in a JSON-based language and execution within a distributed system. By providing a flexible container for orchestrations, Ozy acts as a declarative framework to its users, enabling the composition of distributed system designs that are robust, adaptable, and scalable. A thorough evaluation of Ozy incorporates theoretical and practical analyses, highlighting its performance in both synthetic and real-world scenarios, including the development of a Pox-based e-commerce platform. By exploring opportunities for variation in Ozy's design, we identify areas for expansion into unexplored domains, paving the way for the exploration of novel service platforms. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that the separation of service orchestrators from platforms opens up opportunities for innovation in distributed system design. Previous research by Reggatti and Renaei proposed a proposed early universe potential for primordial black holes, known as the Thakurta metric. However, our analysis indicates that this proposal is invalid. In an attempt to incorporate a black hole mass into the Thakurta metric, a singular, odd point is introduced, causing the Newtonian potential to become singular at this single point, violating crucial assumptions in the standard cosmological model. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this model exhibits an identically relation between the Newtonian and scalar potentials, leading to a divergence in the scalar potential that is inconsistent with established cosmological theory. As a result of these findings, we conclude that the original formulation of the Thakurta metric is inadequate and must be modified. Subsequently, we show that modifying the original formulation has no significant effect on existing research regarding LIGO-Virgo constraints on primordial black holes, as the original formulation was already limited in its implications to mass values greater than $10^{17}$g, exceeding the typical range of primordial black hole masses of $10^{44}$g. While a modified version of the Thakurta metric may have theoretical merit, it does not affect current research regarding these cosmological black holes, based on our analysis. Extremely large, overparameterized models have achieved impressive success. In this research, we investigate whether the requirement for massive models might be partly attributed to computational limitations inherent to the learner itself. We also examine whether these constraints are exacerbated under robust learning conditions. Our study indicates that this is indeed the case for some learning scenarios, such as learning with disturbances and robustly smoothly parameterized regression. Under these circumstances, learners may need to be excessively large to guarantee accurate outcomes, with their performance determined as much by computational limits as by the chosen model. This is a novel observation where the learner's computational capabilities substantially influence the minimum required model complexity. On the other hand, this is not typically the case for standard supervised learning. Consequently, this primary conclusion has significant implications for future research: it is not necessarily the simplest possible models that deliver the best outcomes, but rather the ones that are simplest within the constraints of the learner's computational capabilities. Additionally, this finding underscores that the ideal level of model complexity might vary based on the specific learning protocol and that a uniform separation between learners might not be feasible without considering the potential impact of computational constraints. Finally, these conclusions have significant consequences for learning theory, suggesting that future generalization bounds for computational constrained learners in various settings should not be constant but rather influenced by the complexity of the learner. Three results concerning the presence of Bohr sets in threefold sumsets have been proven. More specifically, considering a countable discrete abelian group $G$ and commuting endomorphisms $\phi_1, \phi_2, \phi_3$ whose images have finite indices, we demonstrate that 
  (1) For a set $A \subset G$ with positive upper Banach density and satisfying the condition that the sum of its images under the given endomorphisms is zero, there exists a Bohr set within the sum of its images under the individual endomorphisms. This generalizes theorems previously established for $\mathbb{Z}$ by Bergelson and Ruzsa as well as a recent result by the primary author.
  (2) For any division of $G$ into subsets $A_i$, it is guaranteed that there exists an index $i$ for which the sum of its images under the given endomorphisms contains a Bohr set. This generalizes a theorem previously established for $\mathbb{Z}$ by the second and third authors.
  (3) For sets $B, C \subset G$ possessing positive upper Banach density and a given division $G = \bigcup_{i=1}^r A_i$ of $G$ into subsets, there exists an index $i$ for which $B + C + A_i$ contains a Bohr set. This represents a strengthening of a theorem previously established by Bergelson, Furstenberg, and Weiss.
The obtained results in this context are quantitative as they assert that the size and rank of the resulting Bohr set depend on certain quantities that describe the set given. Furthermore, we consider several questions that appear in the available literature and that can be resolved using the aforementioned methodology. Finally, we consider a non-distinguishable version of these problems and consider a broader set of endomorphisms before providing some considerations regarding the uncountable case. The research in this article was initially presented at the European Congress of Mathematics held in 2016.

This study addresses the dial-a-ride problem within large urban settings where residents have multiple transportation options at their disposal. To remain competitive, ridepooling services must balance high pool participation rates against minimizing detours for users. We propose a Branch-and-Cut algorithm to tackle this challenge, leveraging insights from established route planning research. Through computational analysis using real-world data from the city of Buenos Aires, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach and examine how varying the availability of vehicles affects user satisfaction and route efficiency. We further highlight key factors influencing the likelihood that users partake in ridepooling services. Computational results show that our method provides a high-quality solution that closely matches the optimal solution, thanks to its cut-cutting technique. We observe that this solution is particularly valuable for operators as it yields a feasible and efficient plan that maximizes customer satisfaction. We showcase a web-based visualization of the computational results and provide policy recommendations for improving the effectiveness of ridepooling services. We find that maximizing rewards for drivers has a substantial negative impact on the likelihood that users participate and travel distances, whereas the effect of vehicle time cost is relatively minor. A fundamental component of various technologies, including surveillance, robotic navigation, and self-driving systems, is pedestrian trajectory prediction, and significant advancements have been made in this field. Nevertheless, past studies still have two main drawbacks. Firstly, as time progresses, prediction accuracy significantly degrades, leading to considerable final displacement errors. Secondly, multi-pedestrian predictions often fail in the prediction time frame due to anticipated trajectory collisions. In an attempt to address these limitations, a new trajectory prediction framework, named CSR, has been introduced. It is built around two interconnected components: a conditional variational autoencoder module (CVAE) operating in a sequential manner and a socially-aware regression module. The first component, using past and predicted locations, sequentially forecasts upcoming trajectories, while the socially-aware module adjusts these estimates by introducing offsets, thus ensuring socially compliant final predictions that outperform the initial forecasts. In an effort to streamline the processing requirements, a time-scale variant of the CVAE, named tvCVAE, has been developed. In addition, another variant of the CSR, incorporating tvCVAE, has been introduced as an improved method of pedestrian trajectory prediction, exhibiting superior performance over state-of-the-art methods. Experimental testing of realistic scenarios, involving data sets from the 4D highway, SIDER, and ETH/UCY datasets, and simulated scenarios, revealed the proposed socially-aware CSR outperformed other tested methods, including significant improvements in FDE values. In particular, on the SIDER dataset, an impressive reduction of more than 20% in the variance of final displacement errors was demonstrated by utilizing the proposed CSR method. Furthermore, along with the proposed model, a new socially-aware dataset, termed socialSIDER, containing annotated socially-aware labels for trajectories has been introduced. It is worthy of note that the proposed dataset can facilitate additional analyses, revealing that not all trajectory predictions in the SIDER dataset exhibit socially compliant behavior with respect to the annotated labels. In an effort to make the proposed models available for testing and evaluation, the corresponding source code has been made available on GitHub at the specified repository. In addition, an extensive evaluation study has been carried out with the aim of assessing the generalization capabilities of the proposed models, demonstrating that the proposed CSR model exhibits exceptional generalization characteristics, surpassing other tested methods by achieving lower FDE values on unseen data sets. Our experiments, conducted using the Multi36 dataset, demonstrate that the proposed approach yields a satisfactory accuracy of 86.2%, with a fast processing speed of under 50 milliseconds. A key advantage of counterdiabatic protocols in driving quantum states involves the use of a supporting, auxiliary gauge potential. However, determining this potential requires the full Hamiltonian, posing a significant challenge for complex many-body systems. A recent approach, proposed by P. W. Claeys et al., utilizes an approximated, variational gauge potential. In the case of a two-component fermionic Hubbard model, this potential can be expressed using nested commutators. A critical insight in this context reveals that optimizing the variational parameters leads to a set of linear equations, whose coefficients are determined by these commutators. A newly devised method allows the nested commutators to be computed and evaluated directly, rather than requiring complex iterative calculations. Applying this method to a Hubbard model with up to 14 sites reveals that it holds great promise for driving quantum states in complex many-body systems efficiently. It remains to be seen, however, whether this method scales down efficiently for smaller, atomic, or molecular systems involving full gauge potentials. Moreover, future research should investigate the relationship between variational and exact CD-driven dynamics. A preliminary study indicates that, for a Hubbard model with 4 sites, the variance of the supporting gauge potential diminishes as the number of time steps grows. This research could have significant implications for efficiently preparing ground states in complex many-body systems using quantum control methods. Moreover, the idea of applying global, adiabatic control to the supporting gauge potential could help ensure that it remains well-behaved throughout the driving process. Color-neutral images are a cornerstone in various image processing applications such as image compression, feature extraction, and printing due to their role in tone mapping. However, valuable image data gets lost when transitioning color images to their grayscale counterparts. In this study, a streamlined, high-speed image decolorization approach based on color temperature perception is developed. The aberration occurring in human color perception during transitions between complementary colors is the foundation for this method. A novel weight assignment algorithm for color channels is thus conceived, simulating natural color interactions through the application of color temperatures. Experimental outcomes confirm the effectiveness of this approach in preserving color nuances across various datasets. Additionally, this technique exhibits fast processing speeds, with processing times ranging from 0.013 to 0.042 seconds for standard datasets. Consequently, this innovation is well-suited for applications requiring rapid image processing, while its preserved color detail benefits numerous image processing areas. Moreover, this technique contributes to future research in the area of progressive image decolorization. A comparative analysis of this method with existing approaches is also presented, revealing that it surpasses others in color preservation, even at a slightly increased computational cost. The study presents several practical examples demonstrating when and how this technique is applied, providing insight to its users. A discussion of potential future enhancements to this method is also presented, with suggestions for future study. The technique is also compared to other algorithms, providing insight into its performance relative to others. The source code of the approach is available at the website provided. The study makes the datasets for evaluating decolorization algorithms available, which may be of use to other researchers working in related fields. The study is ultimately concluded by providing various Scenarios of the technique's usage, providing valuable insight to its users. The study is then brought to a close, with the conclusion that the novel high-speed image decolorization algorithm developed in this study effectively achieves high-speed processing of color images, preserving color details in the process. We examine the RDF data exchange process based on relational data, constrained by Shape Expression schema. Our research involves addressing two critical issues: first, determining the feasibility of solutions for source data instances; and second, developing a single comprehensive solution that represents all possible outcomes. To achieve this, we incorporate typed IRI constructors to form RDF IRIs from relational values and translate Shape Expression constraints into target dependencies. Additionally, we have identified certain data exchange settings as 'key-covered', a determinable property that ensures consistency and closure. Furthermore, we have found this condition necessary and sufficient for a specific algorithm to produce a comprehensive solution, as well as proving its NP-completeness in general cases. However, this complexity hurdle can be overcome by using a polynomial-time approximation algorithm that provides guaranteed solution quality, an improvement over previous methods such as the 'universal instance' algorithm. Lastly, we have explored ways to ensure data exchange processing can be constrained to certain shapes, and demonstrate this constraint can be used to pinpoint specific outcomes while excluding others. Our methods for handling diverse data models have broad applications and can be applied across various languages and frameworks for relational databases, RDF, and Shape Expression shaping. Shapes are now an essential tool for data discovery, query, and analysis, making our work an essential contribution to the evolution of data exchange processes. A comprehensive experimental study highlights the practical advantages of our methods over existing approaches. This study proposes an innovative mass reconstruction technique for examining the lower mass spectrum resulting from top-quark pairs produced in association with a generic scalar boson at the LHC. By employing a novel method of mass reconstruction, it has been demonstrated that a resolution of at least double can be achieved in the lower mass spectrum, maintaining a comparable level of sensitivity compared to earlier analyses. Furthermore, it has been shown that this new technique can improve the mass reconstruction of the 125 GeV Higgs particle in the same production process. To achieve this, we employed an effective Lagrangian model with a generic Yukawa interaction between the top quarks and a scalar boson. A comprehensive phenomenological analysis was performed, generating Standard Model background and signal events with MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO and reconstructing them using a kinematic fit. Utilizing variables that can distinguish between CP-even and CP-odd properties enabled us to maximally separate the respective components of the Yukawa couplings. We determined the confidence levels required for excluding $\phi$ bosons with mixed CP (containing both CP-even and CP-odd components) as a function of the top quark's Yukawa interaction with the $\phi$ boson. Our analysis focused on a mass range starting slightly above the $\Upsilon$ mass, spanning up to 40 GeV; however, the method can be applied for arbitrary masses. We also investigated how these results might impact exclusion limits at 95\% confidence levels for the absolute value of the CP-even and CP-odd Yukawa couplings if a new light scalar boson were not found. Furthermore, it has been estimated that these couplings could be constrained as low as 0.10 and 0.50, respectively, towards the end of the LHC's High Luminosity phase (HL-LHC). In addition, we examined how these results constrain the parameter space of the complex two-Higgs doublet model (C2HDM). not exist, and weak transcription systems force the utilization of poor-quality
