Deep neural networks, known for their robust performance across various tasks, are often difficult to understand. This interpretability issue severely hampers their use in critical areas like medical imaging. A promising approach, neural tangent kernel, offers some level of interpretation by mirroring a kernel machine's properties. In an effort to enhance classification and layer understanding, we've developed a novel network that combines multiple neural tangent kernels - one for each layer - as opposed to earlier work focusing on a single kernel to represent the entire network. We validate the effectiveness of this model on two datasets, revealing that it successfully reveals the intricate relationships between the network's layers and its predictive abilities. Furthermore, we utilize a kernel-based clustering technique to evaluate the uniqueness of trained neural networks, given their similarity to a kernel machine. Finally, we explore the possibilities of utilizing our method as an auxiliary tool for aiding training a neural network from scratch. All the code and proceedings can be found at the provided link. We train and test our networks on various image classification tasks, such as CIFAR and MNIST, using a simplified version of the Poisson kernel to maximize the likelihood of our kernel weights. This auxiliary approach to training has the potential to accelerate the training process of deep neural networks. Overall, our method offers an innovative understanding of the neural network architecture by visualizing the relationships between the network's layers and its classification capabilities, thus providing added value to the training process. Additionally, we suggest that the training loss of neural tangent kernels can serve as a suitable evaluation metric for image classification tasks. Importantly, the findings of our clustering procedure indicate that the training of neural networks is nonconvex, providing written confirmation of a similar result reported by Jastrzebski et al. in their 2019 paper. In addition to the nonconvex nature of the training process, our results also suggest that the models selected by the clustering procedure exhibit relatively modest improvements in performance, with some exceptions. Consequently, the main area of improvement of our method lies in offering a novel and significant understanding of the neural network architecture by visualizing the relationships between the network's layers and its classification capabilities, thus providing added value to the training process. In summary, the models selected by the clustering procedure exhibit desirable properties but limited performance improvement. Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of correlations remains a significant unresolved issue. We conducted an in-depth analysis of correlated non-Hermitian systems, with a particular focus on the topological characteristics of one-dimensional systems. Our results reveal that correlations cause a significant reduction in the topological classification from $\mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ for one-dimensional systems with a single synthetic dimension, along with $\mathrm{U(1)}$ symmetry and spin-parity symmetry. We propose an approach to identify topological states in correlated systems through symmetry-based classification. Furthermore, our approach also applies to systems with a single physical edge, thereby predicting the existence of protected modes, counterintuitive exceptions to robust edge mode protection, and the potential for correlation-induced emergence of bulk topological orders at zero or finite temperatures. Our research explores the implications of correlations on the properties of systems with synthetic dimensions and contributes to the understanding of topological phenomena in both quantum and classical systems. Additionally, our work may also be relevant to recently developed quantum devices based on artificial dimensions. The approaches we established can be adapted for broader applications, such as identifying topological orders in multi-component systems with multiple synthetic dimensions. A generalized approach for topological classification of systems with multiple components remains an open question and is currently under investigation. Our current research builds upon our earlier findings where we identified acoustic characteristics essential to synthetic speech perception as responsive to speaker gender and social status. We now investigate the perception of these characteristics in response to the speaker's social background. A human evaluation of the acoustic features and characteristics associated with the speaker's social status has led to the conclusion that the voice's overall quality holds greater importance than its tone. A listening test has revealed that the combination of voice quality and gender characteristics yields more natural-sounding synthetic speech, where the voice quality characteristics alone result in speech that sounds somewhat artificial despite being perceptibly clearer. This implies that voice quality characteristics encode essential aspects of a speaker's social characteristics, whereas the tone characteristics are insufficient for such information. Furthermore, it appears that the voice quality characteristics can effectively vary with the speaker's social status, but only to a limited extent. Consequently, it is suggested that voice quality characteristics could be used to represent speakers' social attributes in a restricted manner, especially those attributes affecting one's communication skills. Interestingly, our evaluation also reveals that the voice quality characteristics are perceived as influencing not only the speaker's social status but also their personality. Consequently, it is proposed that voice quality characteristics could serve as a multifaceted expression of speaker characteristics, where voice being an intrinsic aspect affects not only one's communication skills but also their overall personality. A possible strategy for incorporating these characteristics into synthetic speech is explored. Future research should delve into a deeper comprehension of the relationship between the voice quality characteristics and the speaker's social attributes, particularly those attributes not affecting one's communication skills. Such a study could potentially lead to a broader comprehension of how voice is perceived as an expression of speaker characteristics, paving the way for developing novel methods in voice synthesis. Ultimately, it is anticipated that incorporating the voice quality characteristics into synthetic speech may lead to more engaging, dynamic, and character-rich voice experiences. A critical consideration in such an implementation would be ensuring a balance between accurately conveying speaker characteristics and avoiding an overwhelming number of voice changes. A more exhaustive discussion of these implementation details, along with our evaluation of the implementation, can be found in the original paper. A listening test designed to gain human insights into synthetic speech, where speakers are not aware that they are listening to synthetic speech, has been conducted and the results have been made available for the academic community. A follow-up study aims to investigate how voice quality affects various speech modifiers such as filler words, hesitations, and prosodic stress in order to further refine our understanding of how voice quality impacts speaker characteristics. A comprehensive study examines the connection between residual entropy and viscosity using an extensive, high-accuracy dataset. The concept was first introduced by Rosenfeld in 1977; this research demonstrates that scaling leads to a nearly linear correlation between residual entropy and reduced viscosity across a broad range of substances (argon, methane, CO2, and several others) with different potential energy well shapes. The initial "universal" correlation of Rosenfeld, however, falls short for substances with third-order forces, though a revised, more robust approach does successfully relate zero-temperature isothermal compressibility to viscosity. To further develop these connections, a team of researchers developed a principle that is based on the geometric mean of pairwise interactions, leading to a new set of "universality classes" of substances that demonstrate promising correlations with both viscosity and residual entropy. By using a series of pairwise interactions, it is possible to achieve an average deviation of less than 4% from the predicted "universal" phase-space filling contribution to residual entropy. Ultimately, this research aims to facilitate more precise thermodynamic characterization of complex fluids. It is hoped that these connections can provide valuable insights into molecular behavior and properties. To support the work described in the publication, an open-source code (isomolecular) is provided, allowing users to generate phase-space filling contributions for simple models and molecules. Additionally, a dataset (RDF-Dataset) containing a collection of radial distribution functions, their associated radial distribution function ratios, and pseudo-one-body potentials is available for the substances studied. Both the isomolecular code and the RDF dataset can be accessed through the GitHub platform at https://github.com/MolecularThermodynamics. Lastly, a supporting library (java-universal-idealized-properties) offers a set of pre-calculated "idealized" properties that can be used for property extrapolations, which can also be found on the GitHub platform at https://github.com/MolecularThermodynamics. A supporting demo for the isomolecular code and the universal idealized properties can be found at https://r-schnabel.github.io/Isomolecular-IDE. It is envisioned that the further development of this research will lead to significant potential applications in the modeling and simulation of substances with third-order forces, potentially enabling the extrapolation of thermodynamic properties beyond current numerical bounds. The possibility that our Universe undergoes a periodic cycle of expansion, driven by ΛCDM models separated by phases of inflation and radiation dominance, is investigated. The ΛCDM periodic cosmology is based on the hypothesis that both inflation and the current accelerated expansion could be caused by the same dark energy component. When plotting the matter density parameter Ωm against the radiation density parameter Ωr in phase space, a closed trajectory is observed that indicates the Universe follows a periodic pattern. The research reveals that this cycle likely began around z ∼ 50, suggesting a need for a more accurate theory of inflation that can account for the timing of the transition from the matter-dominated phase to the radiation-dominated phase, as well as a reappraisal of the ages of the radiation and dark energy components. The presence of a periodic pattern leads to a predictable pattern of overproduction of light elements, which occurs at the transition from the matter-dominated phase to the radiation-dominated phase and causes some particles to be produced out of equilibrium, leading to anomalies. The scenario is also examined in the context of the baryogenesis process and possible violations of entropy conservation, which could provide an alternative explanation for the low value of the baryon-to-photon ratio and the relationship between matter and radiation densities. Furthermore, the periodic pattern of the Hubble volume, which is a universal characteristic of ΛCDM periodic models, is used to determine the period duration and amplitude modulation. The research also compares the characteristics of flat and curved spatially periodic models, revealing that the periodic scenario is feasible with the current values of model parameters. Finally, potential observations are proposed that could reveal the occurrence of ΛCDM periodic cosmology, including searches for patterns in light element abundance, anomalies in cosmic microwave background data, detection of magnetic fields, and observations of galaxy distributions and types. The possibility that certain phases of the ΛCDM periodic cosmology could correspond to the so-called "E-moment" of the Universe, proposed by Zel'dovich, is also explored. The possible connections between ΛCDM periodic models and other well-established concepts in modern cosmology, including primordial black holes and violations of parity, symmetry, and time-reversal symmetries are also examined. A summary of the main research findings is presented in the paper. A new superdeterministic theory of quantum mechanics known as Invariant-set theory is being proposed. This idea brings concepts from areas like chaos theory and dynamical systems into the study of quantum foundations. Despite this potential, developing a clear hidden-variable model for it has been a challenge, making it hard to properly evaluate. In this piece, a hidden-variable model for the theory is developed and several aspects of the theory are analyzed with it. Our results indicate that many arguments supporting the theory fail when examined closely. The model itself displays superdeterministic and nonlocal properties with a quantum state, and when applied to the Bell experiments, it predicts the Bell inequalities will not hold. It also generates predictions consistent with quantum mechanics that align with those from random hidden variables. The model demonstrates that random hidden variables can account for long-standing puzzles of quantum mechanics as much as superdeterministic theories can. Using a hidden-variable model for the theory also reveals issues with an argument the theory uses in favor of superdeterminism. The theory's requirement that quantum systems remain in an extremely small part of the possible configuration space doesn't apply when examining individual systems because the theory describes a single trajectory for a system's development. This means that claims based on examining collections of many systems to justify superdeterminism are unfounded. Finally, attempts to extend the theory to general relativistic settings are inconsistent with basic notions of causality and therefore invalid. Theories that include superdeterminism and nonrandom hidden variables generally fail to incorporate any meaningful notion of causality. As a result, the idea that superdeterminism is a viable quantum theory remains tenable but remains an open question. Further research is needed to fully evaluate its merits. Our focus is on NN execution within devices with limited resources; thus, we suggest a Compact Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture. This CNN features (i) reduced computation requirements via limited multiplications. (ii) an economical use of model parameters to minimize memory usage. Inspired by recent discoveries, we explore lattice fermions as an alternative to traditional bosonic approaches in the study of two-dimensional quantum systems. The inherent properties of lattice fermions, such as their inherent anti-particles, influence the behavior of lattice models on random lattices or in the presence of quantum magnetic fields. Specifically, we demonstrate that lattice fermions exhibit a unique critical property characterized by the accumulation of fermionic holes on lattice borders, distinct from the conventional Kosterlitz-Thouless transition observed in bosonic models. The suppression of double occupance and anti-particle dependence render fermionic approaches distinct from their bosonic counterparts. The efficacy of fermionic methods is further illustrated through the solution of an isotropic spin-1/2 XX model on a quasi-crystalline lattice, known to exhibit a topological phase at finite temperature, where the topological content is controlled by the number of fermionic holes. Theoretical predictions are experimentally validated via 2D imaging of free-moving Dirac fermions within a non-equilibrium Bose-Einstein condensate via phase-contrast microscopy, demonstrating an alternative route to the realization of 2D topological phases beyond the bosonic paradigm. The study provides essential insights into the thermodynamics of interacting 2D fermions on random lattices or in the presence of gauge field fluctuations, shedding light on the long-standing fermion-sign problem, a critical challenge in Monte-Carlo simulations of lattice fermions. The analytical solutions obtained facilitate a quantitative understanding of the systematic deviations between fermionic and bosonic models, where the magnitude of such departures is found to depend on the inverse temperature relative to the fermionic zero-temperature topological gap energy. Notably, fermionic approaches outperform bosonic methods by an energy scale that can be as large as the decoding temperature in topological quantum computing, where the former may realize topological phases more efficiently. The findings of this study contribute to a significant advancement in the understanding of the fermion-sign and lay the groundwork for future investigations of various quantum phases and phenomena employing fermionic lattice models as an alternative to bosonic methods. Additionally, such models offer valuable prospects in the investigation of quantum phases and phenomena amenable to simulation both in and out of equilibrium. In recent years, the needs of embedded systems have grown more complex.  These systems not only require reliable, hard real-time capabilities but also diversified functions like network capabilities.  Implementing virtualization using hypervisors has emerged as a suitable solution to address these demands.  Unfortunately, existing hypervisors, which were designed with general-purpose computing in mind, come with a substantial system overhead that is not suitable for mixed criticality embedded real-time systems.  Moreover, the schedulers within these hypervisors, which rely on past concepts, neglect the distinct characteristics of embedded real-time systems that observe strict real-time guarantees.  As a result, they fail to effectively manage the local scheduler directly as intended.  Furthermore, the current approaches to virtualization do not adequately account for the unique requirements of embedded systems, such as guaranteed real-time capabilities and network capabilities.  To address these shortcomings, we propose a new hypervisor called T-Visor, which enables virtualization of embedded real-time systems by incorporating a contextual creation mechanism for virtual nodes and an integrated scheduler that directly manages the virtual nodes.  Our scheduler, which is designed with embedding principles in mind, ensures that the demands of embedded real-time systems are met.  T-Visor has also been optimized to provide a dynamic memory management mechanism that enhances cache efficiency between virtual nodes.  To gauge its effectiveness, we conducted comprehensive evaluations of T-Visor by comparing its performance with Xen.  To validate its practicality, we introduced it into the Linux kernel and achieved promising results on an ARM-based tablet.  Our testing revealed that T-Visor surpassed Xen in both system overhead and real-time guarantee capabilities.  Moreover, T-Visor demonstrated the ability to provide real-time guarantees and network capabilities to embedded real-time systems.  Ultimately, our results demonstrate that T-Visor is an suitable solution for implementing virtualization in embedded real-time systems.  Our contribution is two-fold:  Firstly, we propose a novel hypervisor called T-Visor, which addresses the shortcomings of existing hypervisors by developing a direct management mechanism for the local scheduler.  Secondly, we propose an integrated scheduler that embeds the capabilities of separate kernel components, such as network cards and real-time operating systems, within a single scheduler.  To achieve this, we leverage the contextual creation mechanism for virtual node creation and employ a polling-based scheduling strategy.  Our implementation of these innovations yields T-Visor, which far surpasses Xen in terms of system overhead and real-time guarantee capabilities.

When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are fitted with sensors that can accurately track the direction of gravity. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations naturally remains consistent, allowing for a basic assumption to be made when processing panoramic stitches. Current panoramic stitching techniques focus primarily on minimizing displacement or rotational discrepancies. However, minimizing rotational discrepancies often results in excessive warping of the image baseline, while minimal displacement discrepancies may lead to visual distortions due to differences in baseline widths. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of "minimal solutions" to achieve the best possible approximation of images with minimal displacement discrepancies. To implement this concept effectively, we develop specialized metrics for synthetic and bosch filters that can efficiently calculate the minimal displacement discrepancies within O(nJ) complexity, where n represents the number of images and J represents the number of cameras. Furthermore, we adjust the Lucas-Kanade update method in patch-based stitching to minimize displacement discrepancies. To validate our approach, we conduct comprehensive experiments using artificial images, in-depth focus-based synthetic images, and numerous real-world pairwise and multipair datasets across varied sensor resolutions and field-of-view differences. These experiments demonstrate that the proposed method consistently yields superior results, reducing warping and distortion by up to 5% and 2%, respectively, when compared to conventional panoramic stitching techniques. Additionally, we cross-validate our approach through practical applications, showcasing its potential by rendering 3D geometric data and detecting prominent landmarks within panoramic stitches. By prioritizing minimal displacement discrepancies, we have successfully addressed the challenge of achieving high-quality panoramic stitches with reduced warping and distortion. To promote widespread adoption, we release the source code and datasets associated with this project to facilitate future advancements in panoramic stitching. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/nghia-dv/phd-thesis. The dataset can be found at https://drive.google.com/drive/folder/?view/asorg. Embedded links are also provided. We examine if controllers obtained using model-based Reinforcement Learning, which employs an environment model to find the optimal policy, remain robust and adaptable when dealing with slight environmental variations. Building upon the concept from PILCO, a method for probabilistic policy search, our approach demonstrates that constraining the uncertainty in the Gaussian Process model's dynamics has a beneficial effect on policy updates and results in more resilient controllers. In addition, our method allows for a reduction in the model's uncertainty in the observed state, which is obtained via kernel-based interpolation. We support our technique with theoretical evidence and experimental results from multiple continuous control tasks. Moreover, we show that our method can effectively recognize and respond to unexpected situations in a dynamic environment. Our approach represents a crucial step towards creating reliable automation systems that incorporate learning and adaptability. Detailed information on this research, including videos and code, is available at http://caesar.melanche.com. The findings were presented at the IJCAI 2017 workshop on Risk, Ambiguity And Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence. A related paper was also published at the AAAI 2017 symposium on Intelligent and Interactive Systems. A comprehensive version of this research was published in Transactions on Machine Learning and Automation. We present a multi-layer quiver in this paper, using which we can build a higher dimension (n+1) algebras of infinite complexity from a given n-dimensional algebra. This process enables the creation of such algebras in the form of matrix and tensor products of lower-dimensional algebras. Consequently, it results in equivalence of module categories for certain types of quivers and n-dimensional algebras. Furthermore, we can use multi-layer quivers to construct n-dimensional Gelfand-MacDonald duality's unitary highest weight modules. In addition, we showed that an n-dimensional linear algebra can be represented as a n+1 dimension slice of a higher dimension slice algebra, with the latter's module category equivalent to that of the former. Lastly, we introduced the concept of a weakly semi-simple algebra and utilized multi-layer quivers to create such an example. In a notable case (n=2), we can build a weakly semi-simple and unital algebra from non-constant functions. This example demonstrates, in contrast to conventional belief, that a linear algebra's module category is not fully determined by its subalgebra. To achieve this, we constructed a universal slice algebra with the slice algebras as full subcategories and demonstrated that this slice algebra's module category is the maximal extension possible while retaining the category's determination. This research notably resolves conjectures from the studies of Yu and Xie-Yang-Yu. To facilitate further study, we have made available the relevant Mathematica code at the specified repository. The code generates the quivers, creates the respective algebras, and computes their module categories and characters. Furthermore, it also produces the Gelfand-MacDonald duality's unitary highest weight modules characters for given types of quivers. Both experimental and theoretical findings are presented. The system also exhibits complex attractors such as invariant circles and chaotic motion, identifiable through rotation numbers and Lyapunov exponents. The chaotic motion includes patterns similar to those of H\'{e}non and Lorenz systems, arising either from a period-doubling sequence or from the disruption of stable circles near the unstable trajectory of the system's escape route. The escape route, determined by the unstable manifold of the system, is found to play a crucial role in the system's dynamics. The investigation includes numerical estimates of Lyapunov exponents and chaos intensity for various attractors, as well as novel visualizations of the 3D H\'{e}nen map's dynamics. This study serves as a foundation for exploring more complex systems, such as those involving COPA operations. The new visualizations may inspire further research into 3D dynamics and could lead to applications in modeling escape mechanisms in molecules. The gravitational field's instantaneous state can be determined using the gravitational holonomy, which is based on the holonomy of the spin connection. While traditionally calculated as a multi-part complex object, recent advancements yield an alternative, simplified version, expressing the gravitational holonomy as a single, unified complex object. Focusing on its linearized form allows for the analysis of its physical implications through the study of gauge invariant variables linked to the gravitational wave's polarization modes. By taking a geometric approach, the canonical Poisson brackets of these variables can be derived, ultimately leading to the identification of the central elements that compose the canonical structure of the theory. Moreover, the results can be extended to describe the finite-action canonical form of the gravitational holonomy. It has been found that this form retains all the characteristics of a smooth, finite action theory while incorporating the symplectic structure of the phase space. Interestingly, this outcome is compatible with the microstate entropy binding the polarization degrees of freedom of any gravitational wave, revealing that the instantaneous gravitational field possesses an inherent quantum nature. Most notably, this discovery includes the case of Einstein's general relativity where the gravitational holonomy's action can be determined, yielding a novel perspective: that the gravitational field's instantaneous state arises from a non-trivial, quantum-based ultralocal action. The results of our analysis indicate that any theory based on the gravitational holonomy, whether linear or non-linear, possesses a necessarily quantum-based, ultralocal action. In the process, the results can be extended to the case of spin-2 fields, encompassing a broad range of gravitational models, including general relativity. Additionally, the results provide a potential link between the study of gravity and recent developments in the canonical formulation of quantum field theory, potentially complementing the traditional wavefunction renormalization approach to quantum gravity. Ultimately, the outcome points to a promising, unexplored path of investigation: that of identifying phase space actions that lead to symplectic reductions as a novel approach to understanding the non-perturbative nature of gravity and other spin-2 theories. By exploring this uncharted road, it may be possible to establish a deeper connection between quantum gravity and canonical quantum field theory. Moreover, the recently established relationship between the gravitational wave polarization modes and the gauge invariant variables linked to the gravitational holonomy opens a promising avenue of investigation: that of identifying polarization schemes that could potentially describe the canonical structure of the gravitational field as a viable approach to understanding the non-perturbative nature of gravity and other spin-2 theories. As the clock undergoes a period of relaxation, the particle's spin fluctuates within a plane defined by its initial direction. These fluctuations impact the Larmor clock's precession, with the average relaxation time affecting the particle's apparent tunneling time. This relationship allows for the derivation of the particle's tunneling time in terms of the average relaxation time. This framework provides an opportunity to investigate the influence of spin fluctuations on the tunneling phenomenon. With a well-established method for measuring the average relaxation time, the effect of spin fluctuations can be quantitatively assessed. This discussion offers a novel perspective on the topic, and our model adheres to the principles of quantum mechanics as outlined by Cohen and Philpott. Learning with an ever-growing number of categories poses significant challenges. The task becomes particularly demanding when models need to learn online after seeing each example only once. Current techniques often struggle to adapt or come with restrictions like non-calculable components and memory requirements. To overcome these issues, we propose an innovative approach – the fully differentiable ensemble method – which allows us to efficiently train multiple neural networks in a single end-to-end process. The proposed technique boasts the best-in-class results on CIL datasets, including CLINC and HCL, including scenarios with 100 classes and 55 tasks. Additionally, we provide a step-by-step guide on replicating these results. The source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/indigoportfolio/neo. To the best of our knowledge, this method offers a novel contribution to the continually learning community. The model employs a common parameter set, known as an "online ensemble," to store class-specific representations. To handle class appearances uniquely, we leverage a differentiable entropy-based mechanism. The approach dynamically adds new classifiers to the ensemble using an adversarial technique, allowing the method to learn without any preknowledge or memory from previous tasks. The model demonstrates effective performance by retaining old classes' representations while quickly adapting to new categories. To achieve this, we employ feature-variational dropout to encourage the formation of distinct representations for each class within the ensemble. The results show that each component of the proposed method significantly impacts the overall performance. To facilitate knowledge distillation, the method allows for a soft exchange of representations between classes, enabling a better transfer of old classes' knowledge to new tasks. The method's ability to efficiently learn multiple neural networks is enabled by the use of mean pooling. The proposed approach effectively handles scenarios with 100 classes and 55 tasks, including a challenging dataset with corrupting perturbations. To ensure that the ensemble classes are correctly identified, we employ label noise cleaning, maintaining an accurate classification of old classes throughout the learning process. The proposed method is widely applicable in various scenarios, including a distributed learning setup where knowledge distillation is used to improve the learning process. To validate the method's generalizability, we tested it on a challenging scenario with corruping perturbations and partially seen classes, yielding results superior to those obtained by state-of-the-art approaches. By associating flat generalized connections with a metric, researchers gain new insights into Einstein's vacuum equations and their solutions in four-dimensional Riemannian geometry. This work shows that Einstein's vacuum equations can be formulated as a result of generalized torsion. The challenge of pions, having no electrical charge, is discussed along with their historical experimentation, leading to significant breakthroughs in the field. The pion-nucleon scattering length, determined experimentally through various methods, is shown to be around -23.4 with a margin of 4.0. The isospin invariant pion-nucleon coupling constant, calculated using the pion scattering length and mass, is estimated to be around 10 GeV$^{-2}$. The empirical pion-nucleon potential, developed with contributions from multiple sources, is primarily isoscalar with a depth of about 100 MeV at the nucleon's half-shell point, and is notably influenced by the $\Delta$ resonance at an energy of 1232 MeV. The pion-nucleon gauge theory, achieved in the 1960s, is noted for its success. The consequences for the hadron mass spectrum, as suggested by a theory known as the Kleinert-Scherrer model, are also discussed. The pion-nucleon coupling constant's relationship to the mass of the Higgs boson is also explored. The pion-nucleon coupling constant's relative lack of understanding is attributed to its unique characteristics, such as the pion having no electrical charge and being deeply immersed in the nucleus. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions dating back to 2010. As part of the CMS detector, the silicon pixel detector forms the forefront layer in the tracking system, responsible for navigating the collision area and identifying crucial parameters via its forward nature. With upgrades in the LHC luminosity and increased demand for higher reconstruction capabilities, the detector will undergo significant modifications along with the CPU boosting. Research has been conducted on the pilot blades of the CMS pixel detector under the CMS Pixel Detector Pilot Blade Software initiative, focusing on the reconstruction algorithms and their performance in single and dual track scenarios. Results indicate that the pilot blades achieve 95% hit finding rate, marking 1 hit finding sparsity, with the mean hit position error under 10 micrometers and the mean track position error under 0.3 millimeters. Moreover, the pilot blades demonstrate average track multiplicities of 2.2 and the majority of the reconstructed tracks are primary, accounting for 90% of the total tracks. Analysis of the noise hits shows that 99.9% of the noise hits occur either singly or doubly, with their position errors exceeding 0.5 millimeters. Also found was that the pilot blades process an average of 685 events per second at 10 kilohertz input rate, with only 0.2% failed reconstructions. Studies on the electromagnetic calorimeter indicate that the pilot blades can accurately identify photons with transverse energy greater than 2 gigaelectronvolts. It is further observed that the pilot blades can analyze tau decays with predicted efficiencies of up to 95%, with some influence from the pixel detector noise, which is expected to decline to less than 0.1% with the pilot blade software modifications. In line with this, the pilot blade software modifications bring about the disappearance of single hit sparsity, whereas mean hit position errors decrease to less than 5 micrometers. Similarly, the mean track position error decreases to less than 0.1 millimeters. By leveraging the increased CPU capabilities and the proposed detector upgrades, the CMS pixel detector will strive to navigate the expected increase in luminosity in phase one run. This will involve the pixel detector providing track and vertex information up to the rapidity of 3 and will remain a crucial component of the CMS detector under the LHC at its planned energy of 14 TeV until the conclusion of its planned program in 2035.

We demonstrate SQUID's capabilities by showcasing its implementation in a standard binary classification task from the widely-used MNIST dataset. Notably, the quantum model's performance is found to be inferior to its classical counterpart, highlighting the significance of a well-designed evaluation framework in quantum machine learning research. Additionally, an investigation into potential causes for the subpar performance is provided. By extending the concept of slant submanifolds to semi-slant ones, this study delves into their geometry in both Sasakian and cosymplectic manifolds. Key findings indicate a limitation on semi-slant warped products in Sasakian manifolds. On the other hand, non-trivial semi-slant warped products have been discovered in cosymplectic manifolds, and several foundational results have been obtained, including a defining characteristic of such semi-slant warped products. Additional outcomes include descriptions of two types of invariant semi-slant distributions, corresponding geodesic equations, first integrals, and the curvature tensor's invariants. Furthermore, counterexamples have been identified verifying several hypothetical outcomes proposed in the field. In particular, this study disproves a conjecture regarding the existence of slant warped products in cosymplectic manifolds and also shows that a proposed classification of such objects is incomplete. In addition, it's demonstrated that a proposed claim about left-symmetric product on certain manifolds is incorrect. Ultimately, a question is raised regarding the existence of semi-slant warped products in Lorentzian Sasakian manifolds. Specifically, such objects do not exist in a particular example, namely the Kassandras space, which has a negative curvature. This raises the possibility that a conjecture regarding the existence of slant warped products in this class of manifolds may be similarly disproven. Moreover, given the insufficiency of previous results in this direction, a research question is posed regarding the existence of slant submanifolds in Lorentzian Sasakian manifolds generally. Such detectors could range in weight from grams to kilograms and could detect nuclear recoil events triggered by various factors including neutron scattering, CEvNS, or interactions with dark matter. Ongoing research, including existing and planned studies, is being conducted to explore the practicality of this technique for multiple applications. The current status of theoretical and experimental efforts related to PALEOCCENE, including small-scale demonstrations with existing technology, is discussed. We examine a system where two active colloidal particles interact within a fluid environment, with both particles producing persistent forces that create differences in activity across the system. By maintaining one parameter constant and allowing the other to fluctuate, we map out a key phase transition, which occurs between a equilibrium state and a regime characterized by persistent two-particle dance patterns, in the presence of a stable, oscillating and chaotic behavior. We derive a simplified equation to represent the long-time behavior of the system and establish its stability by analyzing the dynamics of this reduced model. Additionally, we identify and confirm the existence of unstable states within the two-particle interaction framework, which accounts for fluctuations in both particles' activity levels, by solving a set of differential equations that describe the system's dynamics. Our work contributes to a deeper understanding of how self-driven particles interact with one another in complex environments. It also provides valuable insights that can be applied to the study of more complex systems, which are composed of multiple self-driven particles interacting with heat sources and boundary-driven flows. Such systems are particularly relevant in the study of biological processes and fluid dynamics where complex interactions occur at different scales. It is anticipated that the results of this work, which are connected to other existing theories that describe non-equilibrium systems, will lead to new breakthroughs in the understanding of self-driven particles interacting in non-reversible flows. By utilizing microscopic simulation methods, we are able to accurately reproduce the behavior of the system and validate our analytical findings. Our research demonstrates that the equilibrium approximation can be adequate in certain cases, which is particularly useful because it allows for a much faster computational processing of the system's behavior. For instance, if the system is characterized by a high level of activity non-balancing, the two-particle interaction can be described using a simplified approximation that is comparable to a system where two passive particles interact within a fluid environment, which is then combined with a key parameter that describes the difference in activity between the two particles. The equilibrium approximation that we utilized in the model relies on a key parameter that describes the ratio of the particles' interaction to their movement speed, which we identified as being below a certain threshold. If this parameter exceeds this threshold, we found that the system's behavior is more complex and cannot be described using the equilibrium approximation. By analyzing this more complex scenario, we were able to identify the different possible states that the system can occupy and determine their stability by analyzing the dynamics of the two-particle interaction. We investigate numerically charge-neutral collective excitations in fractional quantum Hall systems, focusing on two specific Jain states, ν=2/7 and ν=2/9 near quarter filling, and the 1/4 Fermi-liquid state, contrasting them with the behavior observed in 1/3 states and those near half filling. Unlike those latter states, ν=2/7 and ν=2/9 each display magnetoroton spectral densities with two peaks rather than one, featuring magnetorotons with a spin of 2, whose chiralities differ for the 2/7 and 2/9 states, but share the same chirality in the 2/9 case. Our calculations also affirm the theoretical prediction that connects the guiding center spin with the spectral properties of the stress tensor. Additionally, we find that the sum rule for the stress tensor's spectral trace is met only closely, with the discrepancy relatively significant for the 2/7 state, but much smaller for the 2/9 state. We discuss the observed outcomes in terms of the Draganopoulos-Erdogan transformation's implications. The findings presented will contribute to understanding the behavior of the stress tensor in the regime of topological phases and support future experimental research using techniques such as ultrafast electron transport to investigate these systems. The outcomes presented can be generalized to other topological phases with exceptional edge excitations. Epidemics on massive contact networks with millions of individuals pose significant challenges for analysis and containment due to their immense scale. However, for networks that can be segmented into groups, describing the spread of an outbreak between these segments is significantly more manageable. Typically, studies have relied on dividing the network into areas based on similar behavior or spatial proximity. This research introduces a mathematical approach for identifying and using these clusters within a network to study the progression of an epidemic. Typically, smaller clusters within the network are more tightly connected than larger groups, although this is not always the case. Nonetheless, this criterion allows us to develop a geometrically representative model. Using SIR modeling as an example, we investigate the implications of varying contact rates between and within these groups on outcomes such as severity, duration, and the likelihood of uncontrolled outbreaks and residual infections. Additionally, we explore trade-offs between controlling outbreaks and resources required for containment, especially in scenarios where a vaccine is not available for immediate acquisition. This research proposes an efficient mathematical method for dividing a network into segments and developing policies to contain an outbreak. Notably, it reveals that a certain level of containment resources allocated can be associated with corresponding levels of control, offering an additional dimension to evaluations of containment effectiveness beyond R0 values. This work provides mathematical insights into practical policies for managing and containing large-scale epidemics. The maximum likelihood estimator used in CMB map-making provides optimal, unbiased results as long as the underlying data model is accurate, but inaccuracies often arise due to sub-pixel structures, instrumentation flaws such as time-varying gain and pointing errors, leading to model inaccuracy in practice. When errors occur, this estimator becomes biased, causing distortions to spread across the scanning pattern through correlations in noise. A notable effect of this distortion is the creation of 'X' shapes surrounding strong point sources in typical scanning patterns. This paper examines why such distortions arise and how to prevent them in CMB data processing. It particularly focuses on overcoming pointing-related distortions, for which two viable solutions exist: (i) improving the CMB map-making model to include pointing errors directly, or (ii) correcting instrument flaws through alternative methods such as pointing correction, data detrending. While the second approach is familiar in the community, describing the first method and its associated benefits is the primary goal of this paper. A mock observation project was implemented to test the effectiveness of this approach, comparing the results to those obtained using traditional techniques for cleaning point source distortions, such as median filtering or priors that rely on internal data. The outcome of this simulation indicates that implementing improved models yields significantly higher signal-to-noise ratios for simulated CMB maps and reduces the distortion phenomenon more effectively than existing techniques. A demonstration of this research's outcomes is available through a interactive presentation on the related NeRF-Windows website. A quick overview of the core concepts and research's findings can also be found in the 2022 TECFA workshop presentation available online.

Interpreting teaching instructions with natural language can be compromised by the complexity of meaning, often leading to misunderstandings. Learners may misinterpret the intentions behind teacher-provided information when object characteristics are ambiguously described, a problem known as referential ambiguity. We utilize Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning (GRL) in a simulated setting to study the effects of referential ambiguity and implement two methods that mitigate these issues: one involves reducing referential ambiguity through object description constraints, and another seeks clarification by generating auxiliary messages. We evaluate our proposed solutions against a baseline that employs GRL without consideration for communication challenges. Experimental results demonstrate that our methods significantly outperform the baseline in most scenarios, especially in situations with increased referential ambiguity. We also observe that auxiliary message generation exhibits desirable qualities, such as natural language fluency and informative content. Ultimately, our research demonstrates effective communication strategies that can adapt to varying levels of referential ambiguity. Quantum process tomography is crucial for building quantum computers, establishing quantum networks, and developing quantum sensors. Like state tomography, characterizing an arbitrary quantum channel necessitates a massive number of measurements, exponentially increasing with the number of quantum bits involved. Recent advancements in shadow tomography, specifically in state measurement, have revealed the possibility of extracting crucial state information using only polynomially many measurements. This study brings the concepts of shadow state tomography to the forefront, addressing the challenge of process characterization and leveraging the Choi isomorphism to derive stricter measurement bounds. Additionally, the research provides exclusive bounds applicable solely to process tomography, along with novel algorithms for its implementation, ultimately leading to new techniques, including channel concatenation and state channel applications. This breakthrough facilitates a significant improvement in understanding large-scale quantum systems. Nevertheless, determining whether these advancements are optimal, and thus setting new standards, remains an open question. Moreover, the research offers a unique perspective on state shadow tomography, enabling a deeper understanding of its own optimality. This study is anticipated to spark future investigations, ultimately paving the way for optimizing quantum mapping algorithms. One notable example is the introduction of a new term, $\mathcal{W}_{\pi}$, within the Gram matrix, whose presence previously went unnoticed in process shadow tomography. This unforeseen term is highly dependent on the specific channel in question and thus cannot be addressed through existing state shadow tomography findings. Consequently, the research is prompted to question whether a comprehensive, universal understanding of shadow tomography remains achievable. This study seeks to answer: what pivotal insights can be gained if we were to establish a singular, all-encompassing theory of quantum information shadowing? While the research seeks to optimize algorithms that have already been implemented, the theoretical implications suggest that achieving a comprehensive understanding of quantum information shadowing might be an unresolvable challenge. To support this assertion, the research provides a concrete example of a property with potentially infinite applications and manifestations, necessitating the determination of a crucial parameter for which there is currently only a single, ambiguous evidence. Consequently, the research is prompted to ask: what is the fundamental limit of knowledge that can be gained through quantum information shadowing? The internet of things encompasses a network of interconnected devices, which includes various non-standard gadgets, traditionally unlinked to the internet, at an exponentially growing pace. Data security and user privacy concerns loom large over the IoT ecosystem, which faces numerous threats from malicious elements. One major obstacle to implementing robust security measures within the IoT is the inherent limitation of devices to support complex cryptographic operations. As a result, light-weight encryption methods become indispensable in the IoT setting. This study assesses the efficacy of existing lightweight algorithms, including those using hash functions, symmetric key encryption, and public key cryptography. Additionally, several hybrid algorithms combining FHE, HMAC, and AES were examined, and a hybrid algorithm based on GCM was proposed and evaluated in terms of security, efficiency, and usability. Finally, a nearly 2-fold reduction in time and energy consumption related to the evaluation of gcmLite in comparison to the hybrid algorithm was observed in the IoT environment. Consequently, the adoption of the proposed algorithm appears an attractive option for the IoT setting. The Ramsey sequence serves as a prime illustration of quantum phase measurement for a spin qubit, and its efficiency in measurements can be enhanced by strategically choosing the duration of phase accumulation, $\tau_a$. A sequential Bayesian experimental approach is employed to determine this duration in low-accuracy Ramsey measurements, and its results are compared to a prior adaptive heuristic method and a randomly selected setup. An efficient data collection system allows for the simultaneous measurement of qubit precession frequencies for multiple atoms, and our findings indicate that the proposed Bayesian strategy: offers the same level of measurement precision as the heuristic method but eliminates the need for a prior atom number, resulting in greater precision when compared to a standard measurement, and can adapt to various physical influences more effectively than a standard measurement or the heuristic method. Consequently, this technique provides a reliable basis for the development of future quantum sensors that combine multiple qubits. Ultimately, the application of the Bayesian method presents a straightforward approach for the design of adaptive low-accuracy Ramsey measurements. Importantly, all of the fundamental principles underlying this technique can be and have been effectively implemented using simple, analog electronic components. Furthermore, a critical examination of our approach, and its accompanying mathematical model, reveals the underlying assumptions that were made, including assumptions regarding qubit accuracy and experimental noise levels. An investigation of the inherent robustness of our model reveals the specific experimental conditions in which our technique is expected to function reliably; in the absence of these conditions, alternative parameter optimization strategies may be more beneficial to explore. Ultimately, the use of our approach is limited to low-accuracy Ramsey measurements in which prior knowledge of qubit accuracy and experimental noise levels is not available. A companion document provides a step-by-step explanation of the underlying mathematical model that was used in this research. The primary advantage of our approach lies in its simplicity, as it allows users to generate adaptive low-accuracy Ramsey measurements independently, even if they are working with pre-existing experimental setups. Specifically, this technique can be applied by simply setting the sampling interval for the qubit accumulation signal, $\Delta\tau_a(t)$, based on the qubit accumulation metric, $M(\tau_a(t),t)$. Furthermore, this technique can be used with a wide variety of qubit accumulation metrics, and can accommodate additional physical influences that may be acting on the qubits during their measurement. Network centrality metrics quantify node importance using various geometric and diffusive characteristics, focusing on distinct scales. From a geometric perspective, a multi-scale centrality is defined by a node's tendency to lie close to shortest paths within its surrounding area. The Gromov centrality metric gauges importance at different network scales based on the size of the neighborhood and recovers well-known metrics as limiting cases. It is demonstrated that the Gromov centrality is sensitive to geometric and boundary constraints of the network, enabling the identification of various node types within random and real-world networks. Furthermore, the Gromov centrality exhibits superior performance in comparing the importance of nodes in comparison to existing metrics. The computational algorithm for calculating the Gromov centrality is discussed along with its limitations, and its applicability to data transfer processes over different network scales is also explored. The Gromov centrality can be used to analyze various networks which are publicly available at https://github.com/athinbill/GromovCentrality. The Python package 'NetworkX' is employed for network analysis and visualization. If you wish to conduct more advanced analysis, you can download the source code at https://www.athenabill.com/lab/resources. The Gromov centrality has practical applications in various fields, and its video illustration can be found at https://vimeo.com/92831478. The research results in this paper are discussed further in a related video presentation. The properties of the Gromov centrality were also analyzed in a research paper by Athinea Bill and Maria Yan, which can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.04231. The Gromov centrality is a multi-scale variant of the Breadth First Search algorithm. The Gromov centrality is a pseudo-metric, a type of similarity measure that does not satisfy the conditions for ultrametric properties. Moreover, a method for identifying the size of the largest bundle that contains a given matrix pencil is developed, and this algorithm is applied to the classification of matrix pencils over specific finite fields. Additionally, a classification of matrix pencils over the field with two elements is also achieved in conjunction with the identification of bundles. Our findings on classification are not dependent on the identification of the polynomial matrix's irreducible components, and this approach is applied to the classification of rings of endomorphism for these matrix pencils. Lastly, particular fields and their corresponding polynomials are defined through their connections with these of another field and its polynomials, and examples demonstrating the diversity of bundles are provided. This study on bundles of matrix pencils and their equivalence classes contributes to the knowledge of this linear systems of partial differential equations' autocorrectability. Specifically, it determines the autocorrectability of these systems, and this study is applied to the classification of certain matrix pencils over finite fields and the identification of their maximal correctors. The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, nilmanifolds, and other examples from topology and topology-inspired quantum field theories. By constructing T-duals from twisted torus bundles with irrational monodromy, we demonstrate its applicability to noncompact cases such as the Seiberg-Witten monopole and the type IIB string on $T^2\times R^3$, with implications for the appearance of irrational monodromy in the later case. Furthermore, we show the appearance of irrational monodromy in torus bundles with base groups of finite rank and nilmanifolds with Lie groups of rank one. Additionally, for certain twisted torus bundles with soluble fundamental group, we establish the existence of nontrivial B-field representatives with zero torsion, thereby providing roots for the Haar measures and thus enabling the computation of T-duals. Finally, for the Seiberg-Witten monopole, we describe in detail the macroscopic geometry of the Seiberg-Witten lift of its $S^1$-invariant parts after T-dualizing the monodromy. After some preliminary considerations, T-duality turns out to be equivalent to computing the dual coactions. A significant role is also played by the classification theorem of twisted torus bundles with irrational monodromy, which has an independent interest. The relevant mathematical objects and concepts can be seen in the accompanying diagram. The considered examples share the property that the topological space has a substructure of trivial fibers, which plays a crucial role in determining its T-dual. An additional instance is provided by torus bundles with connected groups of automorphisms of the torus, which include the action of the groups $SL_2Z$ and $B_2Z$. The substructure of trivial fibers, which appears as a subbundle of the pullback bundle, constitutes the essential component in determining the T-dual. Consequently, T-dualization yields the incidence correspondence of the torus's action group, which reveals that T-dualization implements the Pontryagin dual transformation for the torus's group of unitary characters. For C1-smooth discrete-time systems exhibiting strong monotonicity, the prevailing long-term behavior of linearly stable cycles is established in a probabilistic framework. This research then extends to periodic parabolic equations and reveals new findings regarding the ubiquity of periodic solution convergence. Notably, in Neumann-bound equations defined on convex domains, the set of initial conditions corresponding to homogeneous periodic solutions is shown to be prevalent, while in radially symmetric domains, the set of radially symmetric periodic solution trajectories exhibits prevalence among initial values. These probabilistic analyses also shed light on the prevalence of stable manifolds surrounding unstable invariant sets and the convergent behavior of solutions approaching these manifolds. Ultimately, the prevailing long-term behavior of solutions in radially expanding domains is characterized. This work primarily relies on novel estimates of stable manifold width in domains exhibiting periodic expansion. In addition, the convergence of solutions in radially expanding domains toward the stable manifold is proven to occur with near-unimprovable probability, exceeding 1 - Cε^{1/2}, where ε represents a spatial scaling parameter. Such probabilistic convergence rates closely resemble those established by Blum and Pinsky in their study of long-term behavior for normal diffusion processes. The variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) has shown great potential as a quantum simulation algorithm. Nonetheless, employing VQE on systems requiring large qubit spaces remains challenging. Each evaluation in VQE involves a costly circuit execution followed by a costly classical computation that needs to traverse the entire computational basis. To mitigate this issue, the adaptive VQE (ad-VQE) approach was developed, utilizing problem-specific insights in molecular hydrogen and HeH+ to significantly reduce the number of required computational basis evaluations. Building on ad-VQE, we introduce the Qubit-excitation-based adaptive VQE (qad-VQE) that further optimizes the ad-VQE strategy by incorporating an exciting condition and a criterion for evaluations based on excitation counts. To support the qad-VQE method, we have developed an optimized implementation utilizing QuantumPy, a Python library designed for dynamic quantum computing. Our experimental results showcase that qad-VQE outperforms ad-VQE by lowering the number of required evaluations and can even surpass the state-of-the-art closed-source versions of ad-VQE. Moreover, qad-VQE offers enhanced adaptability through the adaptable selection of the initial variational circuit. With qad-VQE's versatility, we have successfully apply it to simulate multi-excitation states of more complex molecules, such as water and malonaldehyde. Using qad-VQE, we have calculated the ground-state energies of these molecules with significantly fewer qubits and evaluations required. Overall, the proposed qad-VQE approach offers a promising direction for efficiently solving multi-configurational problems in quantum chemistry through the ad-VQE family of algorithms. With an increasing focus on quantum simulation, we believe that qad-VQE will also find applications in solving other classical problems with potentially exciting implications for fields like machine learning and coding theory. Finally, we envision that qad-VQE's optimized implementation could serve as a valuable educational tool to teach the VQE algorithm to students and researchers. The current source code for qad-VQE, which inherits from the QuantumPy library, is now available on GitHub to facilitate future research and educational purposes. In contrast to traditional approaches, we are exploring the potential benefits of treating a deep generative network as a measurement system.  This leads us to a novel statistical estimation technique that relies on maximizing the likelihood of unknown input variables given the network's output.  Unlike traditional backpropagation methods, this approach enables the direct computation of precise, continuous values for the degrees of freedom in a network's random representation.  Through a comprehensive analysis of the statistical efficiency of our technique, we are able to shed new light on the interplay between a network's random representation and its deterministic mapping function.  Our approach has been successfully tested in the contexts of both noise removal and image synthesis, yielding superior results in comparison to conventional methods.  Furthermore, we have applied our technique to the development of an automatic coding strategy for a fully-connected network, thereby facilitating the discovery of efficient feature transformations.  Ultimately, our findings highlight the efficacy of viewing deep generative networks as measurement systems with the potential to accurately recover unknown input variables.  As such, this work marks a significant breakthrough in the field of deep learning.  The accompanying code can be accessed at https://github.com/jordanshue/deep_generative_decoder.  A related movie depicting our technique is available at http://theoraphysics.ucsd.edu/deep_generative_decoder/movies/deep_generative_decoder.html. If such waves exist, their earlier generation during inflation could have been strengthened by the stiff properties of space-time and made more detectable by late-time cosmic acceleration, thus having an amplified impact on the present gravitational wave background, possibly within reach of current observations. We examine the potential consequences of incorporating these amplified gravitational waves on the models aiming to explain the "Hubble tension" and find that incorporating stiff-amplified primordial waves, detectable by both NANOGrav and the LIGO-Virgo Collaboration, could improve the fits to observations by up to two orders of magnitude. Therefore, such an effect could significantly impact the interpretation of gravitational wave data in precision cosmology, and we suggest that existing and future datasets contain information that can help distinguish between different inflationary models with distinct stochastic properties. Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment of a particular aspect within product reviews. Approximately one-quarter of reviews lack explicit opinion words, necessitating the extraction of sentiment from implicit text. Unfortunately, prominently utilized supervised learning methods fall short due to inadequate representation of implicit text. Recent pre-training methods have improved performance on explicit sentiment analysis but have not been effectively applied to implicit sentiment analysis. In an effort to address this gap, a new approach, supervised contrastive pre-training, is proposed to enhance the representation of implicit text. Specifically, a new model, iSSLMP, incorporates instance-level supervised pre-training using a masked pre-training scheme that incorporates a contrastive loss function. Evaluation of the model on existing datasets reveals notable improvements, with significant increases in F1-score values for implicit sentiment analysis. For instance, notable enhancements are observed on the SemEval 2017 Task 2 dataset, with F1-score increases of 8.7% for positive aspects and 10.6% for negative aspects. Similarly, notable enhancements are observed on the Aspect-based Sentiment Dataset, with F1-score increases of 8.6% for positive aspects and 9.4% for negative aspects. Importantly, the proposed model successfully surpasses the best existing benchmarks for implicit sentiment analysis. Furthermore, an analysis of the model's effectiveness reveals that the pre-training process leads to enhanced representations of implicit text, with the masked token being correctly predicted in nearly 90% of cases. Notably, the proposed approach also demonstrates a high capacity for generalization, with results that are two-fold better than the next best approach on the SemEval 2017 Task 2 dataset. This research paper delves into secure communication systems for multiple users that utilize reconfigurable intelligent surfaces to compensate for hardware limitations.
We simultaneously adjust the base station's beamforming vectors and the phase shifts on the RIS to achieve the highest possible weighted minimum secrecy rate under constraints for the base station's power output and RIS element limitations.
To address this optimization challenge, we split the problem into two sub-problems: the first regarding base station power allocation, which is a standard optimization issue, and the second regarding RIS phase shift adjustment, which is a complex non-convex problem.
To resolve these challenges efficiently, we propose simple iterative algorithms for each.
Simulation results confirm the efficacy of the proposed algorithms in enhancing the secrecy rate compared to a risk-averaging algorithm that disregards RIS parameters.
Additionally, we demonstrate the potential of the RIS in enhancing the secrecy rate with reduced base station power, and that the computational complexity of the proposed algorithms is reasonable for implementation. Nonetheless, further enhancements can be achieved by reducing the base station's power requirements, which is a topic we investigate through optimization. A convex optimization algorithm is derived to obtain the analytical solution to this issue, and simulation results are provided to support the case for further research in this area.

This process, which we refer to as the sequence of actions taken by the executive, can be understood as a system that continuously corrects its mistakes from previous stages by selecting and reevaluating key decisions made at different points in the past. To create a self-correcting system of this kind, we build upon two existing ideas: a technique for rapidly improving how well it anticipates the future consequences of its own actions, and a method for condensing a large amount of information into its most essential parts. When we combine these two ideas with each other, we get a more sophisticated version of a decision-making system that we were able to demonstrate effectively tackles our originally defined task. Additionally, we show that the theories we have developed can be applied to other tasks by comparing our system to other algorithms that are different but no less effective. This investigation leads us to the discovery that the process of learning and improving over time that we and many other living things experience is not unique to us after all, and we were able to verify this by studying how the human brain performs its own learning and improvement over time. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of the solar wind particles themselves. Compared to similar data collected by the Helios spacecraft about 40 years ago, our results showed a notable decrease in energy flux but, interestingly, the ratio of energy flux based on electron density versus speed remained consistent at the four different approaches. Furthermore, our research indicated that the different techniques we used to determine the solar wind speed were equally consistent with the overall findings. However, our energy flux calculations based on temperature showed some of the most significant variations. Moreover, our data suggested that the solar wind energy flux follows the square root relationship with the distance from the solar surface, and we found the long-term trend of this parameter to be in line with the predictions of hydrodynamic models. Nevertheless, our research did show some discrepancies with these models that might be attributed to structural changes in the low-frequency MHD waves present during the solar wind development, an effect predicted by wave kinetic models. These observed wave characteristics matched the theoretical models and included measurements of wave speed, direction, orientation, and electrical properties. Moreover, our research revealed that the energy contained in these waves decreased with the distance from the solar surface at a rate consistent with the solar wind energy flux itself. Ultimately, our findings agreed that the solar wind energy flux originates primarily from the structural changes and energetic interactions within the corona, specifically from the 200,000 km region surrounding the solar surface, an area known as the transition region. In a noncommutative setting, where locally compact Hausdorff groups act on C*-algebras in a proper, isometric manner, we introduce the concept of a numerable action possessing certain unwinding properties. This notion is viewed as a noncommutative analog of a numerable fibration in the algebraic topology domain. This framework enables the construction of a noncommutative numerable bundle corresponding to the given group action, characterized by a G-action on a C*-algebra A, which is separable and fully supported. This construction is grounded in the principles of Pimsner's crossed products. Additionally, under specific conditions, when a standard Hilbert space bundle corresponding to the group action is well-dressed, we demonstrate that its corresponding local C*-bundle is a noncommutative numerable bundle, which is topologically isomorphic to a standard numerable bundle in the classical setting. This methodology is illustrated through the examination of two distinct scenarios: (i) when a C*-algebra is generated by its left copies of a group G acting on a Hilbert space H through a linear isometry, corresponding to a noncommutative FRT-bundle; (ii) when a faithful action of an infinite group on a standard Hilbert space is realized, encompassing a subalgebra of secondary Hilbert spaces. This example highlights how the noncommutative numerable bundle, in this case, a noncommutative Whitehead tower, is constructed from a standard numerable bundle (in this instance, a tower of projective spaces). This textual presentation originates from doctoral research conducted at the University of Alcalá, spanning approximately three years, under the supervision of Prof. Alejandro Almeida and Prof. José M. Malmirat. A accompanying thesis document is available for further review. The present account specifically explores the construction of a noncommutative numerable bundle in Section 2.2.2 and the technological groundwork from crossed products found in Chapter 3, relying heavily on the monograph by Fell and Das. Additionally, key concepts related to group actions on C*-algebras as outlined in Chapter 2 and the conventional bundle constructions presented in Section 1 are critical to this research. A accompanying graphics and 3D animations illustrating the group actions and resulting standard numerable bundles can be found online at the associated website. For the purposes of pedagogy, a simplified version of this research focusing on the FRT-bundle is documented in the accompanying PhD dissertation.

We undertook a statistical investigation into tidal features surrounding early-type galaxies of massive proportions, utilizing data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program. Our research is significantly advanced due to the extensive information on tidal features and galaxy properties, as well as the influence of dust and background signal noise levels. Notably, nearly 25% of 3555 galaxies exhibiting a sharp edge in their diffuse light have a central disturbance, while approximately 52% of 1358 galaxies displaying a break in their diffuse light were found to have tidal features. Our results indicate that galaxies of greater mass are more likely to have tidal features, with merged features appearing more common than isolated ones. Additionally, galaxies exhibiting merged tidal features tend to reside closer to their neighboring galaxies. It is found that galaxies of a certain density but without nearby neighbors tend to possess isolated tidal features. Estimates for the merger rates of these galaxies over the past 2 billion years range from 1 billion to 30 billion years, with significant variation. Data on tidal features and galaxy properties is available for access. Further investigation into individual systems using numerical and observational methods would help to better comprehend the processes involved in the formation of these structures. It is observed that a roughly even proportion of tidal features lie along the major axis and at a perpendicular angle to it. No preference for the direction of the tidal features in relation to the direction of the galaxy's nuclear light was found.
