This additional analysis reveals that the strategies derived may not be feasible in real-world investment scenarios where the market factor cannot be accurately represented using a single variable. However, the strategies derived provide a useful approximation, specifically an upper bound, in real-world investment scenarios. This hybrid network creates edges according to a mixture of these rules.  Specifically, when an edge is added, it follows the preferential attachment rule with a certain probability and otherwise forms a connection at random.  This hybrid approach offers a flexible framework for modeling the combination of preferential attachment and uniform attachment mechanisms in real-world networks.  The degree distribution and some fundamental characteristics of this network are analyzed mathematically.  To better understand its properties, a variant of this network called an epsilon-hybrid network is defined.  The variation in the value of epsilon affects the degree distribution and the resulting network.  When epsilon is less than one, the degree distribution and the network behave like those of a purely preferential attachment network, whereas when epsilon is greater than zero, but less than one, the degree distribution and the network incorporate elements of both preferential attachment and uniform attachment.  This variant of the hybrid network provides a useful tool for further investigation of the difference between pure preferential attachment and combined mechanisms, as well as for a deeper analysis of the transition between these regimes of behavior.  The properties of a directed epsilon-hybrid network are further examined.  By further extending this hybrid approach to more complex network structures, it may be possible to evaluate its relevance to real-world networks such as road systems and the world-wide web. Moreover, a directed epsilon-hybrid network exhibits a mean path length that is proportional to epsilon minus the inverse of epsilon, allowing for the identification of the value of epsilon. A critical objective is to rectify these AI errors without compromising their established abilities and ideally without requiring direct human intervention. This report outlines an innovative approach aimed at boosting the cognitive capabilities of individual AI systems by collaborating with other AIs. It synthesizes insights from multi-agent learning and seeks to establish a foundational model for developing unified AI strategies for error correction. Our research involves exploring the thermal behavior of the Bose-Hubbard model in the presence of strong spin-orbit coupling originating from a mean-field state. By introducing a pre-existing triply degenerate spin-orbit coupling configuration, we identify the characteristics of superfluid order parameters and find two second-order phase transition points that separate different phases of the superfluid. The phases include one based on the original spin-orbit coupling configuration and another with a broken modulation symmetry in the superfluid. Through this approach, we develop a Landau theory that predicts critical temperatures consistent with our numerical results, demonstrating good agreement. The predicted critical temperatures show dependence on spin-orbit coupling and interaction strength, with the dependence on interaction strength being the most substantial. The phase diagram of the system can thus be controlled by adjusting the interatomic interaction strength. Our findings contribute to understanding thermal behavior within specific conditions of spin-orbit coupling and interaction strength in the system in question. The results reveal that the system can exhibit distinct superfluid behaviors within separate regions of the interaction strength, specifically multiple superfluid behaviors within regions of weak interactions and a phase with broken modulation symmetry in the system at its lowest filling. For strong interactions, on the other hand, the system exhibits a single superfluid behavior characterized by broken modulation symmetry. The possibility of experimentally observing these thermal behaviors in the system is also discussed. Consider two groups, G_1 and G_2, and suppose a homomorphism \phi from G_1 to G_2 maps a particular element to another element. In the context of graph theory, this leads to the concept of a group G_1 degrading to group G_2, which is investigated within this research. Graph degeneration is found to encompass a particular instance of this group relationship. The paper examines unique properties arising from graph degeneration. To visualize this, it employs a diagrammatic approach representing graphs realized by finite abelian groups. Order relationships within a set of all such graphs realized by a fixed abelian group are also studied, and it is determined that the set forms a partial order. Additionally, it is demonstrated that each graph degrades into a graph of lower order and that its order is the sum of the orders of its prime factor graphs. Finally, it is proven that the set of all graphs realized by a finite abelian group has a well-defined and catacombigous structure of degeneration and partial order. Moreover, it is established that any finite abelian group can be transformed into a group N_2 whose graphs realize a particular subset of all possible graphs realized by the original group, and that this group N_2 is actually a direct product of two circulant matrices. Several further results about the degeneration of graphs realized by 2d abelian groups are derived. Lastly, it is shown that there are instances of graphs N_2 whose graphs realize a particular subset of all possible graphs realized by the original group G, and yet no element maps to another in the group G_1 to G_2, and that in such cases the set of all possible graphs realized by the original group G is equal to the set of all possible graphs realized by the group N_2. This further leads to several further outcomes and questions for future research. Recent breakthroughs in AdS/CFT correspondence research, specifically in low-dimensional settings, are explored, concentrating on AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ and AdS$_2$/CFT$_1$ dualities within massive Type IIA string theory. We first examine the solutions derived in 1908.09851 of AdS$_3$ supergravity, coupled with supersymmetry $\mathcal{N}=(0,4)$. These 2d CFT duals are re-evaluated, in conjunction with surface defect representations in D4-D8 bound state-based 5d fixed-point theories. Next, the solutions derived in 2011.13932 with supersymmetry $\mathcal{N}=4$, specifically AdS$_2$ supergravity, are considered in tandem with the dualized superconformal quantum mechanics. We interpret the solutions through line defect representations, realized in D0-D4 baryon vertices of the 5d Sp(N) 3d fixed-point theory. We also provide an in-depth look at an additional solution with supersymmetry $\mathcal{N}=4$ from 2011.13932, accompanied by additional quantum mechanical analysis and surface defect representations. Lastly, an explored solution of non-trivial T^2 compactification of the 3d free fermion theory, featuring supersymmetry $\mathcal{N}=(4,0)$ through non-canonical kinetic term, is discussed. We conclude with an overview of outstanding challenges and an anticipated research in AdS/CFT correspondence. We also add an additional appendix on an expected Sp(N) 3d fixed-point theory-based surface defect representation of the solutions derived in 1908.09851. Moreover, an additional section discusses an exploration of the solutions derived in 2011.13932 through D0-D4 5d gauge theory defect sessions. Lastly, an additional section delves into an exploration of the solutions derived in 2009.3496 through D4-D8 5d gauge theory defect sessions. We conclude the additional sections with an overview of outstanding challenges and an anticipated future research in AdS/CFT correspondence. Additional sections also serve to provide additional background on surface defect representations in gauge theory for the benefit of the readers. We also provide an additional appendix to delist our contributions in AdS/CFT correspondence research in line with the "first come first served" principle. In numerous Machine Learning applications, selecting an optimal kernel function is a pivotal step. Gaussian Processes excel in regression and classification tasks, largely depending on a well-suited kernel function. Traditionally, Gaussian Process researchers have either designed kernels from scratch, picked them from a predetermined list, or systematically searched for kernel compositions within pre-defined parameter spaces. This paper innovatively leverages Genetic-Programming, utilizing trees of fundamental mathematical expressions to represent kernel functions, thereby broadening the potential solutions, though also introducing new complexities. Our proposed method can successfully address these challenges and uncover kernel models that demonstrate superior performance on common Gaussian Process benchmarks. Moreover, this method can automatically create new kernel models, unlocking novel possibilities for integration. Experiment results indicate that Gaussian Process performance is significantly enhanced across multiple datasets. While computational requirements for training Gaussian Processes with these kernels are substantially higher, recent advancements in parallel training algorithms have greatly mitigated this problem. Our research provides a foundation for future work in automatically designing Gaussian Process operators. As a result, this method is freely available to the public on the TerraHub platform.terahub.com.

Future high-energy muon colliders face a challenge due to in-flight decays of
muons from the beam line, resulting in beam-induced backgrounds (BIB). This
background interference will hinder accurate data analysis and detector
operation unless mitigated. Research focuses on reducing BIB in detector design,
including triggering, data processing, and analysis stages. Studies were carried
out on a detector utilizing a tungsten nose-cone to filter BIB for a 1.5 TeV
energy threshold. In-depth analysis revealed the concept's viability and
highlighted its potential to enhance detector efficiency, particularly in low
luminosity scenarios. This could lead to notable benefits in the form of reduced
processing costs and increased data analysis accuracy. The concept is suitable
for low-energy muon colliders, while high-energy facilities might require an
additional filtering stage due to increased BIB levels. This concept is simple,
cost-effective, and could serve as a potential solution for future high-energy
muon colliders dealing with increased BIB levels. The concept is further explored
in related research papers. The concept is further validated through an
experimental simulation presented at the 2021 Snowmass Workshop. The result of
this validation confirmed that this concept can successfully reduce BIB levels by
more than 3 orders of magnitude. Consequently, this is predominantly useful
for high-energy muon colliders requiring low BIB levels. The concept is
considered useful for muon colliders, especially those handling very high
energies, while tungsten filtering might not be sufficient for low-energy
colliders, which would likely need an alternative beam filtering method. This
concept is considered unique in its simplicity whencompared to other
interpretations of BIB reduction. The concept is considered tenable with
experimental confirmation, which is still needed for tungsten materials.

Introducing Spartan, a novel approach for training neural networks with pre-defined sparsity. This method effectively leverages a combination of two techniques: soft parameter pruning through optimal transportation and hard parameter sparsification during forward passes. This dynamic balance enables initial exploration of various sparsity patterns and gradually shifts towards optimizing parameters with respect to a predetermined sparsity pattern. Spartan offers flexibility in incorporating diverse sparsity policies, encompassing both random and structured sparsity, as well as cost-sensitive allocation guided by per-parameter models. Spartan demonstrates exceptional performance on ImageNet-1K classification, achieving significant sparsity in ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16 models, outperforming state-of-the-art methods like SLAMN by a notable margin. Notably, our approach is compatible with existing frameworks, easily integrable and adaptable for practical use. You can find more information and demos at this website: https://spartan.diffsky.com. Additionally, relevant resources are available at this GitHub repository: https://github.com/kskth/SpaRtAn. Lastly, you can find associated videos with the provided hyperlinks.

The intricate connection between many-body interactions and the spatial dimension of a system plays a pivotal role in various quantum phenomena that emerge from these interactions. A compelling example of this relationship is the behavior of a Bose gas confined to a one-dimensional space, where the presence of one De Broglie wave results in the absence of another. Although the underlying physics in this scenario can be understood through the concept of Pauli blocking, this phenomenon is rarely observed in real-world situations due to the lack of strict Pauli blocking conditions in systems with colloid or atomic components. However, our theoretical research suggests that the emergence of a distinct many-body interaction-induced correction to the single-particle density of states near the critical point of a second-order phase transition in different dimensions has the potential to display distinct characteristics that could be interpreted as Pauli blocking. This prediction was verified via the creation of a 2D Bose-Einstein condensate through a 3D confinement and the subsequent observation of a jump in a specific energy loss measurement as it transitions from a superfluid to a Bose gas. This unexplained spike in energy can be attributed to the simultaneous emission of two photons in conjunction with a third, non-interacting quasicondensate, which can be described through the application of a modified density of states incorporating many-body interaction effects. Essentially, the phenomenon being described here could be referred to as "Higgs-like interaction correction to the density of states." Furthermore, the possibility of reproducing the conditions required to identify the emergence of the interaction correction in experiments involving a Bose gas confined to one-dimensional channels is also explored. If these conditions can be replicated, it may result in the observation of what can literally be referred to as the "Higgs mechanism" in a 2D Bose-Einstein condensate. Even in the event of failing to fully qualify the system for strict Pauli blocking, the interaction correction will still make a substantial contribution to the observed phenomenon. This distinctive characteristic can be attributed to the unique many-body interaction effects observed in this system, which may prove to be a highly effective means of identifying these interactions in various quantum phenomena. To facilitate future experiments, estimates for the duration of the phenomenon being described are also provided. This research incorporates a series of experimental results, including the measurement of spin and collective properties of a 2D Bose-Einstein condensate. These experiments not only confirm the predictions made through a theoretical model but also provide an in-depth analysis of the nature of many-body interactions in a 2D Bose-Einstein condensate

Software developers widely acknowledge the importance of unit testing as a crucial aspect of their work cycle, allowing for swift detection and resolution of coding errors. However, test code can be compromised by suboptimal design or implementation choices referred to as test smells. These shortcomings can significantly undermine the quality of software systems by exacerbating difficulties in comprehension, amplifying maintenance complexities, and making systems more susceptible to bugs and errors. Prior studies have investigated the likely consequences of test smells on test code. Despite their focus, a knowledge gap remains regarding the perspectives of developers regarding these issues. To fill this knowledge gap, a study empirically examined how software developers perceive the level of impact test smells have on test quality. Through a cross-sectional survey involving 264 developers, findings revealed that developers consider test smells to be moderately severe issues in terms of test quality. What was equally noticeable was that developers' views on the degree of impact test smells have varied, with some believing it to be of minor concern and others perceiving it as a substantial issue. A notable insight from the data is that developers' perspectives on the importance of something (in this case, test quality) and their perception of the severity of an issue are unrelated. By distinguishing between these two concepts, a theoretical framework for coding best practices has been developed, providing a foundation for further research. Moreover, implementing a distinction between developers' and maintainers is crucial, with maintainers being more likely to identify and prioritize actual issues. A significant insight from our empirical study is that future research into the opinions and perspectives of software developers regarding coding issues is necessary. By following a consistent research approach, a more comprehensive understanding of these perspectives can be gained. As future work, investigating the opinions of developers regarding the most effective techniques to address specific issues (in this case, test smells) would be a valuable area of study. A study could involve asking developers to evaluate various methods to address these issues, providing insights into the most effective strategies to address these concerns. By deepening our understanding of what works best for software development, a more informed and knowledge-rich software development practice can be realized. Ultimately, a more informed and knowledgeable software development community where researchers and practitioners can provide practical solutions to practical problems in terms of their unique perspectives and expertise can be achieved. To support this, efforts by researchers and practitioners to tackle these concerns from a practical perspective can be undertaken. A key requirement for achieving this goal is for practitioners and researchers to work in close collaboration, with a shared understanding of the unique perspectives and needs of each group being recognized. This paper investigates the existence and uniqueness of solutions to a modified version of the sweeping process, first proposed by J.J. Moreau in the early 1970s as part of plasticity theory. The proposed modification involves a novel combination of the prox-regular moving set and two types of perturbations: a Carathéodory mapping and an integral forcing term with an integrand dependent on time variables. To address this new integro-differential sweeping process, a semi-discretization method is developed and used in conjunction with an original Gronwall-like inequality to prove that it possesses a single, absolutely continuous solution. Furthermore, the solution is demonstrated to be continuous with respect to its initial value. The obtained results have been successfully applied to two significant problems: nonlinear integro-differential complementarity systems, comprising Volterra equations and complementarity constraints, and non-standard electrical circuits with time-varying capacitors and diodes, representing novel aspects of the presented work. The analytical method employed in this research can be seen as a generalization of the classical convex sweeping dynamics, allowing for its application in non-standard systems. The nonconvex moving set and perturbations by a Carathéodory mapping and an integral forcing term render the problem under study unique and distinguish it from previously existing works on differential inclusions and the sweeping process. The contributions of this research consist of the originally introduced integro-differential sliding mechanism and the novel mathematical model of non-standard systems with time-modulated capacitors and diodes. The related problems of numerical semidiscretization and stability analysis with respect to the initial condition have been explored for the first time in the framework of the presented integro-differential sweeping process. The developed method can be easily extended to other types of regular moving sets, such as vector fields and their associated manifolds. Notably, the possibility of extending the results to the multidimensional case, when the vector field becomes a matrix, remains an open question. The obtained results of this research have been successfully tested in the context of numerical examples, highlighting the importance of the obtained findings. We introduce the updated version of the {\tt KKMCee} event generator, version 5.00.2, designed for simulating lepton and quark pair production through high-energy electron-positron annihilation. This upgraded tool offers several enhanced features, encompassing extended QED processes, improved treatment of electroweak corrections in top pair production, fine-tuned final state radiation, and updated leading logarithmic results for heavy top pair production. Additionally, {\tt KKMCee} now includes the ability to model neutron radiation using the {\tt ATLASFAST} module. Furthermore, this pair production event generator is integrated with the {\tt LEPRec} tool to provide recalculation options for corrected cross sections, a feature particularly beneficial for analyzing precision data. As demonstrated through its contribution, {\tt KKMCee} is utilized in the {\tt TGCStudy} event generator for simulating {\tt X,Y,Z} production in the LHC and CLIC experiments. Both {\tt KKMCee} and {\tt LEPRec} are distributed under an open-source license, available for research purposes only. Padhi for their valuable input and assistance in developing the present tools. Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when they are heavily distorted by motion noise, which is common in individuals who are highly active. Researchers working on remote health monitoring and wearable devices have identified signal denoising and IBI estimation as a significant area of focus. Recent breakthroughs have involved the use of deep learning, which has significantly improved signal quality and diagnostic accuracy, far exceeding previous limitations. A novel deep learning approach is being developed using a Tiramisu autoencoder to effectively filter out motion artifact and make ECG signals more interpretable even during high-impact motion. By achieving accurate denoising and IBI estimation, this approach has set a new standard in performance, achieving reduced error rates and providing high-precision IBIs from highly noisy signals. Moreover, the accuracy of heart rate variability measurement has the potential to be significantly enhanced. Experimental testing using synthetic and real-world signals from the CMU-KS dataset has shown that the effects of motion are greatly reduced and that the average IBI estimation error rate is approximately 2 milliseconds when the signal is heavily affected by motion. In comparison, the existing state-of-the-art method yields an average error rate of around 7 milliseconds. Notably, the results of this research are consistent with the show rate of a CMOS sensor, which has a noise floor around 2 milliseconds. Recent findings have also demonstrate that the sample rate of a sensor has a direct impact on the precision of IBIs, with higher rates resulting in more accurate estimates. It has also been discovered that the precision of heart rate can be significantly enhanced, ranging from 61 to 99 percent, which surpasses the existing state-of-the-art value of 56 to 94 percent. These breakthroughs suggest that the technique has the potential to greatly enhance the diagnostic precision of diagnostic systems that rely on ECG signals, which could lead to the development of more accurate and efficient healthcare platforms. Ultimately, the technique has been shown to provide high-precision IBIs from highly noisy signals, which has the potential to greatly enhance the precision of diagnostic systems working with ECG signals. Furthermore, the technique has been found to significantly improve the diagnostic accuracy of heart diseases, which could lead to the development of more accurate and efficient healthcare platforms. To utilize contemporary computing systems efficiently, an important consideration is reducing the communication cost associated with data transfer, especially when calculating the tensor singular value decomposition (t-SVD) in just a few data passes. The prevailing subspace randomized methods used to compute the t-SVD require 2q + 2 passes over the tensor data, where q represents a positive integer variable for iteration refinement. In this paper, we introduce a new randomized algorithm for t-SVD calculation, allowing for an arbitrary number of passes 'q', not constrained to even integers, building upon existing matrix-based approaches adapted to tensors. The error margin of the proposed method has been statistically quantified. Through practical experiments, we demonstrate that the algorithm's efficiency and usability are well-supported, and we apply this method to develop a faster computational method for tensor completion. The associated source code can be found at the repository located at https://github.com/filippo-barbieri/randitens.py. The algorithm's performance is shown in Figs. 9-12, and numerical results are presented in Table 1. The remaining results are listed in Section 6.6. Consequently, the newly developed method can be considered a versatile tool for tensor data processing, distinct from other approaches such as the tensor train (TT) and cp-decomposition methods. Additionally, the experimental results obtained using the randomized algorithm for t-SVD revealed that the reduced 2q passes data transfer efficiency comes at the price of increased central processing unit (CPU) time requirement. However, the main contribution of the proposed method lies in its capability to efficiently handle large-scale tensors on modern graphics processing units (GPUs) with small memory capacities. The proposed method is capable of processing such tensors in GPUs with a capacity of 8 GB that is utilized in the experimental section. Network analytics heavily relies on embedding static graphs in low-dimensional vector spaces to enable node classification, link prediction, and visualization, but this approach struggles to accommodate dynamic behavior exhibited by real-world networks. These networks often undergo changes in their topological structure, feature evolution, and spreading dynamics over time. To capture such dynamics, researchers have proposed various techniques for embedding dynamic graphs over time. These methods face challenges related to modeling temporal changes, incorporating temporal characteristics, and adjusting to varying levels of granularity. This overview survey provides a comprehensive analysis of dynamic graph embedding by detailing its fundamental aspects and latest developments. We formally define dynamic graph embedding and categorize it into problem settings and a novel taxonomy of input and output. We also discuss different dynamic phenomena and categorize them according to topological changes, feature evolution, and network processes. In addition, existing methods and a classification of algorithmic approaches, ranging from matrix factorization to deep learning, random walks, and temporal processes, are discussed, as well as primary applications and some future research opportunities. These discussions are brought together to provide an in-depth overview of the field, its challenges, and future directions. These challenges include developing formal quantitative frameworks for evaluating this task and conducting a detailed comparison of existing techniques. Key future avenues explored include incorporating temporal processes, a broader and more refined notion of time, and multi-modal and heterogeneous data. One of the main future developments discussed is the adaptation of the node-centric and edge-centric viewpoints to accommodate the analysis of temporal network structures. This survey aims to provide valuable insights for researchers working in this field. An extensive dataset of dynamic graph embedding methods has been made publicly available.  https://github.com/hjwang517/emdg_survey/blob/main/emdg_dataset.md)

Notably, expanding the neutron space resulted in a calculated ground state energy of approximately 23.14 MeV, which matched real-world measurement findings of 23.11 MeV with a 0.6 MeV margin of error. Moreover, calculated data for other resonances such as 27.25, 32.42, and 41.02 MeV also corresponded reasonably well with existing experimental results, with a 2 MeV error margin in some cases. Deep Metric Learning methods primarily aim to develop a space where data similarities can be accurately maintained. These methods have made notable improvements in many areas but have failed to account for the broader range of similarity constraints. As a result, suboptimal metrics in the embedded space have been the outcome. The existing research into their performance with noisy labels is still limited. To overcome this limitation, we introduce DOME, a pioneering approach that enables the development of a space where similarities and dissimilarities are accurately distinguished using the concept of displacement divergence. The displacement divergence offers advantages over other divergence metrics as it effectively deals with noisy labels and enables non-linear comparisons of distributions. The effectiveness of DOME was tested on a variety of datasets, demonstrating its capacity to outperform existing techniques of Deep Metric Learning. The source code of DOME is freely accessible on GitHub at the specified link. Additionally, we have made available a new dataset, the ModelNet40-3DDraw dataset, comprising 3D drawings of ModelNet40 objects. The dataset can be found at the provided website. The results of experiments demonstrate the capabilities of DOME to learn nonlinear, noisy-sensitive embeddings in complex domains such as 3D objects classified using deep descriptors. Moreover, we have successfully applied it to learn an optimal metric space for word embeddings in NLP domains. The embeddings obtained can be found on our GitHub repository. The displacement divergence was implemented using the Optimal Transport library, a popular OT solver. The solution repository can be accessed at the provided link. The accuracy of solved OT problems was verified using a new OT verification tool. The source code of the verification tool can be found at the provided link. The results of tests demonstrate the high precision of OT verification tool. The process of matching objects between photometric catalogs can lead to inaccuracies when objects of different brightness are mistaken for the same source. However, incorporating the magnitudes of sources can rectify this issue and improve the accuracy of matching algorithms. A novel approach described here utilizes graphic processing units (GPUs) to accelerate the matching process, which now utilizes magnitudes in addition to astrometry. The method's performance was validated through a comprehensive analysis of multiple catalogs, demonstrating improved results when matching catalogs containing a large number of sources, outstripping even the most precise astrometric reference catalogs. A demonstration of this technique's efficacy is showcased through a study of the photometric properties of the galaxy NGC 4258. Furthermore, a suite of software and sample input/output data are provided to facilitate seamless integration of this technique into the existing legacy pipeline of the Wide-Field Astronomy Plan, enabling accurate source matching and characterization. A comprehensive discussion of incorporating magnitude information is also presented, potentially expanding this technique to support cross-spectral source matching, which could lead to significant advancements in research. A preliminary assessment estimates that processing the entire collection of sources observed by the Gaia space mission at a rate of one GPU per month could yield more than 100 million sources matched precisely. A vertex cover of a hypergraph is a subset of vertices that intersects with every edge of the hypergraph. A vertex cover is considered minimal if none of its proper subsets serve as vertex covers. Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive, formally structured concept relationships called ontologies. In fields like biology and medicine, vast ontologies comprise hundreds of thousands of interconnected concepts. Effective visual representations are particularly crucial when dealing with large, complex ontologies, enabling easier comprehension and exploration. However, existing visualisation tools predominantly focus on hierarchical structures and overlook other types of associations. This paper introduces OntoPlot, an innovative visualisation system designed to seamlessly balance the exploration of all concept relationships and large hierarchical structures. OntoPlot's novel hybrid visualisation incorporates icicle plots, interactive elements, and space-efficient visual compression to enhance understanding and reduce visual clutter. Through a user study involving domain experts, we demonstrated that OntoPlot's novel visualisation significantly enhances association detection and exploration performance. Notably, it surpasses existing visualisation methods, allowing users to efficiently identify and navigate non-hierarchical associations within minutes, as opposed to potentially overwhelming ones with detailed information. The study also revealed that OntoPlot's visual distortions do not impede understanding, and users prefer working with distored rather than compressed views. Following the user study, we incorporated the learning methods presented into OntoPlot, enabling just a few seconds of interaction to produce high-quality visualisation with minimal distortion. The OntoPlot prototype is openly available for further development and contributes to the ongoing development of visualisation tools capable of handling complex associations. The research draws from extensive cognitive modelling studies on concept retrieval, skipping stages that do not affect understanding to rapidly identify relevant associations. We introduce an innovative technique that synergistically combines inter-domain loss and CycleGAN to facilitate semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition. Inter-domain loss aims to derive a common speech-text representation through a shared neural network, whereas CycleGAN aims to learn a common representation by transforming speech and text into a unified domain. However, current inter-domain loss methods only utilize speech-text pairs, which are readily available, but this approach is biased as it doesn't account for the common information shared by speech and text. To address this limitation, we propose leveraging the knowledge of a language model to introduce text-text pairs, thereby expanding the set of available data. Moreover, we propose refining the speech-text and text-text mapping function by minimizing cycle consistency loss. Experimental evaluations on the WSJ, Voxforge, and LibriSpeech datasets reveal a significant improvement in WER. Notably, our method achieves a WER of 12.96% on the LibriSpeech test_clean dataset using only 400 training speech-text pairs, surpassing the baseline WER of 13.83%. Additionally, we compare our approach with the state-of-the-art inter-domain loss method, yielding a notable improvement of over 4 points in WER. To further verify the efficacy of our technique, we performed a comprehensive ablation study that confirms the individual contributions of inter-domain loss and CycleGAN. Moreover, we highlight the benefits of our text-text pair generator as a standalone component, which can be applied to various applications such as speech synthesis and visual speech synthesis. Ultimately, the generated text-text pair is used in a combined loss function to enhance end-to-end automatic speech recognition. To facilitate future research, we release the code on GitHub. A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings and intelligent systems interact with their surroundings. This theory views the world through a lens of active prediction, relying on an intricate dynamic model that breaks down into latent variables, including agents, environments, senses, and sense data. Beliefs about these variables are updated by incorporating sense data, and agents make decisions by inferring the most likely course of action that would lead to expected sense data. Although the original method excels at handling intricate scenarios, its computational complexity has proven challenging to alleviate effectively via traditional approaches. This paper presents a novel approach that incorporates deep active inference, utilizing convolutional neural networks to expedite belief modeling and expectation estimation for sensor data. This approach was applied to a complex navigation task on a legged robot, comparing its performance to more conventional techniques. Results demonstrate that deep active inference delivers accurate predictions and robust decision-making while substantially reducing computational complexity. This ambitious project marks a significant breakthrough, marking the first time a pure theoretical model of mind has been successfully implemented on a physical system with a mind-free architecture. This achievement serves as a stepping stone for developing more sophisticated cognitive architectures. Experimental findings indicate that the approach surpasses baseline methods in terms of precision, with the added benefits of rapid inside-out transformations to lower computational complexity. This deep model's versatility can be leveraged in various applications, from robotics to neurology, with potential future extensions including model interpretability and integrating multi-modal perceptions. One potential innovation could be the incorporation of predictive information in control laws to bypass the estimation of expected sensor data, with the added potential of applying the principles of active inference to the prediction of useful sensor data directly. Another promising area of research could be the prediction of useful sensor data through the estimation of expected sensor data, with the added potential of applying the principles of active inference to the prediction of useful sensor data through the incorporation of novel sensory modules. Analysis of the approaches and their shortcomings may lead to a deeper understanding of the state-of-the-art implementation and the uncovering of unresolved issues to be addressed in future work. A significant challenge for future research could be the development of more sophisticated architectures that incorporate multiple inference processes such as the ones used for object detection, object tracking, or predictive modeling, with the added potential of leveraging multi-modal perceptions. Another promising area of research could be the development of architectures that efficiently use edge devices for real-time active inference, leveraging the principles of active inference to mitigate issues related to transmission bandwidth and significantly reducing the quantity of data to be transmitted. This study presents an innovative method for enhancing low-quality music recordings made on consumer-grade devices, which often include distortions like background noise, echo effects, and microphone distortion. A novel deep learning technique combines two processes: one transforms audio in a specific representation called the mel-spectrogram into a new, more desirable format, and another model generates high-quality audio from this new format using a specific type of deep learning architecture called U-net. Experimental results indicate that our approach surpasses established methods, with samples being made available online. While our technique exhibits exceptional results, it is crucial to acknowledge its limitations, primarily stemming from the need to utilize a separate vocoder to convert the enhanced mel-spectrogram into high-quality audio. Future research aims to integrate this vocoder directly into the method. Additionally, this work showcases a range of applications for the U-net architecture in music enhancement, a field that has yet to be extensively explored. Furthermore, enabling direct audio processing using more complex neural networks would be essential for achieving better results. A related Python project with most of the necessary code for music enhancement has been made available on the GitHub platform. Moreover, a demonstrationauxiliary Python project for generating a fully trained music enhancement model has been provided on the GitHub platform. Lastly, a detailed, informative document outlining the necessary steps for reproducing the study's results using the provided Python project has been included in the study's supplementary materials. Our primary objective is to comprehensively investigate the impact of a virtual ball's Point of Release on viewers' perception of a throwing motion. Our perceptual study revealed that individuals tend to more readily notice errors in underarm throws where the point of release occurs early, in contrast to late releases. Conversely, in the case of overarm throws, participants have a greater propensity to identify errors with a late point of release. Moreover, variations in the viewer's vantage point and the trajectory of the ball influence the overall perception of realism. These research findings can potentially contribute to the improvement of the authenticity of throwing animations in interactive applications such as virtual reality experiences or video games. Ultimately, this knowledge can aid developers in the creation of more immersive and engaging animations that simulate human movement. A novel animation generation method built upon these findings is known as FauxThrow. Our algorithm adjusts the throwing motion according to specific error parameters and generates a faux (false) throwing motion effect. Through user testing, it has been demonstrated that the rendition of throwing motions with errors, as generated by the FauxThrow algorithm, appear more realistic than unaltered animations. Interestingly, even though algorithmically inaccurate, the FauxThrow animations are perceived as more authentic than correct animations. These research findings and the FauxThrow algorithm have the potential to expand the possibilities of animation expression and interaction in the realm of simulations. Moreover, this knowledge can potentially be applied to the manipulation of animations by skilled practitioners of animation. Our research implies that artistically intentionally flawed or distorted animations, where the point of release appears unnatural, can potentially evoke a greater emotional response from viewers and serve as an innovative form of animation manipulation. A more in-depth exploration of these research findings and the FauxThrow algorithm can be found in a published paper in ACM Transactions on Graphics (TOG). The proposed Seq2DRNN architecture synergizes a sequential encoder with tree-structured decoding enhanced by a syntax-aware attention mechanism, connecting sentence structures. Compared to conventional parsers like Viterbi and inside-outside probability, the new Seq2DRNN architecture exhibits superior performance on the task of sentence structure prediction. Furthermore, experiments conducted on the English-Chinese NMT dataset reveal that Seq2DRNN compared to a benchmark cortical-based NMT model yields a 0.9 and 1.1 BLEU points improvement respectively, which serves as a promising Computationally-Efficient NMT Architecture. The corresponding code for Seq2DRNN has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ziyunHZ/Seq2DRNN. The model has also demonstrated its capability to handle out-of-vocabulary words by incorporating word embeddings into neural machine translation systems as detailed in the accompanying main paper publication. In addition, a new evaluation metric has been suggested to assess the capabilities of syntax-based decoding systems to produce correct sentence structures. Specifically, this new metric called Syntactic Normalization has been calculated from the inside-outside probability of the Viterbi parse with a log-linear model, where the coefficients used are those optimized for the NMT task. The inside-outside probability measures the likelihood of observing a given sentence structure, while the coefficient vector provides weights of importance for incorporating various sentence structures in the translation process, as further explained in the paper. The integrity of astrochemical predictions relies heavily on the accuracy and consistency of experimental techniques, especially in determining the binding energy of molecules.  Experimental binding energies are often derived from a limited range of data points obtained through absorption spectroscopy, whereas a more comprehensive understanding can be gained through high-dimensional quantum simulations. This service allows users to input molecules and generate three-dimensional solvation configurations with corresponding binding energy profiles, hosting over 500,000 mbeds for various astrophysical molecules. A multiplicative stochastic process with lognormally distributed lower bounds is studied, where a theoretical model of the process is developed and its distribution, characterized by four parameters, along with its statistical properties, is analytically determined. This model is further validated by demonstrating its compatibility with real-world data through parameter adjustment. Additionally, models for the distribution of individual measurements and extremes are developed, yielding models comparable to the Probit model and a generalized version of the Benoit Court Model, respectively. Applications of the model are explored in the fields of medicine and economics. The medical application involves modeling the distribution of white blood cell counts in patients with chronic myeloid leukemia treated with Pegasvastin, while the economic application entails analyzing the impact of COVID-19 on air traffic in selected European countries and assessing the effects of the Russian-Ukrainian conflict on Estonian air traffic. In both instances, the proposed model exhibits satisfactory performance in modeling the data with its statistical properties such as autocorrelation, trend, and extreme events. Furthermore, the models possess easily interpretable parameters. The developed models propose that the Russian-Ukrainian conflict and COVID-19 are detrimental to Estonian air traffic. Conversely, the models suggest that the Russian-Ukrainian conflict is beneficial to Finnish air traffic. Several scenarios, including modeling the distribution of prices and experts' assessments with the lognormal distribution, are also examined. The study contributes theoretically to the understanding of multiplicative stochastic processes with lower bounds and enhances the availability of user-friendly statistical tools for such processes. Moreover, the results can be utilized in various fields including medicine, economics, and others with minor adjustments in parameters. The provided R code can be directly applied to model and analyze time series with multiplicative stochastic properties and lower bounds. The study's findings are independently validated by means of the ocular hyperemia dataset. A novel method for detecting trends in multiplicative stochastic processes is presented, which is sensitive to changing conditions and can identify shifts in trends. The method is demonstrated by analyzing the dataset from ocular hyperemia and shows that TMT values decrease over the initial 40 minutes before increasing until the end of the experiment. If trend-detecting mechanisms had been used, this increase in TMT values could have indicated that the experiment was unfinished. The study's findings are verified via visual inspections of the data and the calculated autocorrelation function values. The study's results are expanded by showing that the multiplicative stochastic process with lower bounds is an adequate model for the TMT dataset. The study's contributions

In the field of legged locomotion, spring-based actuators can boost energy efficiency and performance but complicate the controller's design. We diverge from conventional methods of developing optimal controllers through in-depth modeling and simulation, instead directly teaching model-free controllers to the actual robot. Initially, gaits are generated through central pattern generators, whose parameters are fine-tuned to rapidly develop an open-loop controller for efficient walking. Following this, we implement reinforcement learning to enhance the controller's resilience and efficacy by introducing corrective control. We thoroughly tested our findings on the elastic quadruped ARCN'3 over numerous real-world runs. Our results not only recovered actuator performance metrics matching simulated models but also revealed intriguing behaviors arising from complex system dynamics, such as gait-tracking on uneven terrain without prior knowledge of the surface. By adopting this approach, developer interaction lengths are significantly reduced, and developmental costs are largely spared, making it easier to adapt this strategy to a wide range of robotic systems. Key Findings:
1. Fast, open-loop learning enables an efficient walking gait on the ARCN'3 over various terrain types, such as carpet, hardwood, carpet ramp, and outdoor terrain.
2. Performance of the learned controller was validated against an extensively detailed model. Moreover, this controller's energy efficiency was comparable to that of an expert-human generated gait.
3. Research on real-world runs of 3 hours long (2.5 kilometers at 2 km/h) showed that the controller's behavior was consistent with expected dynamic model predictions, even on unknown terrain types like sand and snow.
4. Behavioral analysis uncovered a number of previously unanticipated dynamic behaviors: side stepping on slippery surfaces, climbing snowy banks, and navigating on icy surfaces. These behaviors indicate that the complex dynamics of the system can be leveraged for advantage in the right conditions.
5. This work provides critical groundwork for developing "autolearning" control strategies that could optimize performance in the field, free from the need for detailed modeling. 

Future Work
1. The next step will be to test model-free learning in the absence of detailed dynamic models, starting with simpler systems.
2. Developing a "autolearning" strategy that could optimize performance in real-time, without the need for detailed modeling, is another area for future investigation.

Alternative theories of gravity that go beyond the Riemannian framework have been proposed to explore quantum gravity and model systems with non-relativistic symmetry. However, developing these theories involves a complex task: deriving an action principle that accurately captures their behavior. This technical note utilizes the formulation of double field theory to create action frameworks for these alternative gravity theories. By doing so, it resolves the ambiguities associated with their corresponding motion equations. As a result, this note embeds three theories – Torsional Newton-Cartan gravity, Carrollian gravity, and String Newton-Cartan gravity – within double field theory and derives their respective action frameworks for comparison with previously established literature results. The successful embedding also simplifies the formulation of these alternative gravity theories. Furthermore, this method may offer insights for other theories of gravity that exhibit non-Riemannian behavior. Additionally, this note details the version of double field theory called New-Model-Construction, and includes a review of the characteristic features of this construction. Moreover, this note provides a concise overview of the geometry behind Newton-Cartan geometry and T-foliation geometry. Additionally, several relevant references are provided for further exploration. Overall, this paper provides technical support for researchers working with alternative gravity theories and double field theory. To meet growing demands for next-generation home WiFi networks, it is essential to improve their performance capabilities. The increasing presence of high-bandwidth applications such as online gaming, virtual reality, and high-quality video streaming requires networks with enhanced throughput. One effective strategy for achieving this is to deploy a high-density of access points within the home. However, this approach also leads to a more complex network that is harder to manage. To resolve this issue, we propose a solution that leverages the capabilities of IEEE 802.11k/v standards to enable the automation of access point selection. Our proposal suggests using the "Channel Load Map" information provided by the network's connection base stations to determine which access point should serve which device. By only deploying additional base stations in areas with high network loads, we can minimize the overall cost of the network. In addition, our mechanism for "Extender load detection" allows us to accurately assess the performance capabilities of each device. Our evaluation demonstrates that our proposal outperforms conventional techniques in terms of overall network throughput. Notably, our analysis confirms that our proposal can effectively reduce the amount of channel interference within the network, thus resulting in better throughput performance compared to conventional methods. The results of our research also indicate that the traffic load within home networks often exhibits an irregular, dynamic pattern, which necessitates an adaptive network solution. Ultimately, our thesis's conceptual framework and our simulation-based evaluation demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of using the proposed "Channel Load Aware AP/Extender Selection" method. This method can be implemented using the IEEE 802.11k/v standards and can enhance the throughput performance of the network by up to 25% compared to conventional techniques. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the traffic load within the network often changes dynamically, which in turn demonstrates the importance of implementing an adaptive network solution.
